01.1Chapter 1 · Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

Model kya hota hai: Architecture, Data, Code

Model serving samajhne se pehle ek sawaal ka jawab clear hona chahiye — model hota kya hai? Academic definition me model ek mathematical representation ya algorithm hai jo data se patterns seekh kar predictions, decisions ya inference karta hai, bina us kaam ke liye explicitly program kiye gaye. Lekin engineering aur operations ki nazar se model ko dekhne ka tareeka alag hai: hum zyada tar model ko black box ki tarah treat karte hain — training se nikli hui executable files ka ek collection.

Model ke teen hisse

Serving ki duniya me model teen tarah ki files se banta hai — data, architecture, aur execution code:

  • Model data: isme model ke weights, bias aur configuration aate hain. Weights aur bias wahi hain jo model training ke dauraan seekhta hai. Configuration me woh metadata hoti hai jo model chalane ke liye chahiye — jaise embeddings aur label classes (classification models ke liye), max_batch_size property (batch inference ke liye), aur input/output tensors ki details.
  • Model architecture: ye model ki structure aur design hai — kis tarah ki aur kitni layers hain, layers ke beech connections kaise hain, aur model kaunse operations karta hai. Architecture tay karta hai ki model input data ko process karke output prediction ya decision tak kaise pahunchta hai.
  • Model execution code: ye woh code hai jo model ko chalata hai — architecture ko serving framework me initialize karna, weights load karna, aur predictions (ya doosre outputs) run karna.
Yaad rakho: model ko sirf passive data file mat samjho. Model ek executable program hai — isme execution logic, metadata aur woh sab kuch hota hai jo use chalane ke liye chahiye. Model static artifact nahi hai; ye inputs process kar sakta hai, decisions le sakta hai, aur time ke saath evolve kar sakta hai.

Ek practical example: PyTorch me model save/load

Ye structure ek mashhoor PyTorch tutorial ke example se samjho. Pehle architecture ek Python file me define hoti hai — ek class jisme convolutional layers (conv1, conv2), pooling layer, aur fully connected layers (fc1, fc2, fc3) hain, aur ek forward method batata hai ki data layers se kaise guzarta hai. Ye code aam taur par training code wali architecture class ki copy hoti hai.

Dusra, training ke baad weights aur biases ek file me save hote hain, jaise model_weights.pt. PyTorch me learnable parameters state_dict me store hote hain, aur torch.save(model.state_dict(), "model_weights.pt") se save kiye jaate hain.

Teesra, execution code model ko initialize karta hai, weights load karta hai, model ko evaluation mode (model.eval()) me daalta hai, aur phir input par prediction chalata hai (pred = model(inputs)). TensorFlow aur PyTorch jaise alag frameworks ke APIs alag hote hain, lekin model packaging aur structure ke fundamental principles lagbhag ek jaise rehte hain.

Architecture aur data ko alag files me rakho

Poora model ek hi file me save karna possible hai, lekin book ki recommendation hai ki architecture (class definition) aur weights ko alag files me rakho — isse zyada flexibility milti hai. Example ke liye, jab model architecture versions ke beech thoda sa badal jaata hai, to checkpoint ke kuch parameters nayi structure se match nahi karte — inhe nonmatching keys kehte hain. Aise cases me PyTorch partial loading allow karta hai: compatible parameters load ho jaate hain aur incompatible skip ho jaate hain. Ye fine-tuning, model me extra layers jodne, ya bina scratch se retrain kiye incremental architecture updates roll out karne me bahut kaam aata hai.

Aakhir me, practice me model files par aksar additional optimizations bhi lagayi jaati hain taaki serving performance behtar ho — khaas taur par LLMs ke liye. Ye optimizations book ke aage wale chapters me detail me aayengi.

SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

01.2Chapter 1 · Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

Model Lifecycle: Training se Serving tak

Serving me ghusne se pehle zoom out karke dekho — serving poori ML lifecycle me kahan baithta hai? AI par zyada tar discussion training par hoti hai — data collect karna, architecture design karna, accuracy badhana. Lekin real-world systems me training sirf journey ka ek hissa hai. Model ki value tabhi realize hoti hai jab use deploy kiya jaaye, reliably serve kiya jaaye, aur scale par efficiently operate kiya jaaye.

Lifecycle ke chhe stages

  • Data collection: raw data user interactions, sensors, logs, documents ya third-party providers se ikattha hota hai. Phir use clean, label aur curate karke training aur evaluation datasets banaye jaate hain.
  • Training aur fine-tuning: models data se patterns seekhte hain. Aaj ke systems me isme aksar bade foundation models ki pretraining aur phir domain-specific data par fine-tuning hoti hai, taaki application ki requirements poori hon.
  • Evaluation: trained models ko offline metrics — accuracy, loss, ya task-specific benchmarks — par validate kiya jaata hai. Is stage se tay hota hai ki model production ke liye ready hai ya nahi.
  • Deployment: trained model ko package karke production environment me release kiya jaata hai. Is point par model ek software artifact ban jaata hai jise version karna, test karna aur existing systems se integrate karna padta hai.
  • Serving (is book ka focus): deployed model applications, users ya doosre systems ke liye accessible banaya jaata hai — aam taur par APIs ya services ke through — taaki woh naye, unseen data par real time ya scale par predictions (inference) generate kar sake.
  • Optimization aur iteration: jab model live traffic serve karne lagta hai, to teams continuously serving performance, reliability aur cost optimize karti hain. Training side par, production usage se mila feedback aksar aur fine-tuning, retraining ya architecture changes ki taraf le jaata hai — aur lifecycle phir se shuru ho jaata hai.
Yaad rakho: model train karna aur use production me chalana ek hi kaam nahi hai. Jaise hi model real users ko serve karne lagta hai, constraints, goals aur engineering challenges poori tarah badal jaate hain. Training me jo cheez matter karti thi, production me uski jagah latency, reliability, cost aur scale le lete hain.

Ye lifecycle deep learning aur LLMs ke aane se bahut tezi se accelerate hua hai — data collection aur training se lekar deployment, monitoring aur continuous iteration tak, poora flow ab pehle se zyada tez aur zyada complex hai. Aur isi liye serving ko lifecycle ka ek side-task samajhna galat hai: trained model ki business value tabhi banti hai jab woh users tak sahi latency, reliability aur cost ke saath pahunche.

SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

01.3Chapter 1 · Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

Model Serving kya hai?

Engineering terminology me model serving ka matlab hai ML model ko production environment me deploy karna, jahan woh naya data process karke predictions generate kar sake. Isme zaroori software aur hardware infrastructure set up karna padta hai taaki model input le sake, inference execute kar sake, aur results efficiently, scalably aur reliably wapas de sake. Book me model serving, model inference aur prediction terms interchangeably use hote hain.

Teen serving scenarios — teen examples

Model serving local (on-device), in-cluster (on-premises), ya remote (on-cloud) — kahin bhi ho sakta hai, business requirements aur infrastructure constraints par depend karta hai:

  • Warehouse robot (on-device): ek real-time object detection model (jaise YOLO) robot ke onboard computer par deploy hota hai — maan lo ek chhota board jisme AI accelerator chip lagi ho. Robot visual input ko turant process karke autonomous decisions le sakta hai, bina cloud ka wait kiye.
  • Document search (on-premises): company ke internal data par semantic search index banane ke liye ek language model (jaise sentence embeddings wala model) company ke apne computing cluster ke andar serve hota hai. Isse documents ke dense vector embeddings bante hain, aur data security aur compliance bhi bani rehti hai kyunki bada data bahar transfer nahi hota.
  • Customer support chatbot (on-cloud): jab customer query bhejta hai, to chatbot use — relevant documents ke saath — ek remote LLM ko bhejta hai jo kisi vendor ke hosted ya managed service par chal raha ho, jaise ek bade cloud provider ka managed inference endpoint.

Serving engineers kis par focus karte hain?

Model serving context me ML aur DevOps engineers model ke internal details — architecture, training methods, file formats — par kam focus karte hain aur model ko black box ki tarah treat karte hain. Iski wajah ye hai ki aaj ke model serving frameworks model execution ki complexity ko handle karke high-level abstraction de dete hain, jisse predictions chalana simple aur efficient ho jaata hai. (LLMs iska exception hain — unke liye architecture samajhna zaroori hai, ye aage aayega.)

Serving me focus in cheezon par hota hai:

  • Deployment: sahi hardware chunna aur model ko training pipeline (ya open source options) se available karwana taaki woh input consume karke predictions de sake.
  • Scalability aur availability: kuch hazaar se lekar millions requests efficiently handle karna, jabki customer experience consistent rahe.
  • Latency: predictions jaldi dena — real-time use cases me milliseconds me.
  • Monitoring: model performance, data drift aur system health ko track karna.
  • Versioning: model updates aur rollbacks manage karna bina clients ko disrupt kiye.
  • Security: sensitive data protect karna aur model tak access control karna.
  • Cost-to-serve: sabse decisive factor. Alag-alag serving approaches aur trade-offs evaluate karne ke liye cost-to-serve ko key factor mana jaata hai.
Yaad rakho: practice me serving engineers zyada tar deep learning models ko deployed software artifacts ki tarah treat karte hain aur focus karte hain ki inference workloads ko kaise package, deploy, scale, monitor aur optimize kiya jaaye — taaki models business SLAs (service-level agreements) meet karte hue applications aur end users ko value dein. Ye kaam naye learning algorithms invent karne se zyada systems engineering, infrastructure design aur hardware-software stack par end-to-end performance optimization ka hai.

LLM serving ke liye LLM ki samajh zaroori hai

Effective LLM serving aur optimization ke liye AI algorithms — khaas taur par Transformer — ki solid samajh essential hai. LLM serving techniques ki saari advancements LLM execution ke bottlenecks ko overcome karne ke liye design ki gayi hain. Isliye LLM architecture ki strong grasp se woh intuition milti hai jo throughput aur latency optimize karne ke liye chahiye. Aane wale chapters is foundational knowledge ko detail me cover karenge.

SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

01.4Chapter 1 · Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

Serving kyun padhein? Optimize kyun karein?

Model serving critical hai — is par sab agree karte hain. Lekin log aksar poochte hain: apna serving system banana ya customize karna seekhna kyun zaroori hai? Is section me book teen aise sawaalon ke jawab deti hai jo real experience se aaye hain.

Sawaal 1: Cloud vendors se hi models consume karte hain — apna system kyun banayein?

Cloud vendor platforms par models deploy aur host karna bahut si situations me achha option hai. Cloud services hardware management aur software patching jaise kaam sambhal leti hain aur quick proof of concept (POC) enable karti hain. Lekin inhe bina soche-samjhe consume nahi kar sakte. Pehle, products aur features itne zyada hain ki best fit chunna mushkil hota hai. Dusra, vendor services ko existing infrastructure aur client applications se integrate karne me extra engineering lagti hai. Teesra, vendor services ko apne business use case aur performance requirements ke hisaab se optimize aur fine-tune karna padta hai.

Cloud vendors apne solutions ko alag-alag customers ki needs ke hisaab se general-purpose offerings ki tarah package karte hain. Example: ek bade cloud provider ka managed ML service single-model aur multi-model endpoints jaise multiple serving options deta hai, aur har option ke alag customization levels, trade-offs aur costs hote hain. Model serving design, challenges aur use cases ki clear samajh ke bina suboptimal choices karna aasan hai — jo cost badha sakti hain ya flexibility limit kar sakti hain. Short me: serving system kaise banta aur operate hota hai, ye samajhna hi aapko cloud vendors ke options ka best use karne me madad karta hai.

Sawaal 2: Foundation LLMs hi kaafi powerful hain — apna stack kyun maintain karein?

LLMs AI field ki sabse badi inventions me se ek hain, lekin business me apply karte waqt bahut nuance hai. Pehle, cost: businesses kabhi ek hi LLM se saare use cases solve nahi karte. Real world me businesses jitna ho sake chhote aur saste models use karna prefer karte hain aur LLMs ko complicated requests ke liye rakhte hain. Jab usage badhta hai, to lower-cost LLM serving adopt karna chahte hain — example ke liye, ek open source LLM ko cloud virtual server (EC2 instance) par chalana managed serving solution ke mukable 30% se 60% sasta ho sakta hai, aur reserved instance par 70% tak discount bhi mil sakta hai.

Ek typical chatbot app ek chhote intent-classification model se customer questions triage karti hai, ek embedding model se questions encode karke answers search karti hai, aur ek LLM se request ko actions (backend API calls) me todkar human-friendly interaction generate karti hai. Dusra aspect data privacy aur security hai: sensitive ya proprietary data handle karne wali company ko data breach ya compliance issues se bachne ke liye in-house solution chahiye ho sakta hai. Teesra, zyada tar foundation-model vendors aapka fine-tuned model serve karne ki functionality dete hi nahi, ya bahut zyada price charge karte hain — book likhte waqt ek bade vendor fine-tuned model serve karne par 50% zyada charge karta tha. Isi beech chhote models zyada powerful ho rahe hain aur custom data par fine-tuning, faster inference, behtar aur consistent results aur lower cost-to-serve de rahe hain. Apna serving solution (on-cloud ya on-premises) open source LLM ke saath business ko lower cost par critical edge deta hai.

Sawaal 3: Apna stack banana aur maintain karna mehenga hai — worth it kab hota hai?

Serving costs kam karna ek everlasting effort hai. Jaise industry develop hoti hai, koi guarantee nahi de sakta ki serving ko outsource karna hamesha business goals meet karega. Do scenarios samjho. Pehla: education sector ka ek Series A startup, jiski app LLMs se students ka homework grade karti hai aur personalized study plans banati hai. Shuruaat me fully managed LLM provider ke saath kaam karna development accelerate karne aur business model validate karne ke liye great hai. Lekin jaise usage scale hota hai, serving costs unsustainable hone lagte hain. Tab customized serving solution — open source LLMs, optimized serving frameworks, inference performance fine-tuning — costs significantly kam kar sakta hai jabki user experience achha bana rehta hai.

Dusra: ek CRM company jo LLMs se sales recommendations deti hai — text inputs (emails, messages, customer notes), unstructured audio (voice calls, meeting transcriptions) aur structured CRM databases (past sales records, customer interactions) ko process karke. High volume LLM inference requests aur sensitive customer data ke saath, fully outsourcing se data-security risks aur operational costs badh sakte hain. In-house stack own karna aur optimize karna cost per inference kam karne, security regulations (jaise GDPR aur HIPAA) comply karne aur behtar performance aur latency control ke liye zaroori ho jaata hai. Lekin in-house stack ke liye specialized hardware me significant upfront capital investment aur engineers me ongoing investment chahiye. Isliye build vs outsource ka decision sirf security aur privacy par nahi, project ki maturity, expected scale aur organization ki operational complexity sustain karne ki ability par bhi depend karta hai. Experience ye kehta hai: outsourced solutions great starting point hote hain, lekin businesses ko continuously assess karna chahiye ki in-house serving long-term competitive advantage deta hai ya nahi — cost savings, security aur flexibility ke terms me.

Yaad rakho: model serving ka koi one-size-fits-all ya "eternal" architecture nahi hota. Model algorithms aur serving technologies evolve karti rehti hain, aur businesses ko pace rakhna padta hai. Fundamentals ki solid samajh hi aapko naye innovations ko samajhne, unke pros aur cons assess karne aur sahi technical choices karne ke layak banati hai — bina kisi specific framework ya vendor me lock hue.

Optimize kyun karein — khaas taur par LLMs ke liye?

Jab model successfully deploy ho jaata hai, to functional standpoint se woh "done" lagta hai — sahi outputs deta hai, requests ka jawab deta hai. Lekin LLMs ke liye naively deployed serving system practice me jaldi fail ho jaata hai: load ke neeche latency badhti hai, throughput hardware capacity se bahut neeche plateau kar jaata hai, aur serving costs usage ke saath linearly — ya usse bhi zyada — scale hote hain. Demo ya pilot me chalne wala setup real users aate hi economically ya operationally infeasible ho jaata hai.

Model serving optimization ka matlab hai serving performance improve karna — serving latency kam karna, throughput (per unit time me process hone wale predictions ki sankhya) badhana, aur resource utilization optimize karna — taaki serving efficiency maximize ho jabki costs control me rahein. LLMs itne bade aur complex hain ki unhe significant computing power chahiye, jo operational costs ko chhote businesses ke liye unaffordable bana sakti hai. Ek estimate ke mutabik, ek LLM request chalana traditional keyword search se 10 guna zyada mehenga ho sakta hai — potentially billions me additional costs. Isliye LLMs ke liye optimization lagbhag must hai: ye costs kam karta hai, faster response se user experience enhance karta hai, aur slow ya expensive inference solutions wali companies par competitive edge deta hai.

Training framework vs serving framework — aur vLLM ka example

Ek common sawaal hai: training wala setup hi serving ke liye kyun na use karein? Dono me model load karke architecture execute karni hoti hai — lekin goals aur requirements poori tarah alag hain. Training ka objective loss function minimize karke parameters (weights) seekhna hai — extremely compute-intensive, backpropagation aur gradient updates ke saath, bade data batches parallel process karke high throughput prefer karta hai. Example: ek bahut bada model 16,384 high-end GPUs par train hua tha. Serving ka objective naye input par efficiently prediction (inference) generate karna hai — sirf forward propagation, koi backpropagation ya model updates nahi, per-request low latency par optimized, aksar single ya chhote batches par, CPUs, edge devices ya inference-specific GPUs par.

Isi liye serving-specific frameworks use hote hain, jaise vLLM — ek optimized LLM serving engine jo high-throughput, low-latency inference ke liye design hua hai. Ek example command me ek 20-billion-parameter model ko ek 80 GB GPU par chalaya gaya: precision bf16, GPU memory utilization 0.9, max concurrent requests 16, max batched tokens 16384, aur model do GPUs par share (tensor-parallel-size 2). vLLM team ke 2023 ke experiments me PagedAttention ke saath throughput Hugging Face Transformers se 24 guna tak zyada aur ek doosre generation framework (TGI) se 3.5 guna tak zyada mili — ek chart me 8.5x–15x aur 3.3x–3.5x ke gains dikhaye gaye. Ek aur experiment me ek bade reasoning model ko vLLM par host karte hue sirf do configuration changes se — FP8 kernels enable karke aur batch size badhakar — throughput 38 tokens per second se 600 tokens per second tak pahunch gayi, lagbhag 15x ka jump. Har configuration option ek potential optimization technique hai, aur sahi configurations performance me bahut bada farq la sakti hain. Production LLM systems ke liye optimization must-have hai — ye sirf extra performance squeeze karne ke baare me nahi, business SLAs meet karne ke baare me hai, sustainable cost par.

SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

01.5Chapter 1 · Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization

Serving Paradigms: Edge, Single, Multi, Platforms

Is section me model serving ke sabse common paradigms explore karte hain — on-device (edge) se shuru karke single-model, phir multi-model, aur aakhir me full serving platforms tak. Har design pichle concept par build hota hai, aur har ek ke apne trade-offs hain. Practical design principles aur hands-on examples aane wale chapters me aayenge.

On-device (edge) serving

On-device serving ka matlab hai model ko user-side devices par hi chalana — smartphones, drones, robots, cameras, VR headsets — remote web services par depend kiye bina. Data wahin process hota hai jahan generate hota hai, isliye constant internet connectivity ki zaroorat nahi aur real-time computation possible hota hai. Iske chaar key benefits hain: cost-effective (local inference se cloud API fees bachte hain, jaise smart speaker local voice recognition karke), efficient (on-device compute se response fast aur power-efficient hota hai, jaise mobile photo-enhancement apps real-time results deti hain), private (data device se bahar hi nahi jaata — health-tracking app personal biometric data locally analyze kar sakti hai), aur personalized (models user-specific data se device par hi continuously update aur fine-tune ho sakte hain, jaise keyboard app aapki typing style seekh kar suggestions improve kare bina keystrokes upload kiye).

On-device AI app ke do key components hain: model runtime aur model wrapper. Model runtime ek specialized software framework hai jo ML models ko alag-alag hardware platforms par efficiently execute karta hai — trained model aur device hardware ke beech intermediary layer. Ye alag-alag hardware (smartphones, drones, robots) aur operating systems (iOS, Android, Linux) par execution ki complexity abstract karta hai aur hardware-specific optimizations deta hai. Zyada tar runtimes delegates support karte hain — ek software component jo compute-intensive operations ko CPU se specialized hardware jaise GPU par offload karta hai. Popular runtimes me LiteRT, ONNX Runtime aur Core ML aate hain. Model wrapper application developers ka banaya hua component hai jo model inference interfaces deta hai — input preprocessing, model ko runtime me load karna, execution, aur output postprocessing — taaki application logic ko low-level details se deal na karna pade.

Model ko on-device ke liye ready karne ka workflow: pehle trained model ko training format se runtime ke required format me convert (compile) karo (jaise ek ResNet PyTorch model ko LiteRT ke .tflite format me). Phir numerical accuracy validate karo target device par — wahi inputs training server aur local device dono par chala kar outputs compare karo, taaki conversion aur optimization se accuracy degrade na hui ho. Phir performance measure karo ki local hardware business requirements meet karte hue model efficiently execute kar sake. Aakhir me optimized model ko application installation ya update ke part ke roop me package karke customers ko release karo. Ye process tedious lag sakta hai, lekin kuch tools compilation, optimization aur validation ke key steps automate kar dete hain.

On-device kab sahi hai? Privacy-first workloads (biometric authentication, personal health data), ultra-low-latency applications (gesture recognition, robotics control loops, AR/VR, real-time audio — network latency se bachna), disconnected ya intermittent environments (industrial equipment, remote sensors, vehicles, drones), aur IoT, smart cities aur robotics (power efficiency aur task specificity). Lekin constraints bhi hain: computation aur storage constraints (limited CPU/GPU/memory — bade models nahi chal sakte; edge ke liye chhote models jaise 270-million-parameter wale models bane hain, lekin ye har model ke liye feasible nahi), power consumption (deep neural networks battery jaldi drain karte hain — real-time video enhancement local nahi chalate), limited update aur maintenance (har device ko update install karna padta hai — banking app ko fraud-detection model improve karne ke liye frequent app updates release karne padte), aur inconsistent hardware support (kuch devices me NPU, kuch me sirf CPU — ek phone ke neural engine ke liye optimized model doosre phone ke processor par efficiently nahi chal sakta).

Single-model service

Ye classic aur sabse widely used cloud-based pattern hai: har model aur uske har version ko ek dedicated web service ki tarah deploy kiya jaata hai, jo HTTP ya gRPC par prediction API expose karta hai. Architecture standard microservices design follow karta hai — saamne ek API component web prediction requests receive karke backend workers ya containers me se kisi ek ko route karta hai, aur backend workers actual model execution karke result wapas dete hain.

Modern serving ki foundation containerization hai — application ko uski saari dependencies, libraries aur configurations ke saath ek isolated environment (container) me package karna, taaki woh developer ke laptop, test server ya production — har jagah consistently chale. Zyada tar server-side model execution container ke andar hota hai: model management, resource management aur model execution logic ko ek Docker container (ya Kubernetes Pod) me encapsulate karke model ki prediction/serving function ko gRPC ya HTTP interface se expose kiya jaata hai.

Serving container ke andar teen main components hote hain: API-Server (HTTP/gRPC par inference functionality expose karta hai), Model Management (model download karna, local storage me extract karna, inference backend me load karna — initialization steps), aur Inference Backend (actual model execution — serving frameworks ya libraries use karke). Deployment me training pipeline ya Ops team trained model ko cloud storage par upload karti hai; Model Management component naya model detect karke har serving container me model automatically refresh kar deta hai.

Routing: API component ka kaam hai saare containers ko prediction workloads se equally saturate karna. Simple round-robin load balancing (pehli request container 1 ko, dusri container 2 ko, teesri container 3 ko, phir repeat) me ek key limitation hai — ye request processing times ke variation ko account nahi karta. Ek LLM request 5,000 tokens ke payload ke saath 100-token input se zyada time leti hai; high-resolution images wali request chhoti images se zyada resources khati hai. Isse container 1 abhi bhi badi request process kar raha hota hai, container 2 free ho chuka hota hai, lekin agli request phir bhi container 1 ko route ho jaati hai — bottleneck ban jaata hai. Isliye sophisticated routing strategies use hoti hain: weighted round robin (bade servers ko zyada weight, zyada requests), least connections (sabse kam active connections wale server ko), least response time (sabse kam response time wale server ko), aur dynamic load balancing (CPU, GPU, memory usage ya queue length jaise metrics se distribute karna).

Scaling: traffic badhne par serving containers ke zyada instances multiple machines par deploy karte hain — ye horizontal scaling (scaling out) hai. Production me autoscaling enable karte hain: infrastructure management system CPU/memory usage, inference latency aur active requests jaise metrics monitor karta hai, aur thresholds exceed hone par additional instances dynamically spin up karta hai. Kubernetes me Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) real-time demand ke hisaab se serving pods ki sankhya adjust kar sakta hai. Bade deep learning models ke liye, jinhe ek machine ki GPU memory me load karna possible nahi, vertical scaling (scaling up) use hota hai — zyada powerful GPUs aur multiple GPUs ya machines par distributed serving. Frameworks distributed serving ko abstract kar dete hain — ek command me tensor-parallel-size 4 dekar model 4 GPUs par serve ho sakta hai. Behtar performance, easier management aur lower latency ke liye intra-node serving (ek machine par multiple GPUs) ko inter-node serving (multiple machines) par prefer karo — inter-node me network overhead latency aur synchronization complexity badhata hai.

Single-model service default starting point kyun hai? Best performance (koi resource contention nahi, lower latency), easy scaling (har model independently scale hota hai), simple deployment aur debugging (isolated logs, metrics, updates), reliability (ek model crash ho to doosre affect nahi hote), aur optimized hardware per model se behtar cost control. Lekin kami hai resource efficiency aur cost me: imagine ek agent platform jahan 100 customers har ek 10 models deploy karte hain — 1,000 separate model services! Itni services maintain, patch, deploy aur monitor karna overwhelming hai, aur kai models kabhi use hi nahi hote — compute waste hota hai. Isi liye multi-model service aata hai.

Multi-model service

Multi-model service multiple models ko ek serving container me co-host karta hai — GPU/CPU aur memory share karke — aur incoming traffic ke hisaab se models ko dynamically load aur unload karta hai. Isse significant cost savings aur best price-performance milti hai. Agent-platform example me 1,000 models ko ek saath GPU aur memory me load karne ke bajaye on-demand approach adopt karte hain: model tabhi load karo jab customer prediction request kare, aur inactive hone par ya naye model ke liye memory free karne ke liye unload kar do.

Multi-model container single-model container se do components me alag hai: model server inference backend aur model cache management. Model server inference backend multiple types ke models ko black-box manner me handle karta hai — model ke algorithm aur version se farq nahi padta, unified web prediction API se serve karta hai. Trick ye hai ki model server ke andar multiple inference backends hote hain, har backend ek type ka model handle karta hai — jaise TensorFlow, ONNX ya PyTorch. Ye khud se build karne ki zaroorat nahi: robust open source solutions hain, jaise NVIDIA Triton Inference Server — jo TensorRT, TensorFlow GraphDef, TensorFlow SavedModel, ONNX, PyTorch, Caffe2 NetDef aur aur formats par unified API deta hai. Model cache management ke do responsibilities hain: model ko model storage se model server inference backend me load karna, aur least recently used (LRU) cache maintain karke least-used models unload karna jab container resource utilization high ho.

On-demand workflow: prediction request aane par, agar model loaded hai to request backend ko forward hoti hai; agar nahi hai to management component model download karke load karta hai aur phir request forward karta hai; agar memory aur disk consumption specified threshold (jaise 80% memory usage) se upar hai to least-used model unload karke cache aur disk se remove kar diya jaata hai.

Routing aur autoscaling ki challenges: pehli problem — request routing: models kisi bhi container me host ho sakte hain, to request us container ko route karni chahiye jisme model pehle se loaded ho, warna cold start (request wait kare jab tak model load ho) ya model swapping (purane models memory se nikaal kar naya load karna) se extra latency aati hai. Dusri problem — per-model scaling: sab models ko barabar traffic nahi milta; "hot" models ke liye zyada instances chahiye. Solution: frontend API layer me routing component enhance karo — model ke metadata me replica attribute jodo (kitne instances host honge) aur ek route map introduce karo jo track kare ki model prediction request kis container ko jaani chahiye. Example: Model A ki replica count 2 hai to routing logic containers C1 aur C3 ko host chunegi aur saari Model A requests un dono ko evenly route karegi. Router replica count ko real time me traffic ke hisaab se up-down bhi adjust kar sakta hai, aur naye replicas add karte waqt sahi container chunna bin packing problem jaisa hai.

Multi-model service kab zaroori hota hai aur kab struggle karta hai? Ye sabse cost-efficient method hai kyunki shared resource pool se zyada models host kar sakte hain bina sab ko ek saath host kiye. Lekin struggle karta hai jab: models itne bade hon ki ek GPU me fit na hon (bahut model unloading aur cold-start latency), individual models ko high traffic aur low latency chahiye aur model hamesha loaded rehna chahiye (tab single-model behtar hai), models ki security policies alag hon, ya operational complexity high ho (deployment, debugging, monitoring complicated — model cache management, per-model routing aur scaling, model compatibility, dependency conflicts). Single-model aur multi-model complementary hain — practice me platforms dono ko combine karte hain.

Model serving platforms

Jaise business badhta hai, serving demand surge hoti hai aur requirements complex ho jaati hain. Single-model aur multi-model services ko sirf saath rakhna kaafi nahi rehta. Do badi challenges aati hain: pehli, kai tasks ke liye multiple models ko saath kaam karna padta hai — jaise ek voice assistant ko ek voice command ka jawab dene ke liye speech recognition, NLP, recommendation models aur text-to-speech synthesis integrate karne padte hain. Dusri, kai AI applications ek platform par chal rahi hon to GPUs, CPUs aur memory ko models ke beech efficiently allocate karna critical ho jaata hai, jabki scalability aur cost-effectiveness bani rahe aur resource contention minimum ho.

Model serving platform design in challenges ko do tareekon se address karta hai. Pehle, resource groups se alag applications aur business scenarios ke prediction workloads ko segregate karta hai — har resource group ko apni CPU, GPU aur memory quotas milti hain, business requirements ke hisaab se performance aur cost optimize karne ke liye. Dusra, ek graph execution component (jaise workflow engines) multistep inference workflows support karta hai — har app team apna inference workflow define karke graph execution engine par deploy karti hai; prediction time par graph engine request le kar predefined workflow chalata hai aur har inference step ke liye routing component se sahi serving group aur service dhoondhta hai. Practice me platform design aur bhi complicated ho sakta hai — security aur access control, metrics aur monitoring, deployment aur DevOps integration jaise components bhi hote hain — lekin diagram me focus core serving concepts par rakha gaya hai.

02.1Chapter 2 · Large Language Model Serving

Transformer ke andar: Evolution, Autoregressive, Decoder-Only

Chapter 1 me serving paradigms samajh liye — ab LLM ke andar jhaankte hain. Serving systems ki complexity se darne ke bajaye book ka approach hai fundamentals se shuru karna: bare minimum code se LLM serve karo, token generation ka mental model banao, aur phir dheere-dheere advanced topics ki taraf badho. Is chapter ka goal hai LLM architecture, token generation process, attention mechanisms, prefill/decode aur KV cache jaise core concepts dena — taaki aap bottlenecks diagnose kar sako aur performance improvements me contribute kar sako. Deep mathematical knowledge zaroori nahi hai — serving par focus hai, isliye math ko intuitive explanations me abstract kar diya gaya hai.

LLM evolution: Word2Vec se Transformer tak

Language models ka evolution sirf history nahi hai — ye model design choices, architectural patterns aur execution behaviors ki insight deta hai, jo inference aur optimization workflows ke liye fundamental hain. Late 2000s me deep learning ne NLP me turning point laaya. 2013 me Word2Vec aaya — words ki dense vector representations ek continuous space me, jo semantic relationships capture karti thi aur language samajhne ki ability ko dramatically aage badhaya.

Bhasha ki sequential nature model karne ke liye 2013 me recurrent neural networks (RNNs) popular hue — temporal dependencies aur contextual information capture kar sakte the, sentiment analysis aur text generation jaise tasks ke liye suited the. RNNs ki long-term dependencies wali struggle ko overcome karne ke liye 2014 me LSTM networks aur GRU aaye — gating mechanisms aur memory cells ke saath, lambi sequences par information behtar retain aur manage kar sakte the. Lekin RNN-based models ki critical limitations bani rahi: woh input ko sequentially process karte the — ek time step at a time — jisse parallelize karna inherently mushkil tha. Isse GPUs jaise modern hardware par scalability aur efficiency hinder hoti thi, aur long-range dependencies capture karne me bhi struggle rehta tha.

2017 me Transformer architecture aayi, jisne sequence modeling ko revolutionize kar diya. Recurrent layers ko self-attention mechanisms aur positional encoding se replace karke Transformers parallel processing enable karte hain jabki long-range dependencies ko efficiently capture karte hain. Iske baad do influential model families aayi: BERT (bidirectional encoder — text ko dono directions me simultaneously padhta hai, text classification ya contextual embeddings jaise tasks ke liye effective) aur GPT (unidirectional decoder — preceding context se next token predict karke text generate karta hai, generative tasks ke liye suited). Ek pivotal innovation ye thi ki har task ke liye scratch se train karne ke bajaye large-scale unlabeled text par pre-training ki jaane lagi (unsupervised learning objectives se), jisse models ko language ki broad, generalizable understanding milti hai, jise phir specific downstream tasks ke liye fine-tune kiya ja sakta hai.

GPT architecture ne text generation, summarization, translation aur question answering me exceptional versatility dikhayi. Researchers ne discover kiya ki model size aur training data dono ko scale up karne se performance significantly enhance hoti hai — isse few-shot aur zero-shot learning jaisi capabilities unlock hui, jahan models naye tasks little ya no additional training ke saath perform kar sakte hain. Scale ka trend saaf hai: pehle generation ke model me 117 million parameters the, do saal me teesri generation 175 billion tak pahunch gayi, aur haal me ek reasoning model 671 billion parameters tak gaya. Isi liye large language model term aaya — tens ya hundreds of billions of parameters wale powerful pre-trained models ke liye.

Yaad rakho: is chapter me LLM aur Transformer ka matlab specifically decoder-only Transformer architectures hai — models jo original Transformer design ke sirf decoder stack ka use karte hain. Aur LLM ki definition static nahi hai — ye evolve karti rehti hai. 2018 me kuch hundred million parameters wale models "large" mane jaate the; 2023–24 tak kuch models trillions of parameters aur multi-modal capabilities tak pahunch gaye. Aaj LLMs ko sirf coherent text generate karne se judge nahi kiya jaata — complex instructions follow karna, tools ke saath interact karna aur human-aligned behavior bhi expectations me shamil hai.

Autoregressive nature: ek token at a time

LLMs ki defining characteristic hai unki autoregressive nature: woh text ek token at a time generate karte hain, har naya token sabhi pehle generated tokens par based hota hai. Ye step-by-step process coherence aur context maintain karta hai — har word pehle generate hue content ke saath meaningfully align hota hai. Ye bhasha ke natural construction ko bhi mirror karta hai — progressively, har word prior context par depend karta hai.

Example se samjho: prompt hai "Write a short introduction about the US capital city." Step 1 me model pehla output token generate karta hai: Washington. Step 2 me ye generated token original input me append ho jaata hai, aur updated sequence phir se model me feed hoti hai agla token produce karne ke liye: D.C. Step 3 me prompt me Washington aur D.C. dono shamil hain, jisse model agla token generate karta hai: is. Step 4 me sequence me "is" jud jaata hai, aur model agla token generate karta hai: the. Ye iterative process tab tak chalta hai jab tak stopping condition na mile — jaise maximum length pahunchna ya special stop token generate hona — aur output sequence token by token banti jaati hai.

Book me input text, input sequence aur prompt terms interchangeably use hote hain — sabka matlab LLM ko diya gaya input hai. Token term ko bhi word ke saath interchangeably use kiya gaya hai, lekin practice me token tokenizer algorithm se define hota hai — text ko chhoti units me todne ka tareeka. Tokenizer aur language par depend karke token poora word, subword ya punctuation bhi ho sakta hai. Average me ek token English me lagbhag 0.75 words ke barabar hota hai.

Decoder-only Transformer architecture: teen components

Decoder-only Transformer ko conceptually teen key components me toda ja sakta hai: tokenizer, Transformer (decoder) blocks, aur language modeling (LM) head.

Step 1 — Tokenizer aur embedding: tokenizer raw input text (prompt) ko fixed vocabulary ke hisaab se discrete tokens me todta hai, un tokens ko token IDs (numerical representations) me convert karta hai, aur phir embedding layer se un IDs ko vector embeddings me map karta hai, taaki Transformer blocks input ko samajh sakein. Example: input "Write a short introduction about the US capital city" 11 tokens me tootta hai, har token ka ek ID hota hai (jaise 1100, 10930, 261...), aur har ID ek embedding vector se map hota hai (jaise [-0.12, 0.55, 0.98, ...]).

Step 2 — Transformer (decoder) blocks: ye model ka heart hai — yahin zyada tar computation (aur learning) hoti hai, serving aur training dono ke dauraan. Decoder blocks stack hote hain (jaise 12, 24 ya zyada layers), jisse model prompt aur previous outputs ki rich contextual understanding build karta hai — token by token — agla token predict karne se pehle. In blocks ke outputs hidden states hote hain — input tokens ki contextualized representations. Ye tensors hote hain shape [N, d] ke, jahan N input sequence me tokens ki sankhya hai aur d hidden state size hai (jaise 768, 2048, 4096, model par depend). Zyada tar cases me sirf final hidden state — last token ke corresponding — use hota hai agla token predict karne ke liye.

Step 3 — Language modeling (LM) head: LM head do kaam karta hai: pehle, hidden states ko vocabulary logits me map karta hai — token vocabulary ke liye ek probability distribution. Dusra, in logits (probabilities) ke basis par output token select karta hai — aam taur par sabse zyada probability wala token agla output banta hai. Example me LM head "Washington" select karta hai, alternatives jaise London, New York aur Cat ke upar.

Ek real model ki configuration: Qwen 2.5

Model ke saath kaam karne se pehle — khaas taur par LLM ke saath — uski configuration inspect karna common aur recommended practice hai. Configuration me architecture ki valuable details hoti hain: layers ki sankhya, hidden dimensions, attention heads, vocabulary size, aur aur bhi. Ye information compute resources estimate karne (jaise GPU memory), serving strategies chunne (jaise quantization ya batching) aur performance optimization plan karne (jaise layer-wise parallelism ya model sharding) me madad karti hai.

Ek chhote open model ki configuration dekho: hidden size 896, number of layers 24, number of attention heads 14, intermediate size 4864, vocabulary size 151936, maximum position embeddings 32768, total parameters lagbhag 494 million. Configuration ko upfront inspect karke aap behtar decisions le sakte ho deployment strategies par — quantized models use karein, multi-GPU setups, ya offloading techniques.

Transformer (decoder) block ke andar

Decoder blocks LLM architecture ki sabse critical aur computation-heavy layers hain. Har block me do primary components hote hain: self-attention layer aur feedforward neural network (FFN). Self-attention layer Transformer models ka novel component hai — ye input tokens ko unke meaning aur relative positions ke basis par dynamically correlate karke contextual information incorporate karta hai. Simple shabdon me, self-attention layer model ko saare previous tokens par consider karne aur agla word generate karte waqt har ek ko alag-alag importance assign karne deta hai.

FFN ek given token ki understanding ko stronger representation me refine karta hai — token ka contextual meaning, aam taur par ek dense, high-dimensional vector (jaise 768 ya 4,096 dimensions). Ye per-token transformation apply karta hai: attention layer se mili context information leverage karta hai, training me seekha hua knowledge incorporate karta hai, aur prediction se pehle refined token representation deta hai.

Ek real decoder layer ki structure inspect karne par dikhta hai: attention module (jisme query, key, value aur output projections ke liye linear layers hain), MLP (gate, up aur down projections aur ek activation function ke saath), aur do layernorms (ek attention se pehle, ek uske baad). Ye decoder layer structure jaanna model optimization ya serving plan karte waqt crucial hai — example ke liye, attention-heavy blocks ko fused attention kernels ya custom GPU implementations se fayda ho sakta hai.

import torch
import gc
import time

# Unload models and clean up gpu memory cache
def free_gpu(model):
  if model:
    # Removes the reference to the model's memory,
    # making it eligible for garbage collection.
    del model

  # Release any cached GPU memory that's no longer needed.
  torch.cuda.empty_cache()

  # Trigger garbage collection to ensure memory is fully released.
  gc.collect()

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from pprint import pprint

model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_name,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    device_map="auto"
)

# Print all configuration parameters
config = model.config
print("\n=== Model Configuration Parameters ===")

# Architecture parameters
print("\nArchitecture Parameters:")
print(f"Hidden size: {config.hidden_size}")  # Size of the hidden layers
print(f"Number of layers: {config.num_hidden_layers}")  # Number of transformer blocks
print(f"Number of attention heads: {config.num_attention_heads}")  # Number of attention heads
print(f"Intermediate size: {config.intermediate_size}")  # Size of the MLP intermediate layer

# Tokenizer parameters
print("\nTokenizer Parameters:")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {config.vocab_size}")  # Size of the vocabulary
print(f"Maximum position embeddings: {config.max_position_embeddings}")  # Maximum sequence length

# Print model size
total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"\nModel Size:")
print(f"Total parameters: {total_params:,}")

# Model-specific parameters
print("\nModel-specific Parameters:")
for key, value in config.to_dict().items():
    if key not in ['architectures', 'model_type', 'torch_dtype']:
        print(f"{key}: {value}")

# Free GPU memory
free_gpu(model)

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from pprint import pprint


# Load the model
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    device_map="auto"  # This will automatically handle device placement
)

print(f"\n=== {model_name} Architecture ===")
print("\nModel Configuration:")
# pprint(model.config.to_dict())

print("\nModel Structure:")
def print_module_structure(module, prefix=''):
    for name, child in module.named_children():
        # Skip certain internal modules for clarity
        if name in ['_orig_mod', 'wrapped_model']:
            continue

        # Print the current module
        print(f"{prefix}{name}: {type(child).__name__}")

        if "Qwen2Attention" in name.lower():
          print(f"\nFound attention module: {name}")
          print(f"Type: {type(module).__name__}")

          # Print attention-specific attributes
          if hasattr(module, 'num_heads'):
              print(f"Number of attention heads: {module.num_heads}")
          if hasattr(module, 'head_dim'):
              print(f"Head dimension: {module.head_dim}")
          if hasattr(module, 'hidden_size'):
              print(f"Hidden size: {module.hidden_size}")
          if hasattr(module, 'rotary_emb'):
              print(f"Has rotary embeddings: {module.rotary_emb is not None}")

        # If it's a container module (has children), recurse
        if list(child.children()):
            print_module_structure(child, prefix + '  ')

print_module_structure(model)

free_gpu(model)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    device_map="auto"
)

print(f"\n=== Detailed {model_name} Attention Analysis ===")

# Find all attention layers
attention_layers = []
for name, module in model.named_modules():
    #if "attention" in name.lower():
    if "Qwen2Attention" in type(module).__name__:
        attention_layers.append((name, module))

print(f"\nFound {len(attention_layers)} attention layers")

# Analyze each attention layer
for i, (name, module) in enumerate(attention_layers):
    print(f"\nAttention Layer {i}: {name}")
    print("=" * 50)

    # Basic information
    print(f"Type: {type(module).__name__}")

    # Attention parameters
    if hasattr(module, 'num_heads'):
        print(f"Number of attention heads: {module.num_heads}")
    if hasattr(module, 'head_dim'):
        print(f"Head dimension: {module.head_dim}")
    if hasattr(module, 'hidden_size'):
        print(f"Hidden size: {module.hidden_size}")

    # Rotary embeddings
    if hasattr(module, 'rotary_emb'):
        print(f"Rotary embeddings: {type(module.rotary_emb).__name__ if module.rotary_emb else 'None'}")

    # Attention projections
    print("\nAttention projections:")
    for sub_name, sub_module in module.named_children():
        if hasattr(sub_module, 'weight'):
            shape = sub_module.weight.shape
            print(f"  {sub_name}: {type(sub_module).__name__}, Shape: {shape}")

    # Additional attention-specific attributes
    print("\nAdditional attributes:")
    for attr_name in dir(module):
        if not attr_name.startswith('_') and not callable(getattr(module, attr_name)):
            try:
                value = getattr(module, attr_name)
                if not isinstance(value, (torch.Tensor, torch.nn.Module)):
                    print(f"  {attr_name}: {value}")
            except:
                pass

# Print model's attention-related configuration
print("\nAttention-related configuration:")
config = model.config.to_dict()
attention_config = {k: v for k, v in config.items() if 'attention' in k.lower()}
pprint(attention_config)

free_gpu(model)



def calculate_model_memory():
    # Constants
    hidden_size = 896
    num_layers = 24
    num_heads = 14
    intermediate_size = 4864
    vocab_size = 151936
    max_position = 32768

    # Memory for embeddings
    embedding_memory = vocab_size * hidden_size * 4  # 4 bytes per float32

    # Memory for each transformer block
    # Self-attention
    qkv_memory = hidden_size * hidden_size * 3 * 4  # Q, K, V projections
    attention_output_memory = hidden_size * hidden_size * 4  # Output projection

    # MLP
    mlp_input_memory = hidden_size * intermediate_size * 4  # First MLP layer
    mlp_output_memory = intermediate_size * hidden_size * 4  # Second MLP layer

    # Layer norms
    norm_memory = hidden_size * 4  # Layer normalization parameters

    # Total memory per layer
    layer_memory = (qkv_memory + attention_output_memory +
                   mlp_input_memory + mlp_output_memory +
                   norm_memory * 2)  # 2 layer norms per block

    # Total model memory
    total_memory = (embedding_memory +
                   layer_memory * num_layers)

    # Convert to MB
    total_memory_mb = total_memory / (1024 * 1024)

    return {
        "Embedding Memory (MB)": embedding_memory / (1024 * 1024),
        "Memory per Layer (MB)": layer_memory / (1024 * 1024),
        "Total Model Memory (MB)": total_memory_mb,
        "Total Model Memory (GB)": total_memory_mb / 1024
    }

# Calculate and print memory usage
memory_stats = calculate_model_memory()
print("\n=== Memory Usage Analysis ===")
for key, value in memory_stats.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value:.2f}")

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from pprint import pprint

# prompt: use bertviz library to visualize the attention result of the input prompt "write a short introduction about US capital city"
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from bertviz import head_view

# Your input text
text = "The tiny animal was overwhelmed by the confetti and it attempted to bat away the glitter with its little paws."
model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, output_attentions=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, output_attentions=True).eval().cuda()

# Tokenize input and get token strings
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
tokens = tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(inputs['input_ids'][0])

# Generate outputs with attention
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_attentions=True)

# Get attention weights
attention = outputs.attentions

# Use bertviz to visualize
head_view(attention, tokens)

← Previous01.5 · Serving Paradigms: Edge, Single, Multi, Platforms→ Next02.2 · Attention: token context kaise capture hota hai
02.2Chapter 2 · Large Language Model Serving

Attention: token context kaise capture hota hai

Context language processing tasks ke liye critical hai. Example lo: sentence "I saw a dog chasing a squirrel, and it climbed up the tree" — bina context ke unclear hai ki "it" dog ko refer kar raha hai ya squirrel ko. Transformer ki self-attention hi woh mechanism hai jisse har token sequence ke doosre tokens ko "dekh" sakta hai aur apni representation compute karte waqt unki relevance weigh kar sakta hai.

Attention kaam kaise karta hai — ek example

Jab LLM prompt "Write a short introduction about the US capital city" process karta hai, to token capital par self-attention model ko ye karne deta hai: peeche US ko dekh kar samajhna ki capital ka matlab ek desh ki capital hai, financial capital nahi; introduction ko consider karke writing ko concise aur general rakhna; aur Write se jaanna ki overall task instructional hai. Yehi context hai jo models ko words aur sentences ka matlab surrounding information ke basis par samajhne, ambiguity kam karne aur coherent interpretation enable karne deta hai.

Attention calculation: Q, K, V

Nutshell me: har token ke liye LLM teen vectors compute karta hai — query (Q), key (K) aur value (V). Ek token ka attention score calculate hota hai us token ke query aur input sequence ke saare tokens ke keys ke beech dot product lekar, result ko scale karke, softmax apply karke weights nikal kar, aur phir un weights se value vectors ka weighted sum compute karke. Ye result token ki updated representation banta hai, poori sequence ke context se enriched. Attention mechanism ko is equation se summarize kiya jaata hai:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) · V

Yahan d_k key vectors ki dimension hai — scaling factor jo dot products ko bahut bada hone se rokta hai. Detailed explanation ke liye book ek mashhoor paper ke scaled dot-product attention wale section ki taraf point karti hai, lekin serving ke liye is high-level samajh se kaam chal jaata hai.

Multi-head attention

Model ki understanding ko aur enhance karne ke liye, ek token ke liye ek attention calculation karne ke bajaye model multiple attention calculations karta hai — inhe heads kehte hain — har head ke apne Q/K/V projections hote hain. Isse model alag-alag tarah ke relationships (jaise syntactic, positional aur semantic) ko parallel me capture kar sakta hai. Saare heads ke outputs ko phir concatenate karke ek linear layer se pass kiya jaata hai, jisse final attention output banta hai.

Attention ko visualize karna

Practice me attention kaise kaam karta hai, ye dekhne ke liye book ek visualization library ka use karti hai: input sequence "write a short introduction about the US capital city" par ek chhote model ke har decoder layer ki attention visualize ki jaati hai. Model ko output_attentions=True ke saath chalakar attention weights fetch kiye jaate hain, aur phir ek head view se tokens ke beech relations dikhaye jaate hain.

Visualization me har line do tokens ke beech ek attention connection represent karti hai — line ki thickness attention weight ki strength dikhati hai, aur color alag-alag attention heads ko distinguish karta hai. In connections ko examine karke dekh sakte ho ki ek given token sabse strongly kis tokens ko attend karta hai. Example me, layer 10 par token capital ka US aur write ki taraf strong attention dikhta hai — ye suggest karta hai ki ye tokens us layer par capital ki contextual representation shape karne me influential hain.

Yaad rakho: attention ki mathematical details se darne ki zaroorat nahi hai — ML engineers ke liye jo LLM serving par focus karte hain, attention ko conceptually samajhna practical bhi hai aur aksar preferable bhi. Serving perspective se sabse important ye jaanna hai ki attention compute-intensive hai, khaas taur par prefill phase ke dauraan, aur iski memory aur latency costs input sequence length ke saath scale hoti hain. Ye samajh critical hai jab aap inference performance tune kar rahe ho, KV caching implement kar rahe ho, ya workloads ko GPUs par distribute kar rahe ho.

Book ye bhi saaf karti hai ki yahan di gayi attention computation intentionally high-level aur conceptual hai — token aur embedding dimensions, har attention head ke andar matrix shapes, aur output aggregation ki exact mechanics jaise implementation details abstract kar diye gaye hain. Ye simplification deliberate hai: ML engineers ke liye attention kaise kaam karta hai aur tokens kaise generate hote hain, ye samajhna typically sufficient aur practical hota hai. Gehraai me jaane ke liye book kuch mashhoor blogs aur books suggest karti hai jo transformers aur attention ko detail me samjhate hain.

02.3Chapter 2 · Large Language Model Serving

LLM Generation step-by-step: Qwen run

Architecture aur attention samajh liye — ab dekhte hain ki LLM generation under the hood kaise execute hoti hai, hands-on code ke saath. Is section ka goal Transformer theory sikhana nahi hai, balki ek serving-oriented mental model banana hai ki inference ke dauraan LLM kaise execute hota hai — kyunki ye execution pattern hi LLM serving systems ke lagbhag har design decision ko drive karta hai. Demo me single-request aur single-sequence example use hota hai; ye code production settings ke liye recommended nahi hai — aane wale chapters dikhayenge ki serving systems isi execution pattern ko scale par batch, stream aur optimize kaise karte hain.

Shuruaat: sabse simple tareeka — pipeline

Ek chhote open model ko chalane ka sabse simple tareeka ek text-generation pipeline object use karna hai — ye underlying complexity ka zyada hissa abstract karke ek straightforward generator() API deta hai. Prompt "Write a short introduction about the US capital city." par output kuch aisa aata hai: "The United States of America is the largest country in the world by area... The city is also home to many other important institutions, including the National Mall, the White House Museum, and the National Archives." Pipeline convenient hai, lekin andar kya hota hai, ye samajhne ke liye generator() ke peeche jhaankna padta hai.

Model prediction, line by line

Manual walkthrough me pipeline ke bajaye model ko directly load kiya jaata hai, taaki generation configuration, inputs aur decoding strategies par full control rahe. Steps ye hain:

  • (1) Tokenizer aur model load karo: model ka naam aur tokenizer load karo, aur model ko available device (GPU ho to GPU, warna CPU) par daalo.
  • (2) Input prompt define karo: woh text jise model complete karega.
  • (3) Prompt ko tokenize karo: prompt ko model ki samajh wale input format me convert karo — token IDs ki sequence. Ye initial input sequence hai LLM generation ke liye.
  • (4) Main generation loop — tokens ek-ek karke generate karo: har iteration me chaar sub-steps hote hain. (A) current context set karo — ab tak ki poori sequence. (B) Model chalao — model input sequence ke basis par agle token ke candidates produce karta hai; logits har token prediction ke raw prediction scores hote hain. (C) Agla token select karo — sirf last token ke logits lo, softmax se probabilities me convert karo, aur probability distribution se ek token sample karo. (D) Naya token input sequence me append karo. (E) Check karo ki end-of-sequence (EOS) token generate hua ya nahi — agar haan, to generation complete.
  • (5) Poori generated sequence ko decode karo: token IDs ko wapas human-readable text me convert karo, special tokens skip karke.

Do cheezein dhyaan do: pehli, LLM ek token at a time generate karta hai; dusri, har newly generated token previous input sequence me append ho kar agle prediction step ka naya input banta hai.

Latency ka pattern: har token dheere kyun hota hai?

Demo me har token ki latency bhi track ki gayi. 100 tokens generate karne me kul 9.1205 seconds lage — average lagbhag 0.09 seconds per token. Lekin ek pattern dikhta hai: pehle token ke alawa, per-token generation time dheere-dheere badhta jaata hai. Ye expected hai — kyunki har newly generated token input sequence me append hota hai, model ko har step par lamba context process karna padta hai. Nateeja: computation time aur resource usage har token ke saath badhte hain.

ML engineers ke roop me inefficiency turant pehchan sakte ho: model har naya token generate karne ke liye saare previous tokens ki attention dobara compute karta hai. Ye repetitive computation known tokens par costly aur unnecessary hai. Kya hum previous tokens ke liye wahi attention dobara calculate karne se bach sakte hain aur computation sirf newly generated token par focus kar sakte hain? Yahi sawaal agle section — KV cache — ki taraf le jaata hai.

Yaad rakho: execution time par dhyaan do, sirf ye nahi ki har line code kya karti hai. Token-level execution, prefill vs decode, aur cached state jaise concepts poori book me wapas aayenge — jab batching, streaming, KV cache optimization aur serving frameworks ki baat hogi.

import torch
import gc
import time

# Unload models and clean up gpu memory cache
def free_gpu(model):
  if model:
    # Removes the reference to the model's memory,
    # making it eligible for garbage collection.
    del model

  # Release any cached GPU memory that's no longer needed.
  torch.cuda.empty_cache()

  # Trigger garbage collection to ensure memory is fully released.
  gc.collect()


from transformers import pipeline
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
import torch

# Initialize the text generation pipeline
generator = pipeline('text-generation', model='Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B')

# Define your prompt
prompt = "Write a short introduction about US capital city."

# Generate text
generated_text = generator(prompt, max_length=50, num_return_sequences=1)

# Print the generated text
print(generated_text[0]['generated_text'])

free_gpu(generator.model)

import torch
import time
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

first_token_generated = False

# (1) Specify the model and load tokenizer and model
model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True).to("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

# (2) Define the input prompt - a text about communication history
prompt = """The history of human communication is a story of innovation. From ancient cave paintings and spoken language to the invention of writing systems, humans have constantly developed new methods to express ideas and share knowledge. The printing press revolutionized the spread of information, enabling books to be produced and distributed at an unprecedented scale. Centuries later, the invention of the telegraph, radio, and television further transformed how we connect with one another. But perhaps no advancement has reshaped communication more profoundly than the internet.
Today, digital platforms allow billions of people to share messages, media, and experiences in real time. Social media, messaging apps, and video conferencing have broken down geographical barriers and created new ways of building communities. At the same time, these technologies raise important questions about privacy, information overload, and the nature of human interaction.
Looking ahead, emerging technologies such as virtual reality, brain-computer interfaces, and artificial intelligence promise to once again redefine how we communicate. As we reflect on this history and anticipate the future, one question arises:

How might the next wave of communication tools shape our relationships, societies, and sense of identity?"""

# (3) Convert (Tokenize) prompt to the input format that model understands
max_new_tokens = 100
# tokenize the input prompt for the first output token
# PS: prompt is the initial input sequence for LLM generation
idx = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(model.device)
start_time = total_time = time.time()
times = []

# (4) Main generation loop - generate tokens one by one
for _ in range(max_new_tokens):

    # (A) Set the current context for generation
    idx_cond = idx
    with torch.no_grad():
        # (B) Generate predictions (token candidates) for next token
        outputs = model(idx_cond)
        # Get the logits (raw prediction scores) for each token predictions
        logits = outputs.logits

    # (C) Select next token from the predictions generated in step (B)
    logits = logits[:, -1, :] #  Select only the logits for the last token
    probas = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1) # Convert logits to probabilities using softmax
    # Sample the next token from the probability distribution of the predicted tokens from step (B)
    idx_next = torch.multinomial(probas, num_samples=1)
    print("Next Token is:", tokenizer.decode(idx_next[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
    time_cost = time.time() - start_time
    times.append(time_cost)

    # Track time spent in token generation
    if not first_token_generated:
        print(f"Time taken for generating the first token: {time_cost:.4f} seconds")
        first_token_generated = True
    else:
        print(f"Time taken for generating a token: {time_cost:.4f} seconds")

    start_time = time.time()

    # (D) Append the new token to the input sequence
    idx = torch.cat((idx, idx_next), dim=1)

    # (E) Check if end-of-sequence token was generated
    if idx_next.item() == tokenizer.eos_token_id:
        print("\n[Generation completed - EOS token reached]")
        break

# Decode the entire generated sequence
generated_text = tokenizer.decode(idx[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
print(f"Total time take for next token: {time.time() - total_time:.4f} seconds")
print(generated_text)

# Free GPU memory
free_gpu(model=model)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# First chart: First bar red, others blue
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))
# plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.bar(range(len(times)), times, color=['red'] + ['blue'] * (len(times) - 1))
plt.xlabel("Token ID")
plt.ylabel("Time Spent in Token Generation")
plt.title("LLM Generation Times for each token")

# # Second chart: Exclude the first element
# plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
# plt.bar(range(len(times) - 1), times[1:])
# plt.xlabel("Token ID")
# plt.ylabel("Time Spent in Token Generation")
# plt.title("Token Generation Times (Excluded the initial prompt tokens)")

# plt.tight_layout()
# plt.show()

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True, use_cache=True) \
            .to("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True).to("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

prompt = """The history of human communication is a story of innovation. From ancient cave paintings and spoken language to the invention of writing systems, humans have constantly developed new methods to express ideas and share knowledge. The printing press revolutionized the spread of information, enabling books to be produced and distributed at an unprecedented scale. Centuries later, the invention of the telegraph, radio, and television further transformed how we connect with one another. But perhaps no advancement has reshaped communication more profoundly than the internet.
Today, digital platforms allow billions of people to share messages, media, and experiences in real time. Social media, messaging apps, and video conferencing have broken down geographical barriers and created new ways of building communities. At the same time, these technologies raise important questions about privacy, information overload, and the nature of human interaction.
Looking ahead, emerging technologies such as virtual reality, brain-computer interfaces, and artificial intelligence promise to once again redefine how we communicate. As we reflect on this history and anticipate the future, one question arises:

How might the next wave of communication tools shape our relationships, societies, and sense of identity?"""

num_interations = 100
times_with_cache = []

first_token_generated = False
input_ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(model.device)
idx = input_ids
start_time = total_time = time.time()

# (1) Define Key/Value Cache for faster generation
past_key_values = None

for _ in range(num_interations):
    print("input_ids size: " + str(input_ids.size()))
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids,
          past_key_values=past_key_values, # (2) Use KV-cache from previous iteration
          use_cache=True, # (2) Enable KV caching
          max_new_tokens = 100,
          min_new_tokens= 100)


        logits = outputs.logits
        # (3) Update KV Cache
        past_key_values = outputs.past_key_values
        torch.cuda.synchronize()

    logits = logits[:, -1, :]
    probas = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    generated_token_id = torch.multinomial(probas, num_samples=1) # Sample instead of argmax

    # (4) Update input_ids with only the new token (using KV-cache)
    input_ids = generated_token_id  # Note: Not concatenating with previous tokens due to KV-cache

    print("Next token:", tokenizer.decode(generated_token_id[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
    idx = torch.cat((idx, generated_token_id), dim=1)

    time_cost= time.time() - start_time
    times_with_cache.append(time_cost)
    if not first_token_generated:
        print(f"Time take for first token: {time_cost:.4f} seconds")
        first_token_generated = True
    else:
        print(f"Time take for next token: {time_cost:.4f} seconds")
    start_time = time.time()

    if generated_token_id.item() == tokenizer.eos_token_id:
        print("\n[Generation completed - EOS token reached]")
        break

generated_text = tokenizer.decode(idx[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
print(f"Total time take for next token: {time.time() - total_time:.4f} seconds")
print(generated_text)

free_gpu(model=model)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))

# Display the time cost of LLM token generation without KV Cache
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.bar(range(len(times)), times, color=['red'] + ['blue'] * (len(times) - 1))
plt.xlabel("Token ID")
plt.ylabel("Time Spent in Token Generation")
plt.title("LLM Generation Times (No Cache) for each token")


# Display the time cost of LLM token generation with KV Cache
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.bar(range(len(times_with_cache)), times_with_cache, color=['red'] + ['blue'] * (len(times_with_cache) - 1))
plt.xlabel("Token ID")
plt.ylabel("Time Spent in Token Generation")
plt.title("LLM Generation Times (with Cache) for each token")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

import torch
import time
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)\
          .to("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

prompt = """The history of human communication is a story of innovation. From ancient cave paintings and spoken language to the invention of writing systems, humans have constantly developed new methods to express ideas and share knowledge. The printing press revolutionized the spread of information, enabling books to be produced and distributed at an unprecedented scale. Centuries later, the invention of the telegraph, radio, and television further transformed how we connect with one another. But perhaps no advancement has reshaped communication more profoundly than the internet.
Today, digital platforms allow billions of people to share messages, media, and experiences in real time. Social media, messaging apps, and video conferencing have broken down geographical barriers and created new ways of building communities. At the same time, these technologies raise important questions about privacy, information overload, and the nature of human interaction.
Looking ahead, emerging technologies such as virtual reality, brain-computer interfaces, and artificial intelligence promise to once again redefine how we communicate. As we reflect on this history and anticipate the future, one question arises:

How might the next wave of communication tools shape our relationships, societies, and sense of identity?"""

max_new_tokens = 50
context_size = 2048 # Define the context size as needed for Qwen

first_token_generated = False
idx = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(model.device)
start_time = total_time = time.time()

for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
    # Take the latest "context_size" tokens as model input
    idx_cond = idx[:, -context_size:]
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(idx_cond)
        logits = outputs.logits

    # select next token from candidates based on probabilities.
    logits = logits[:, -1, :]
    probas = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    idx_next = torch.multinomial(probas, num_samples=1)
    print("Decode text generated:", tokenizer.decode(idx_next[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

    idx = torch.cat((idx, idx_next), dim=1)

    if idx_next.item() == tokenizer.eos_token_id:
        print("\n[Generation completed - EOS token reached]")
        break

generated_text = tokenizer.decode(idx[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
print(f"Total time take for next token: {time.time() - total_time:.4f} seconds")
print(generated_text)

# Free GPU memory
free_gpu(model=model)
