02.4Chapter 2 · Large Language Model Serving

KV Cache + Prefill/Decode phases

Pichle section me dekha ki bina optimization ke model har token ke liye poori sequence dobara process karta hai. Ab imagine karo ki saare previous tokens ke intermediate results — khaas taur par attention mechanism se compute hue key aur value vectors — cache kar liye jaayein. Phir har naye token ke generation step me sirf newly added token process karna padega, poori sequence ki attention dobara compute karne ke bajaye. Yahi KV cache karta hai: ye optimization har layer par previously generated tokens ke liye compute hue attention keys aur values store karti hai, jisse decoding ke dauraan redundant computations skip ho jaati hain.

KV cache: memory ke badle compute ki bachat

KV cache LLM calculation ko full-sequence recomputation se incremental, cache-augmented workflow me badal deta hai — increased memory usage ke badle significant compute savings. Ye technique redundant computation ko dramatically kam karti hai aur bahut tez token generation enable karti hai.

Code me farq saaf hai. KV cache wale version me teen key changes hote hain: pehle, ek past_key_values variable define karo jo cache hold karega (shuruaat me None). Dusra, model ko call karte waqt pichli iteration ka cache pass karo (past_key_values=past_key_values) aur caching enable karo (use_cache=True). Teesra, har token generation ke baad cache update karo (past_key_values = outputs.past_key_values). Aur sabse important: agle step ka model input sirf newly generated token hota hai (input_ids = generated_token_id) — previous tokens se concatenate karne ki zaroorat nahi, kyunki unki information cache me hai.

Numbers: cache se kitna farq padta hai?

Demo ke numbers bahut kuch kehte hain. Bina cache ke 100 tokens generate karne me 9.1205 seconds lage. KV cache ke saath wahi kaam 3.1416 seconds me ho gaya — lagbhag 3 guna tez. Time comparison me pattern bhi saaf hai: bina caching ke generation time steadily badhta hai, kyunki model har step par badhti hui input sequence ko reprocess karta hai. Iske contrast me, KV cache enable karne se compute time significantly kam ho jaata hai — previously computed key-value pairs reuse karke — jisse pehle token ke baad generation speed zyada stable aur efficient ho jaati hai.

Practice me KV caches ko design, manage aur optimize karne ke liye kai advanced techniques propose hui hain. Yahan mili foundational intuition se aap un methods ko explore aur apply karne ke liye behtar equipped ho. Book KV cache optimization strategies ko aage wale chapters me detail me cover karti hai.

Prefill aur decode phases

Ab tokens generate hone ka tareeka dekh liya, to agle do phases samajhne ka time hai — prefill aur decode. Ye terms LLM serving domain me widely use hote hain, khaas taur par performance optimization aur scalability ke context me.

  • Prefill phase (prompt processing bhi kehte hain): model poora input prompt ek saath process karta hai. Ye phase compute-intensive hai kyunki attention prompt ke saare tokens par compute hoti hai — sequence length ke respect me quadratic complexity.
  • Decoding phase (token-by-token generation): model ek token at a time generate karta hai aur har naye token ke liye repeat karta hai. Sequence badhti hai, lekin (attention) computation typically sirf sabse recent token par focus hoti hai — baaki KV cache se aata hai.

Example: jab user prompt submit karta hai, prefill phase me model prompt ke saare tokens ko simultaneously process karta hai, parallelism leverage karke relatively efficient computation karta hai. Prefill complete hone ke baad decoding phase shuru hoti hai — model ek-ek karke tokens generate karta hai response banane ke liye, jaise Washington, D.C., is, aur the.

Time comparison me farq saaf dikhta hai: pehla token generate karne ka time — jo prefill phase se correspond karta hai — significantly zyada hota hai, kyunki model ko poora prompt ek saath process karna padta hai. Uske baad ke bars (decoding phase) bahut chhote aur consistent token-generation times dikhate hain, kyunki model pehle steps se cached information use karke ek token at a time generate karta hai.

Yaad rakho — prefill vs decode jaanna kyun matter karta hai: prefill aur decoding phases ke alag-alag compute patterns samajhna informed optimization aur resource-planning decisions ke liye critical hai. Prefill compute-intensive hai (multiple prompt tokens ka parallel processing); decoding memory-intensive hai (model weights ka frequent loading aur badhta hua KV cache). Kaunsi phase dominate karti hai, ye jaanna aapko sahi bottlenecks target karne me madad karta hai. Example: 500+ page ki PDF process karne jaise long prompts wale scenarios me prefill expensive ho jaata hai. Dusri taraf, short prompts aur long generations — jaise chatbot replies ya story generation — me decoding bottleneck ban jaata hai. Phases ko distinguish karke aap system design aur optimization efforts ko apne application ki performance characteristics ke saath behtar align kar sakte ho.

import torch
import gc
import time

# Unload models and clean up gpu memory cache
def free_gpu(model):
  if model:
    # Removes the reference to the model's memory,
    # making it eligible for garbage collection.
    del model

  # Release any cached GPU memory that's no longer needed.
  if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()

  # Trigger garbage collection to ensure memory is fully released.
  gc.collect()

free_gpu(None)

02.5Chapter 2 · Large Language Model Serving

vLLM se serving, performance comparison, streaming & batching

Ab tak inference scratch se implement karke dekha — model manually load karna aur tokens step by step generate karna. Ye under-the-hood insight ke liye valuable hai, lekin real-world applications typically custom-built inference pipelines ke bajaye serving frameworks par rely karte hain. Is section me vLLM ko practical example ki tarah use karke dikhate hain ki production-ready libraries ke saath LLM inference kaise execute hoti hai.

Serving framework kya deta hai?

vLLM aur SGLang jaise model serving frameworks purpose-built systems hain jo pre-trained language models load karke unhe APIs (typically REST ya gRPC) ke through real-time ya batch inference ke liye expose karte hain. Training frameworks (jaise PyTorch aur TensorFlow) model development aur gradient-based learning par focus karte hain; serving frameworks efficient, scalable aur low-latency inference ke liye optimized hote hain.

Serving frameworks sirf inference chalane ki ability se bahut zyada dete hain: KV-cache reuse ke saath efficient decoding, request scheduling (batching ya micro-batching), multi-user concurrency support, aur token streaming, cancellation aur interruption handling. Ek well-designed serving framework latest research optimizations — jaise paged attention aur speculative decoding — ko continually integrate karta hai, jabki low-level infrastructure concerns ko abstract kar deta hai. Isse developers har model architecture ke liye inference logic dobara implement karne ya latest academic papers ke peeche bhaagne ke bajaye applications banane par focus kar sakte hain.

vLLM se LLM serve karna

vLLM se LLM serve karna bahut simple aur efficient hai. Kuch hi lines me model load karke inference chala sakte ho: LLM(model=...) se model load karo, SamplingParams se inference parameters define karo (jaise temperature 0.8, top_p 0.95, max_tokens 128), aur llm.generate([prompt], inference_params) se text generation chalao. LLM() aur generate() functions bahut saari complexity abstract kar deti hain, jisse LLMs ke saath quick experimentation possible hoti hai.

Simplicity ke bawajood, vLLM extensive configuration options deta hai performance aur behavior ko specific application needs ke hisaab se fine-tune karne ke liye. Advanced configuration me shamil hain: memory management (CPU swap space size GB me, maximum model length), PagedAttention settings (block size, prefix caching enable), KV cache management (maximum number of sequences, maximum sequence length), performance optimizations (chunked prefill, CUDA graph), aur system settings (distributed serving ke liye worker framework, custom all-reduce). Sampling parameters me bhi bahut kuch hai: temperature (randomness control karta hai — 0.0 deterministic), top_p (nucleus sampling), top_k, max_tokens, stop sequences, frequency penalty, presence penalty, repetition penalty, aur skip_special_tokens. vLLM ek mashhoor text completion API ke parameter conventions follow karta hai, jisse adopt karna familiar aur easy hota hai.

Performance comparison: vLLM vs Hugging Face Transformers

Convenience ke alawa, vLLM substantial performance improvements bhi deta hai. Kai benchmarks me ye ek mashhoor library ke .generate() API se 10 se 20 guna zyada throughput achieve karta hai. Side-by-side comparison me, wahi prompt aur wahi model: vLLM ko 1.12 seconds lage, jabki doosri library ko 19.58 seconds — single prompt par 17x speedup. Aur performance gap sirf badhta hai jab aap concurrent ya batched inference tak scale karte ho.

Best practice: real-world development me teams ease of use ke liye prototyping ek general-purpose library se kar sakti hain, phir production usage ke liye vLLM jaise frameworks par migrate kar sakti hain aur serving configuration ko behtar latency, throughput aur concurrency ke liye fine-tune kar sakti hain. Serving parameters ko apne specific model aur use case ke hisaab se tune karne dekar frameworks minimal engineering overhead ke saath enterprise-grade performance dete hain.

Streaming serving basics

vLLM example me ek problem dikhti hai: LLM internally tokens ek-ek karke generate karta hai, lekin llm.generate() call poora output generate hone tak wait karti hai, koi result return karne se pehle. Web service — jaise chatbot — ke context me iska matlab hai user ko koi response milne se pehle lamba delay — kuch seconds se minutes tak, output length par depend. Conversational interfaces (chatbots) ya real-time feedback chahne wale applications (live captioning, summarization) ke liye ye delay user engagement ko significantly impact karta hai — slow response users ko frustrate karta hai, retention kam karta hai, aur ultimately business goals meet nahi hote.

Solution hai streaming: har token jaise hi generate ho, use turant return kar do — poora output complete hone ka wait karne ke bajaye, incrementally token by token (ya chhote chunks me) return karo. vLLM me streaming AsyncLLMEngine class se enable hoti hai (standard LLM class ke bajaye). generate() function ek asynchronous stream object return karti hai, jisse async for loop se newly generated tokens ek-ek karke pull kiye ja sakte hain — har chunk ko print ya web service ko yield karte hue.

Streaming ka ek aur valuable benefit hai: users generation ko beech me cancel kar sakte hain agar output galat direction me ja raha ho. vLLM me ye engine.abort(request_id) call karke hota hai, jahan request_id us specific generation request se associated unique identifier hai. Ye na sirf user experience improve karta hai (irrelevant ya incorrect completions se bachakar), balki compute resources bhi conserve karta hai — production environments me ye khaas taur par important hai jahan efficiency aur cost control critical hain.

Batch serving basics

Ab tak ke examples me ek time par ek prompt LLM ko bheja gaya. Prototyping ke liye simple aur effective hai, lekin high-throughput scenarios me ye bottleneck ban jaata hai — jaise 100,000 documents summarize karna, 5,000 PDF files index karna, ya 20,000 concurrent chatbot users serve karna. Ek time par ek input process karna scale nahi karta.

Is performance limitation ko address karne aur GPU compute resources ko fully utilize karne ke liye batching chahiye: multiple input requests ko group karke ek hi forward pass me simultaneously process karna. Ek prompt at a time handle karne ke bajaye, batching model ko multiple prompts ke outputs parallel me generate karne deti hai, throughput significantly improve karti hai. Batching zyada tar ML models par apply ho sakti hai, lekin LLMs ke liye ye khaas taur par crucial hai unki compute characteristics ki wajah se.

Transformer-based LLMs input batches ko efficiently process kar sakte hain kyunki unki computations — jaise matrix multiplications aur attention — sequences par parallelize ho sakti hain. Shared model weights aur GPU ki parallel compute capability ki wajah se batching minimal overhead ke saath multiple requests simultaneously handle kar leti hai.

Experiment ke numbers: chaar prompts ka batch process karne me vLLM ko 1.0626 seconds lage; wahi chaar prompts ek-ek karke process karne me kul 2.3865 seconds lage — batching se 2.2x throughput improvement. Aur optimization techniques se throughput aur bhi badhaya ja sakta hai jabki latency simultaneously kam hoti hai. Aisi hi ek technique hai continuous batching — jahan naye requests dynamically add ho jaate hain jaise hi doosre complete hote hain. Ek 2023 ke study me dikhaya gaya ki continuous batching LLM inference throughput ko 23 guna tak improve kar sakti hai, saath me p50 latency significantly kam karke.

import torch
import gc
import time

# Unload models and clean up gpu memory cache
def free_gpu(model):
  if model:
    # Removes the reference to the model's memory,
    # making it eligible for garbage collection.
    del model

  # Release any cached GPU memory that's no longer needed.
  if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()

  # Trigger garbage collection to ensure memory is fully released.
  gc.collect()

free_gpu(None)

import asyncio
from vllm.engine.arg_utils import AsyncEngineArgs
from vllm.engine.async_llm_engine import AsyncLLMEngine
from vllm.sampling_params import SamplingParams

# Initialize the engine arguments
engine_args = AsyncEngineArgs(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B",
    dtype="float16",
    tensor_parallel_size=1,      # Number of GPUs to use
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.9,  # GPU memory utilization
    max_num_batched_tokens=32768, # Maximum number of tokens to process in a batch
    max_num_seqs=256,           # Maximum number of sequences to process
    disable_log_requests=True,   # Disable request logging
    disable_log_stats=True,      # Disable stats logging
)

# Create the vLLM async streaming engine
engine = AsyncLLMEngine.from_engine_args(engine_args)

async def generate_text(prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 100, request_id="id"):
  try:
    # Define sampling parameters
    sampling_params = SamplingParams(
        temperature=0.0,
        max_tokens=max_tokens,
        stop=["\n"],  # Stop at newline
    )

    # Generate text in async and streaming fashion
    results_generator = engine.generate(
        prompt=prompt,
        sampling_params=sampling_params,
        request_id=request_id
    )

    # Process the results
    final_output = None
    async for request_output in results_generator:
        final_output = request_output
        # Print each token as it's generated
        print("chunk \n")
        for output in request_output.outputs:
            print(output.text, end="", flush=True)
        print()
    print()  # Newline at the end

    # This will only be reached if all tokens are generated
    print("\nGeneration completed successfully")

    return final_output
  except asyncio.CancelledError:
    print("\nGeneration was cancelled")
    return None
  finally:
    # Always clean up
    try:
      await engine.abort(request_id)
    except:
      pass

request_id = "any_id"
await generate_text(prompt, 10000, requtest_id)

import asyncio

from vllm.engine.async_llm_engine import AsyncLLMEngine
from vllm.sampling_params import SamplingParams

# Initialize the vLLM async streaming engine arguments
engine_args = AsyncEngineArgs(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B",
    dtype="float16",
    tensor_parallel_size=1,      # Number of GPUs to use
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.9,  # GPU memory utilization
    max_num_batched_tokens=32768, # Maximum number of tokens to process in a batch
    max_num_seqs=256,           # Maximum number of sequences to process
    disable_log_requests=True,   # Disable request logging
    disable_log_stats=True,      # Disable stats logging
)

# Create the vLLM async streaming engine
engine = AsyncLLMEngine.from_engine_args(engine_args)

# Define the async function to generate text in streaming mode
async def generate_text(prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 100):
    try:
        # Define sampling parameters
        sampling_params = SamplingParams(
            temperature=0.0,
            max_tokens=max_tokens,
            stop=["\n"],  # Stop at newline
        )

        # Generate text
        request_id = "test-request"  # Unique ID for this request
        # Generate tokens in streaming mode
        results_generator = engine.generate(
            prompt=prompt,
            sampling_params=sampling_params,
            request_id=request_id
        )

        # Process the results
        final_output = None
        async for request_output in results_generator:
            final_output = request_output
            # Print each token as it's generated
            for output in request_output.outputs:
                print(output.text, end="", flush=True)
            print()  # Newline at the end of each output

        return final_output
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        # Handle cancellation gracefully
        print("\nGeneration was cancelled")
        return None
    finally:
        # Always clean up
        try:
            await engine.abort(request_id)
        except:
            pass

03.1Chapter 3 · Model Serving System Design: A Deep Dive

Online serving service from scratch: design goals + architecture

Chapter 1 me serving paradigms aur Chapter 2 me LLM inference samajh liya — ab dono ko jod kar production engineering ki taraf badhte hain: code aur infrastructure ko kaise organize kiya jaaye taaki single-model aur multi-model scenarios ke liye complete serving systems ban sakein. Model serving rapidly evolving field hai — hundreds of open source serving frameworks aur commercial solutions available hain. Kisi specific framework se shuru karne ke bajaye, book first principles se intuition build karne par focus karti hai. Serving systems fundamentally kaise structured hote hain, ye samajhkar aap kisi bhi framework ya managed service ke baare me behtar reason kar sakte ho.

Isi liye chapter me do simplified lekin representative serving systems develop kiye gaye hain: ek single-model LLM serving ke liye aur ek multi-model serving ke liye. Ye implementations intentionally streamlined hain — ye production frameworks ko replace karne ke liye nahi hain — lekin ye core components aur architectural decisions capture karte hain jo real-world systems ko define karte hain. In examples se dikhta hai ki batching, streaming, routing, isolation aur resource management practice me kaise fit hote hain.

Design goals: ek online LLM serving service

Modern serving frameworks bahut saari complexity abstract kar dete hain — lekin woh abstractions important architectural trade-offs bhi chhupa dete hain. Performance, cost aur scalability ke baare me effectively reason karne ke liye, framework par rely karne se pehle serving system ki core mechanics samajhna essential hai.

Is exercise me aap ek model serving service banayenge jo startup par ek single LLM load karta hai aur batch aur streaming dono ke liye concurrent generation requests support karta hai. Example intentionally simplified hai — sirf ek LLM ke liye kaam karta hai jo CPU par chal sakta hai — lekin isme saare essential components cover hote hain jo multi-node, generalized production-grade system tak scale karne ke liye chahiye, future me advanced model optimization techniques ke saath.

Approach ye hai ki complex, production-ready service banane ke bajaye core components implement kiye jaayein, taaki ye critical aspects samajh aayein: web APIs generation requests kaise handle karti hain (batching aur streaming samet), typical LLM request-processing workflow kaisa dikhta hai, service internally kaise structured hai taaki alag-alag LLM models ki flexibility aur scalability support ho, concurrent requests batches me kaise group aur process hote hain, streaming generation under the hood kaise kaam karta hai, batching aur streaming ek hi system me kaise coexist kar sakte hain, aur LLM serving me key performance bottlenecks kahan appear hote hain.

Plan hai: pehle minimal generation service, phir incrementally batching aur streaming capabilities add karna, aur aakhir me dikhana ki vLLM batching ko practice me kaise handle karta hai. Dono approaches samajhkar aap single-model serving architectures ke baare me reason karne, framework choices evaluate karne aur real-world systems me informed design trade-offs karne ke liye behtar equipped honge.

Service architecture: chhe core components

Sample LLM serving service ke chhe core components hain:

  • API server: HTTP API endpoints aur request/response handling karta hai.
  • LLM engine: high-level orchestrator — inference ko end-to-end operate karta hai.
  • Workload manager: request queuing aur batch management handle karta hai.
  • Model executor: processes manage karta hai aur model-worker execution coordinate karta hai.
  • Model worker: apne process me model inference execution karta hai.
  • Model manager: model ko load aur cache karta hai.

LLM engine ek orchestra conductor ki tarah kaam karta hai — stage set karta hai aur coordinate karta hai ki sab kuch kaise chalega. Ye saare core components initialize karta hai, LLM model load karne samet, aur phir orchestrate karta hai ki generation requests kaise handle hongi.

Service concurrent web requests manage karne ke liye design hai, batching aur streaming dono ke support ke saath — isliye ek workload manager introduce kiya gaya hai jo generation request me shamil har prompt ka status track karta hai aur determine karta hai ki model ko process karne ke liye agle batch me kaunse prompts hone chahiye. Ye critical point hai jahan throughput optimize karne ke liye alag-alag batching strategies apply ki ja sakti hain.

Yaad rakho — multi-process setup overkill kyun nahi hai: model worker apne separate process me model loading, hosting aur execution handle karta hai, jabki model executor model workers initialize karta hai, worker groups (inter-worker communication samet) set up karta hai, aur cross-process calls karke inference trigger karta hai aur workers se generation results retrieve karta hai. Simple example ke liye ye multi-process setup overkill lag sakta hai, lekin ye real-world LLM serving systems ka common aur practical pattern reflect karta hai — LLMs typically GPU devices par chalte hain, aur standard practice hai model execution ko specific GPU devices se bound dedicated processes me isolate karna. Main web service CPU par rehti hai, concurrent request management aur orchestration par focus karti hai. GPUs expensive hain, aur aap nahi chahte ki GPUs idle baithe rahein jabki CPUs input preprocessing, output postprocessing, tokenization aur de-tokenization jaise kaam kar rahe hon. Multi-process setup me saare compute-intensive tasks alag processes me move ho jaate hain, CPU–GPU interaction ke liye dedicated CPU resources chhodkar — isse optimal GPU utilization ensure hoti hai.

from typing import List, Dict, Any
from .workload_manager import WorkloadManager, Sequence
from .model_executor import ModelExecutor
import asyncio
import json
import atexit
import threading
import time
import uuid
from vllm import LLM as VLLM
from vllm import SamplingParams

class LLMEngine:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model_executor = ModelExecutor()
        self.workload_manager = WorkloadManager()
        self.max_tokens = 20
        
        # Initialize the model
        self.model_executor.setup_worker("facebook/opt-125m")
        
        # Initialize vLLM model
        self.vllm_model = VLLM(model="facebook/opt-125m")
        
        # Start processing loop in a separate thread
        self.thread = threading.Thread(target=self.requests_processing_loop, daemon=True)
        self.thread.start()
        
        # Register cleanup
        atexit.register(self._cleanup)
    
    def requests_processing_loop(self):
        """Process requests in a loop."""
        while True:
            try:
                active_sequences = self.workload_manager.get_next_batch(is_streaming=True)
                if not active_sequences:
                    time.sleep(0.1)
                    continue
                    
                # Process batch through model, forward pass.
                prompts = [{'prompt': seq.prompt, 'request_id': seq.id} for seq in active_sequences]
                prompts_results = self.model_executor.execute_forward_batch(prompts)
                
                # Stream tokens back to respective clients
                for result in prompts_results:
                    seq = self.workload_manager.get_sequence(result['request_id'])
                    if result['is_finished'] or seq.token_count > self.max_tokens:
                        # Use run_coroutine_threadsafe to safely put None in the main loop's queue
                        asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(
                            seq.client_stream.put(None),
                            seq.loop
                        )
                        seq.finished = True
                        self.workload_manager.remove_finished_sequence(result['request_id'])
                    else:
                        # Use run_coroutine_threadsafe to safely put data in the main loop's queue
                        asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(
                            seq.client_stream.put(
                                json.dumps({"token": result['token'], "sequence_id": result['request_id']})
                            ),
                            seq.loop
                        )
                        self.workload_manager.update_sequence_output(result['request_id'], result['token'])
                
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Error in processing loop: {e}")
                time.sleep(0.1)
    
    def _cleanup(self):
        """Cleanup function to be called when the program exits."""
        # The thread will be automatically terminated since it's a daemon thread
        pass

    # process 1 request with only one prompt at a time.
    def basic_generate(self, prompt: str) -> str:

        sequence = Sequence(str(uuid.uuid4()), prompt, None, None)
        
        # Execute the batch
        results = self.model_executor.execute_batch([sequence])
        
        return results[1][0]['generated_text']
    
    def _is_batch_finished(self, request_ids: List[str]) -> bool:
        for id in request_ids:
            if not self.workload_manager.is_sequence_finished(id):
                return False
        return True

    # process multiple prompts in a request
    def generate(self, prompts: List[str]) -> List[str]:
        # Add all requests to workload manager
        request_ids = []
        for prompt in prompts:
            request_id = self.workload_manager.add_request(prompt)
            request_ids.append(request_id)
        
        # Process requests in batches (from LoadManager) until all prompts of the request are finished
        while not self._is_batch_finished(request_ids):
            # Get next batch of requests
            sequences = self.workload_manager.get_next_batch()
            if not sequences:
                time.sleep(0.1)
                continue
                
            # Execute the next batch in one go, it may not be the same prompts as the prompts in the request.
            results = self.model_executor.execute_batch(sequences)
        
            # Update results in workload manager
            for result in results[1]:
                self.workload_manager.remove_active_sequence(result['request_id'])
                self.workload_manager.update_sequence_output(result['request_id'], result['generated_text'], is_finished=True)

        # Remove finished sequences from workload manager
        generated_texts = []
        for request_id in request_ids:
            generated_texts.append(self.workload_manager.get_sequence(request_id).output[0])
            self.workload_manager.remove_finished_sequence(request_id)

        return generated_texts 
    
    async def event_generator(self, loop, prompt: str):
        
        asyncio.set_event_loop(loop)
        # Create a queue for this client's stream
        queue = asyncio.Queue()
        
        # Add streaming request to workload manager with the queue
        seq_id = self.workload_manager.add_streaming_request(prompt, queue, loop)
        
        print(f"Created queue for sequence {seq_id} in loop {id(loop)} and queue {id(queue._get_loop())}")  # Debug print
        
        try:
            while True:
                print(f"Waiting for data in queue for sequence {seq_id}")  # Debug print
                # Get next token from queue
                data = await queue.get()
                print(f"Received data in queue for sequence {seq_id}: {data}")  # Debug print
                if data is None:  # End of stream
                    print(f"End of stream for sequence {seq_id}")  # Debug print
                    break
                yield f"data: {data}\n\n"
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error in stream for sequence {seq_id}: {e}")
        finally:
            # Clean up
            self.workload_manager.remove_finished_sequence(seq_id)
            print(f"Cleaned up sequence {seq_id}")  # Debug print

    def generate_vllm(self, prompts: List[str]) -> List[str]:
        """
        Generate text using vLLM for multiple prompts.
        
        Args:
            prompts: List of prompts to generate text for
            
        Returns:
            List of generated texts
        """
        # Configure sampling parameters
        sampling_params = SamplingParams(
            temperature=0.7,
            top_p=0.95,
            max_tokens=self.max_tokens
        )
        
        # Generate text for all prompts
        outputs = self.vllm_model.generate(prompts, sampling_params)
        
        # Extract generated text from outputs
        generated_texts = [output.outputs[0].text for output in outputs]
        
        return generated_texts

import multiprocessing as mp
from typing import List, Dict, Any
from .model_worker import ModelWorker
import logging
import sys

# Set up logging with stream handler
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
formatter = logging.Formatter('%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
handler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.addHandler(handler)

class ModelExecutor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.task_queue = mp.Queue()
        self.result_queue = mp.Queue()
        self.worker_process = None
        logger.debug("ModelExecutor initialized with queues")
    
    def setup_worker(self, model_name: str):
        logger.debug(f"Setting up worker with model: {model_name}")
        self.worker_process = mp.Process(
            target=ModelWorker.run,
            args=(model_name, self.task_queue, self.result_queue)
        )
        logger.debug("Starting worker process")
        self.worker_process.start()
        logger.debug("Worker process started")
    
    def execute_batch(self, prompts: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        if not prompts:
            logger.debug("Empty batch received")
            return []
        
        logger.debug(f"Sending batch to worker: {prompts}")
        # Send batch to worker
        self.task_queue.put((prompts, False))
        
        # Get results
        logger.debug("Waiting for results from worker")
        results = self.result_queue.get()
        logger.debug(f"Received results from worker: {results}")
        return results
    
    def execute_forward_batch(self, prompts: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        if not prompts:
            logger.debug("Empty batch received")
            return []
        
        logger.debug(f"Sending streaming batch to worker: {prompts}")
        # Send batch to worker with streaming flag
        self.task_queue.put((prompts, True))
        
        # Get streaming results
        logger.debug("Waiting for streaming results from worker")
        result_type, results = self.result_queue.get()
        logger.debug(f"Received streaming results from worker: {results}")
        
        if result_type == 'stream':
            return results
        else:
            raise Exception("Unexpected result type from worker")
    
    def __del__(self):
        if self.worker_process:
            logger.debug("Terminating worker process")
            self.worker_process.terminate()
            self.worker_process.join()
            logger.debug("Worker process terminated")

import os
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

class ModelManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model_dir = "model_cache"
    
    def load_model(self, model_name: str = "facebook/opt-125m") -> tuple[AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer]:
        # Create model directory if it doesn't exist
        os.makedirs(self.model_dir, exist_ok=True)
        
        # Load model and tokenizer
        model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name)
        tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
        
        return model, tokenizer

import multiprocessing as mp
from typing import List, Dict, Any, Generator
from .model_manager import ModelManager
import torch
import logging
import sys

# Set up logging with stream handler
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
formatter = logging.Formatter('%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
handler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.addHandler(handler)

class ModelWorker:
    def __init__(self, model_name: str):
        self.device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
        logger.debug(f"Loading model {model_name} on device {self.device}")
        self.model, self.tokenizer = ModelManager().load_model(model_name)
        # Initialize state for streaming
        self.stream_states = {}  # request_id -> (input_ids, attention_mask, past_key_values)
    
    def generate(self, prompts: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        logger.debug(f"Received prompts: {prompts}")
        
        # Extract prompts and request IDs
        prompt_texts = [p.prompt for p in prompts]
        request_ids = [p.id for p in prompts]
        
        # Tokenize all prompts in batch
        inputs = self.tokenizer(
            prompt_texts,
            return_tensors="pt",
            padding=True,
            truncation=True,
            max_length=512
        ).to(self.device)
        
        logger.debug(f"Batch input shape: {inputs.input_ids.shape}")
        
        # Generate text for all prompts in one batch
        with torch.no_grad():
            outputs = self.model.generate(
                inputs.input_ids,
                attention_mask=inputs.attention_mask,
                max_new_tokens=50,  # Generate up to 50 new tokens
                num_return_sequences=1,
                pad_token_id=self.tokenizer.eos_token_id
            )
        
        # Decode all outputs
        generated_texts = self.tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)
        logger.debug(f"Generated texts: {generated_texts}")
        
        # Map results back to request IDs
        results = [
            {
                'request_id': request_id,
                'generated_text': generated_text
            }
            for request_id, generated_text in zip(request_ids, generated_texts)
        ]
        
        return results

    def generate_forward_batch(self, prompts: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Generate one token for each prompt in the batch."""
        logger.debug(f"Received streaming prompts: {prompts}")
        
        # Add padding token to the tokenizer if not present
        if self.tokenizer.pad_token is None:
            self.tokenizer.pad_token = self.tokenizer.eos_token
        
        # Tokenize all prompts in batch
        encoded = self.tokenizer(
            [p['prompt'] for p in prompts],
            return_tensors="pt",
            padding=True,
            truncation=True,
            max_length=512
        ).to(self.device)
        
        logger.debug(f"Batch input shape: {encoded.input_ids.shape}")
        
        # Generate next token
        with torch.no_grad():
            outputs = self.model(
                input_ids=encoded.input_ids,
                attention_mask=encoded.attention_mask,
                use_cache=False
            )
            
            # Get next token logits and sample
            next_token_logits = outputs.logits[:, -1, :]
            next_token = torch.multinomial(
                torch.softmax(next_token_logits / 0.7, dim=-1),
                num_samples=1
            ).squeeze(-1)
            
            # Prepare results
            results = []
            for i, prompt_data in enumerate(prompts):
                token = self.tokenizer.decode(next_token[i].unsqueeze(0), skip_special_tokens=True)
                logger.debug(f"Generated token for prompt '{prompt_data['prompt']}': '{token}'")
                results.append({
                    'request_id': prompt_data['request_id'],
                    'token': token,
                    'is_finished': token == self.tokenizer.eos_token
                })
            
            return results

    @staticmethod
    def run(model_name: str, task_queue: mp.Queue, result_queue: mp.Queue):
        # Enable remote debugging
        logger.debug("Waiting for debugger to attach...")
        logger.debug("Debugger attached!")
        
        worker = ModelWorker(model_name)
        logger.debug("Worker initialized")
        
        while True:
            logger.debug("Waiting for batch from queue...")
            batch_data = task_queue.get()
            logger.debug(f"Received batch: {batch_data}")
            
            if batch_data is None:  # Shutdown signal
                logger.debug("Received shutdown signal")
                break
            
            batch, is_streaming = batch_data
            
            if is_streaming:
                # Handle streaming generation
                result_queue.put(('stream', worker.generate_forward_batch(batch)))
            else:
                # Handle regular generation
                result_queue.put(('complete', worker.generate(batch)))
python — ch03/single_model_llm_serving/llm/workload_manager.py — poora file (GitHub: https://github.com/orca3/llm-model-serving/blob/main/ch03/single_model_llm_serving/llm/workload_manager.py)
import uuid
from typing import List, Dict, Any, Optional
from queue import Queue
import asyncio

class Sequence:
    def __init__(self, seq_id: str, prompt: str, client_stream, loop):
        self.id = seq_id
        self.prompt = prompt
        self.output = []
        self.finished = False
        self.loop = loop
        self.client_stream = client_stream
        self.token_count = 0

class WorkloadManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.incoming_queue: Queue[Sequence] = Queue()
        self.active_sequences: List[Sequence] = []
        
        self.incoming_streaming_queue: Queue[Sequence] = Queue()
        self.active_streaming_sequences: List[Sequence] = []
        self.batch_size = 4  # Process up to 4 sequences at a time
        self.sequence_map: Dict[str, Sequence] = {}
    
    # for basic generate and batch generate        
    def add_request(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
        sequence = Sequence(request_id, prompt, None, None)
        self.incoming_queue.put(sequence)
        self.sequence_map[request_id] = sequence
        return request_id
    
    # for streaming generate
    def add_streaming_request(self, prompt: str, client_stream, loop) -> str:
        request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
        sequence = Sequence(request_id, prompt, client_stream, loop)
        self.incoming_streaming_queue.put(sequence)
        self.sequence_map[request_id] = sequence
        return request_id
    
    def get_next_batch(self, is_streaming: bool = False) -> List[Sequence]:
        if is_streaming:
            while len(self.active_streaming_sequences) < self.batch_size and not self.incoming_streaming_queue.empty():
                sequence = self.incoming_streaming_queue.get()
                self.active_streaming_sequences.append(sequence)
        
            return self.active_streaming_sequences
        else:
            while len(self.active_sequences) < self.batch_size and not self.incoming_queue.empty():
                sequence = self.incoming_queue.get()
                self.active_sequences.append(sequence)
                
            return self.active_sequences
    
    def remove_active_sequence(self, seq_id: str):
        if seq_id in self.sequence_map:
            sequence = self.sequence_map[seq_id]
            if sequence in self.active_sequences:
                self.active_sequences.remove(sequence)
            if sequence in self.active_streaming_sequences:
                self.active_streaming_sequences.remove(sequence)
    
    def remove_finished_sequence(self, seq_id: str):
        if seq_id in self.sequence_map:
            sequence = self.sequence_map[seq_id]
            if sequence in self.active_sequences:
                self.active_sequences.remove(sequence)
            if sequence in self.active_streaming_sequences:
                self.active_streaming_sequences.remove(sequence)
            del self.sequence_map[seq_id]
            
    def is_sequence_finished(self, seq_id: str) -> bool:
        if seq_id in self.sequence_map:
            sequence = self.sequence_map[seq_id]
            return sequence.finished
        return False
    
    def get_sequence(self, seq_id: str) -> Optional[Sequence]:
        return self.sequence_map.get(seq_id)
    
    def update_sequence_output(self, seq_id: str, token: str, is_finished: bool = False):
        if seq_id in self.sequence_map:
            sequence = self.sequence_map[seq_id]
            sequence.output.append(token)
            sequence.prompt += token
            sequence.token_count += 1
            sequence.finished = is_finished
            return sequence
        return None
python — ch03/single_model_llm_serving/main.py — poora file (GitHub: https://github.com/orca3/llm-model-serving/blob/main/ch03/single_model_llm_serving/main.py)
from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks, Depends
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel
from llm import LLMEngine
from typing import List
import asyncio
import multiprocessing
import atexit
import signal

# Create FastAPI app
app = FastAPI()

# Create LLM instance
_llm = None
_llm_lock = multiprocessing.Lock()

def cleanup():
    global _llm
    if _llm is not None:
        try:
            _llm._cleanup()
        except:
            pass
        _llm = None

def get_llm():
    global _llm
    with _llm_lock:
        if _llm is None:
            _llm = LLMEngine()
            # Register cleanup
            atexit.register(cleanup)
        return _llm

class GenerateRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str

class GenerateResponse(BaseModel):
    generated_text: str

class BatchGenerateRequest(BaseModel):
    prompts: List[str]

class BatchGenerateResponse(BaseModel):
    generated_texts: List[str]

@app.post("/generate_stream")
async def generate_stream(request: GenerateRequest, llm: LLMEngine = Depends(get_llm)):
    async def event_generator():
        loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
        async for token in llm.event_generator(loop, request.prompt):
            # token = 'data: {"token": " a", "sequence_id": "8310f5e1-6f6f-480e-b2f9-c8144a12cc17"}\n\n'
            yield token
    
    return StreamingResponse(
        event_generator(),
        media_type="text/event-stream"
    )

# process 1 request with only one prompt at a time.
@app.post("/basic_generate", response_model=GenerateResponse)
async def basic_generate(request: GenerateRequest, llm: LLMEngine = Depends(get_llm)):
    generated_text = llm.basic_generate(request.prompt)
    return GenerateResponse(generated_text=generated_text)

# process multiple prompts in a request
@app.post("/generate", response_model=BatchGenerateResponse)
async def generate(request: BatchGenerateRequest, llm: LLMEngine = Depends(get_llm)):
    generated_texts = llm.generate(request.prompts)
    return BatchGenerateResponse(generated_texts=generated_texts)

@app.post("/generate_vllm", response_model=BatchGenerateResponse)
async def generate_vllm(request: BatchGenerateRequest, llm: LLMEngine = Depends(get_llm)):
    """
    Generate text using vLLM for multiple prompts.
    This endpoint uses vLLM's efficient batched inference capabilities.
    """
    generated_texts = llm.generate_vllm(request.prompts)
    return BatchGenerateResponse(generated_texts=generated_texts)

def signal_handler(signum, frame):
    cleanup()
    exit(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn
    # Register signal handlers
    signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, signal_handler)
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, signal_handler)
    
    # Initialize LLM before starting the server
    get_llm()
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

03.2Chapter 3 · Model Serving System Design: A Deep Dive

Single request handling, batching, streaming with batching

Architecture samajh liya — ab service implement karte hain. Pehle ek single generation request handle karenge, phir progressively batching aur streaming support add karenge. Har step me components kaise judte hain, ye dekhna hi is section ka point hai.

Single generation request handling

Shuruaat core components initialize karke hoti hai: LLMEngine class me ek ModelExecutor aur ek WorkloadManager bante hain, aur max tokens (example me 20) set hota hai. Phir model executor ek model worker set up karta hai — example me ek chhota open model load hota hai. Model executor worker se do event queues ke through communicate karta hai: task_queue (model request queue) aur result_queue (model result queue). Prompt requests task_queue se worker ko bheji jaati hain aur generation results result_queue se receive hote hain.

ModelWorker model ko ek model manager ki madad se load karta hai — model aur tokenizer dono — aur device choose karta hai (GPU available ho to GPU, warna CPU). Worker apne process me ek while loop chalata hai jo continuously task_queue monitor karta hai. Jab request aati hai, to woh prompt ko task_queue se nikaalta hai, model inference karta hai, aur generation result ko result_queue me daal deta hai.

Web API endpoint /basic_generate ek single prompt ko request payload ke roop me accept karta hai aur generated text ko plain string ke roop me return karta hai. Orchestration logic LLMEngine.basic_generate me hai: pehle prompt ko ModelExecutor ko bhejo, executor prompt ko task_queue se ModelWorker tak pass kare, jab executor ko result_queue se generated result mile to use wapas LLMEngine ko do, jo use web API ko return kare. Worker ke andar inference logic model ka generate chalata hai aur output ko tokenizer se decode karke generated text banata hai. Ek test case se verify karte hain: /basic_generate par prompt "Hello, I am" bhejkar dekho ki response sahi aata hai ya nahi.

Agar service ko aise hi roll out kar do, to pehli challenge hogi low throughput. Current inference service me users ek time par sirf ek prompt bhej sakte hain, aur model worker ek inference call me ek prompt process karta hai. LLMs multiple prompts ko ek saath batch me process karne ke liye well-suited hain, isliye compute resources underutilized rehte hain. Agla step hai batching support add karna.

Batching: prompts ko group karo, outputs ko map karo

Naya /generate API ek prediction request me prompts ki list accept karta hai aur generated texts ki list wapas deta hai — input array ke same order me. Batching implement karne me do key challenges solve karni padti hain. Pehli: alag-alag requests ke prompts ko kuch batches me combine karo, taaki LLM prompts ko per-request nahi, bade batches me execute kare — resource utilization maximize ho. Dusri: generated outputs ko accurately wapas unke corresponding original requests se map karo, taaki service results sahi users ko sahi order me return kar sake.

Iske liye do cheezein introduce hoti hain: har prompt ke liye ek tracking data structure jise Sequence kehte hain, aur ek naya component WorkloadManager. Workflow chhe steps me chalta hai: (1) Request intake — API server requests receive karke har payload se individual prompts extract karta hai. (2) Prompt queuing — API server requests ko LLM engine ko pass karta hai, jo unhe workload manager ko forward karta hai. (3) Prompt tracking aur batching — workload manager har prompt ko unique ID assign karke Sequence object me wrap karta hai, saare active sequences ki in-memory tracking maintain karta hai, aur determine karta hai ki agle batch me kaunse prompts group hone chahiye. (4) Batch execution — LLM engine workload manager se agla prompt batch lekar model executor aur worker ko inference ke liye bhejta hai. (5) Model inference — model worker poora batch ek inference call me process karta hai aur generated texts return karta hai, har ek apne prompt ID ke saath. (6) Response mapping — LLM engine prompt IDs use karke har generated text ko uske originating web request se map karta hai.

Workload manager ki implementation me do key aspects highlight karne layak hain. Pehla, woh first-in, first-out (FIFO) strategy use karta hai ye determine karne ke liye ki agle batch ke liye kaunse prompts select honge. Dusra, maximum batch size cap ki gayi hai — example me LLM ek time par 4 prompts tak process kar sakta hai. LLMEngine.generate pehle saare prompt IDs collect karta hai, phir batches execute karta rehta hai jab tak request ke saare prompts complete na ho jaayein, aur phir prompt IDs se corresponding generated text retrieve karta hai. Batching individual requests ke liye latency introduce kar sakti hai — kuch ko wait karna pad sakta hai — lekin ye resources ko requests ke across optimize karke overall service throughput significantly improve karti hai.

Yaad rakho: har prompt ko individually track karna LLM serving me ek common technique hai. Ye user ki web request ko actual model execution se decouple kar deti hai, jisse system backend me prompts ko zyada efficient processing ke liye reorganize kar sakta hai. Ye abstraction serving service ko flexibility deti hai dynamic batching aur prioritization jaise optimization techniques apply karne ki. Is example me user request ka har prompt ek Sequence object ban jaata hai, jo LLM execution workload manage karne ki fundamental unit hai. Practice me batch size aur batching strategy ka inference throughput par significant impact hota hai — sahi configuration ke liye careful tuning chahiye, jo model, prompt characteristics, web traffic ki nature aur hardware par depend karti hai. Real serving frameworks continuous batching, dynamic scheduling aur memory-efficient KV cache management jaise techniques use karte hain GPU utilization maximize karne ke liye jabki latency control me rehti hai.

Streaming with batching: dono ek saath

Batching code saare prompts fully process hone tak wait karta hai results return karne se pehle — isse significant latency aati hai aur user experience kharab hota hai. LLMs inferences ek token at a time generate karte hain, isliye latency kam karne ke liye tokens ko jaise hi produce hon, users ko stream back karna chahiye — jabki internally har generation step par requests ko batch bhi karna chahiye. Isse high throughput bani rehti hai aur real-time experience bhi responsive hota hai.

Ek timeline se samjho: T0 par user A ka prompt aata hai — backend batch me sirf Prompt1 hai, stream hota hai "a". T1 par user B ka prompt aata hai — backend batch [Prompt1, Prompt2] ho jaata hai; Prompt1 ko "a", "student" stream hote hain, Prompt2 ko "see". T2 par user C ka prompt aata hai — batch [Prompt1, Prompt2, Prompt3]; Prompt1 complete hokar "[end]" stream karta hai, Prompt2 ko "see", "a", Prompt3 ko "eat". T3 par A finish ho jaata hai aur D join karta hai — batch [Prompt2, Prompt3, Prompt4] ban jaata hai. Prompts alag-alag times par aate hain, service unhe backend me inference ke liye batch karti hai, har prompt ke generated tokens ko individually track karti hai, aur jaise hi tokens produce hote hain, unhe real time me stream back karti hai. Jab prompt complete hota hai, to use backend batch se remove kar diya jaata hai naye requests ke liye jagah banane ke liye.

Implementation me batching design ke mukable kuch changes aate hain: generation API ab asynchronous hai, taaki users ko token updates jaise hi generate hon, mil sakein; ModelWorker ek inference step me ek token generate karta hai, poora output ek call me produce karne ke bajaye; WorkloadManager partial outputs track karta hai aur har prompt ko newly generated tokens se real time me update karta hai; har prompt ki apni event queue hoti hai, jisse LLMEngine tokens ko ModelWorker se async API layer tak efficiently pass kar sakta hai; aur LLMEngine me ek dedicated batch-processing thread hai jo prompts par token-level inference orchestrate karta hai.

Background thread (requests_processing_loop) continuously WorkloadManager se prompts ke batches pull karta hai aur ModelExecutor/ModelWorker ko bhejkar agle tokens generate karwata hai. Phir LLMEngine tokens ko unke prompt IDs se corresponding request thread ko route karta hai — har prompt se associated event queue (client_stream) ke through. Agar result finished hai ya token count max tokens se zyada ho gaya, to finish signal (None) queue me push karke sequence ko finished mark kiya jaata hai aur workload manager se remove kar diya jaata hai; warna token ko queue me push karke sequence ka output update kiya jaata hai.

Har web request ki handling thread me, ek event_generator incoming prompt ke liye ek event queue banata hai aur use workload manager ke saath register karta hai. Request phir is queue par tokens ka asynchronously wait kar sakti hai. API server /generate_stream endpoint expose karta hai, jo tokens ka wait karta hai aur unhe Server-Sent Events (SSE) ke through StreamingResponse (media type text/event-stream) se client ko stream karta hai. Har token data: {"token": " a", "sequence_id": "..."} format me aata hai. Core idea ye hai: har prompt ki execution ko dedicated event queue se track karo aur newly generated tokens ko unke respective channels par dispatch karo, taaki timely aur orderly delivery ensure ho.

Batch serving with vLLM: 10 lines me wahi kaam

Ab tak batching manually implement ki gayi taaki serving system ki internal mechanics expose hon. Ab dekhte hain ki production-grade framework vLLM wahi problem kaise handle karta hai. Manual implementation ko replace karne ke bajaye, ye section us par build karta hai: pehle simplified batching system khud banakar request grouping, scheduling aur concurrency control ki coordination challenges visible hui; ab dekh sakte hain ki vLLM inhi responsibilities ko kaise abstract aur optimize karta hai.

vLLM wali architecture streaming design se bahut straightforward hai — saara heavy lifting vLLM ko delegate kar diya jaata hai. LLMEngine sirf vLLM ko model ke saath initialize karta hai aur generation requests seedha use forward kar deta hai. Sampling parameters configure karo (temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, max_tokens), vllm_model.generate(prompts, sampling_params) call karo, aur outputs se generated texts extract kar lo — batch inference sirf 10 lines ke code me enable ho jaata hai. Isi liye aise serving frameworks model serving implementation me itne prevalent hain.

Lekin frameworks ko customize karna bhi zaroori hai — vLLM serving ki complexity ka zyada hissa abstract kar deta hai, lekin jab tak aap default values se OK na hon, customize karna padta hai. Isi liye under the hood kya hota hai, ye samajhna essential hai. Serving systems kaise kaam karte hain, ye jaanna aapko framework ki full potential unlock karne aur use apne system requirements, traffic patterns aur service-level objectives (SLOs/SLAs) ke hisaab se tailor karne me madad karta hai. Kai model optimization techniques seedha vLLM ke configuration options se correspond karti hain — batching latency aur throughput ko kaise affect karti hai, ye samajhkar aap max_batch_size aur max_num_seqs jaise settings ko real-time responsiveness aur batch efficiency ke beech sahi balance ke liye fine-tune kar sakte ho. Kai frameworks do tareekon se deploy ho sakte hain: library ki tarah apni custom serving application ke andar embed karke (tight integration aur execution flow par zyada control), ya standalone web server ki tarah (REST ya streaming API expose karke). Sample code me simplicity ke liye library-based approach adopt ki gayi hai, lekin real-world deployments me aksar standalone web server mode use hota hai.

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_generate_stream(async_client):
    print("Starting test_generate_stream...")
    
    prompt = "Hello, I am"
    # Create a streaming request with stream=True
    async with async_client.stream("POST", "/generate_stream", json={"prompt": prompt}) as response:
        assert response.status_code == 200
        
        # Collect all tokens
        tokens = []
        sequence_ids = set()
        
        # Process the response stream directly
        async for chunk in response.aiter_bytes():
            if chunk:
                # Convert bytes to string and split by newlines
                lines = chunk.decode().split('\n')
                for line in lines:
                    if line.startswith("data: "):
                        data = json.loads(line[6:])
                        token = data["token"]
                        print(f"Received token: {token}")  # Debug print
                        tokens.append(token)
                        sequence_ids.add(data["sequence_id"])
        
        # Verify we got some tokens
        assert len(tokens) > 0
        # Verify we got a sequence ID
        assert len(sequence_ids) == 1
        # Verify tokens form a coherent text
        generated_text = "".join(tokens)
        assert len(generated_text) > 0
        print(f"Final generated text: {prompt} {generated_text}")

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_generate_stream_concurrent(async_client):
    print("Starting test_generate_stream_concurrent...")
    
    async def make_stream_request(prompt):
        tokens = []
        async with async_client.stream("POST", "/generate_stream", json={"prompt": prompt}) as response:
            assert response.status_code == 200
            async for chunk in response.aiter_bytes():
                if chunk:
                    lines = chunk.decode().split('\n')
                    for line in lines:
                        if line.startswith("data: "):
                            data = json.loads(line[6:])
                            token = data["token"]
                            print(f"Received token for prompt '{prompt}': {token}")
                            tokens.append(token)
        return tokens

    # Create two concurrent requests
    prompt1 = "Hello, I am"
    prompt2 = "I would like to"
    
    # Run both requests concurrently
    tokens1, tokens2 = await asyncio.gather(
        make_stream_request(prompt1),
        make_stream_request(prompt2)
    )
    
    # Verify results
    assert len(tokens1) > 0, "No tokens received for first prompt"
    assert len(tokens2) > 0, "No tokens received for second prompt"
    
    # Verify tokens form coherent text
    generated_text1 = "".join(tokens1)
    generated_text2 = "".join(tokens2)
    
    print(f"Generated text 1: {generated_text1}")
    print(f"Generated text 2: {generated_text2}")
    
    assert len(generated_text1) > 0, "Empty generated text for first prompt"
    assert len(generated_text2) > 0, "Empty generated text for second prompt"
    
    # Verify the generated texts are different
    assert generated_text1 != generated_text2, "Generated texts should be different for different prompts"

03.3Chapter 3 · Model Serving System Design: A Deep Dive

Single-model serving ka general design

Sample service implement karke aur under the hood dekhkar ab aapke paas single LLM serving service ka solid foundational understanding hai. Chapter 1 me single-model services ka general design pattern introduce hua tha — lekin single-model serving ki importance ko dekhte hue, khaas taur par modern LLM serving ke context me, ab ek design dekhte hain jo specifically LLMs ke liye tailored hai.

Requirements: production-grade serving system se kya chahiye?

Kisi bhi production-grade model serving system ko ye general requirements meet karni hoti hain:

  • Low latency: system ko jaldi respond karna chahiye — model inference complete karke minimal delay ke saath results return karna, taaki user engagement bani rahe.
  • High throughput: concurrent requests ka high volume handle karna chahiye. Throughput maximize karna — queries per second (QPS) ya tokens per second (TPS) me measure hota hai — scale par serve karne, operational costs kam karne aur resource utilization improve karne ke liye essential hai.
  • Scalability: system ko fluctuating traffic ke saath horizontally scale karna chahiye — peak demand me seamlessly scale out aur quiet periods me scale in.
  • Reliability aur availability: production system highly available aur fault-tolerant hona chahiye, taaki consistent aur uninterrupted service mile.
  • Resource efficiency aur cost management: ML models — khaas taur par GPUs par LLMs — serve karna resource-intensive hai. Hardware (CPU, GPU, memory) ka efficient utilization cost per query manageable rakhne ke liye critical hai.
  • Observability: robust monitoring aur logging essential hai — latency, throughput aur error rates jaise key performance indicators (KPIs) ke saath-saath prediction confidence jaise model-specific metrics track karna. Ye visibility bottlenecks identify karne aur SLOs meet karne me madad karti hai.

LLM serving ki unique challenges

General requirements ke alawa, LLM serving kuch unique challenges introduce karta hai:

  • Large model size aur memory footprint: LLMs ko aksar tens se hundreds of gigabytes memory chahiye hoti hai, isliye GPU resources aur memory allocation ki careful management zaroori hai.
  • KV cache management: long context windows aur efficient stateful decoding support karne ke liye serving systems ko multiple requests aur sessions ke across KV caches effectively manage karne padte hain.
  • Streaming responses: interactive applications ke liye tokens ko jaise hi generate hon, client ko stream back karna important hai.
  • Concurrency aur batching with variable-length workloads: LLM requests ke input aur output lengths aksar vary karte hain. Serving systems ko in heterogeneous workloads ko intelligently batch aur schedule karna padta hai taaki high throughput aur GPU utilization bani rahe.
Yaad rakho: zyada tar traditional deep-learning model serving relatively stable hoti hai — model ko black box ki tarah treat karke latency aur scalability ke liye standard engineering solutions kaafi hote hain. Iske contrast me, LLM serving zyada dynamic aur model-aware handling maangti hai. LLM serving ki requirements frequently change karti hain jaise model architectures aur capabilities evolve hoti hain, aur aksar model-specific hoti hain. LLM input aur output lengths alag user scenarios me vary karte hain — example ke liye, KV cache behavior user input ke size aur model ke attention mechanism (jaise multi-head vs multi-query attention) par depend karke vary karta hai. Isliye LLM serving system design karte waqt evolving components ko stable infrastructure se isolate karna crucial hai — model-specific needs ke liye flexibility bhi, aur core serving logic me robustness bhi.

General design: teen areas me separation

Core design idea hai serving requirements ko teen distinct areas me group karke har ek ko separately address karna:

  • Service infrastructure management: scaling, availability, monitoring aur efficient resource allocation par focus.
  • Business logic handling: customer use-case integration, request batching aur streaming responses cover karta hai.
  • Model serving performance: serving latency, throughput aur LLM-specific performance optimizations target karta hai.

Part A — Infrastructure: model serving logic ko ek replicable unit — jaise Docker container ya Kubernetes Pod — me encapsulate kiya jaata hai, aur infrastructure-level responsibilities ek distributed compute system ko delegate kar di jaati hain. Ye system key tasks manage karta hai: traffic demand ke hisaab se service replicas ko horizontally scale up ya down karna, unhealthy instances restart karna, resources dynamically allocate karna, aur logging aur monitoring interfaces expose karna. Ye capabilities zyada tar modern compute platforms me standard features hain — public cloud providers aur open source solutions jaise Kubernetes samet. Infrastructure concerns ko serving logic se abstract karke model serving ko availability, fault tolerance aur resource provisioning jaise low-level details se decouple kar diya jaata hai. Is setup me end users individual service instances se directly interact nahi karte — requests ek load balancer se route hoti hain, jo traffic ko available instances par transparently distribute karta hai, internal scaling ki complexity chhupakar aur backend details expose kiye bina elasticity enable karke.

Part B — Serving frontend (business logic): har model serving instance ke andar ek serving frontend component hota hai jo web service interface handle karta hai aur model serving ki core business logic manage karta hai. Is layer ki responsibilities hain: customer applications se requests ko authenticate aur authorize karna; external ya internal systems se integrate karna (jaise user customer data, model metadata, audit logs, payment systems); models download aur set up karna; model configuration aur runtime context manage karna; inference requests preprocess karna (request validation, normalization aur batching logic samet); aur traffic control (rate limiting aur logging). Ye component customer-facing interfaces aur backend model inference engine ke beech middle layer ki tarah kaam karta hai — customer logic ko backend inference operations se cleanly separate karte hue, secure, flexible aur context-aware integration enable karta hai, jaise customer-facing chatbot ke liye.

Part C — Serving backend (inference): yahan actual model inference hoti hai. Ye component typically ek separate process ki tarah chalta hai jiska access sirf serving frontend ko hota hai, aur ye poori tarah high-performance model execution par focused hota hai. Serving backend wide variety ki model architectures aur optimization strategies ko understand aur support karne ke liye design hota hai. Practice me developers aksar mature, production-grade model serving frameworks par rely karte hain — jo high throughput aur low latency inference engines (LLMs ke liye tailored), advanced optimization techniques (quantization, KV cache management, variable-length sequences ki continuous batching samet), efficient GPU utilization aur ongoing evolution aur strong community support dete hain. Model execution ko is backend component me isolate karne se modular, scalable architecture milti hai jo business logic ko inference performance concerns se cleanly separate karti hai.
