04.2Chapter 4 · Model Serving Best Practices

RAG + CAG + agents serving kaise use karte hain

Agents ko external knowledge ki zaroorat kyun padti hai? Kyunki LLM powerful hote hue bhi teen badi limitations rakhta hai: uska knowledge limited aur static hota hai (training data ek cutoff date par frozen hai), woh hallucinate kar sakta hai (fluent lekin factually galat content generate karna), aur usme specialized ya up-to-date information ki kami hoti hai (domain-specific gaps). Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) inhi problems ko solve karta hai — query ke time par external knowledge retrieve karke LLM ke response ko enrich karna.

RAG: index-building workflow (offline)

RAG ke do workflows hain. Pehla index building hai — ek offline data process jo typically periodically schedule hokar chalta hai. Isme raw knowledge documents (HTML ya PDF) ko clean aur parse karke plain text banaya jaata hai, phir text ko chunks me toda jaata hai — typically lagbhag 1,000 tokens per chunk. Chunking sirf preprocessing nahi hai: ye retrieval ki granularity define karta hai (system ek baar me kitna text consider kar sakta hai) aur wahi stage hai jahan offline batch inference hota hai — poore documents ko on-demand embed karne ke bajaye, system har chunk ki embeddings bulk me precompute kar leta hai, jisse query-time retrieval bahut faster aur efficient ho jaata hai. Har chunk ko embedding model se dense vector representation me encode kiya jaata hai, aur ye chunk embeddings vector database me index hokar store ho jaati hain — online query workflow me efficient similarity search ki foundation.

Fine vs coarse chunking: chhote chunks zyada precision dete hain (retrieval narrowly relevant passages par focus karta hai) lekin aggressively split karne par context kho sakta hai. Bade chunks richer context dete hain lekin unrelated content include karke precision dilute kar sakte hain. Optimal balance application domain aur LLM ke context window par depend karta hai.

RAG: query workflow (online)

Doosra workflow query/retrieval hai — real-time online process. Jab agent ko query milti hai, to pehle query text ka embedding vector banaya jaata hai, phir database me un vectors ko search kiya jaata hai jo query vector ke sabse close hain (jaise cosine similarity se). Sabse relevant document chunks retrieve karke user query ke saath LLM ko bhej diye jaate hain, jo final answer generate karta hai. Ye basic, "naive" RAG pipeline hai — production-grade RAG systems me additional complexity hoti hai, jaise chunking, ranking, deduplication aur multisource retrieval. Aur ek basic sawaal — text ko chhote chunks me kyun todna? — ka jawab context window hai: LLM ek baar me limited tokens process kar sakta hai (input + output), isliye sirf kuch highly relevant chunks hi context ke roop me bheje jaate hain.

Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG)

RAG powerful hai, lekin uski apni challenges hain: LLM call se pehle extra steps aur latency, limited tokens me relevant documents galat select ho jaane ka risk, aur ek complicated search system build aur maintain karne ki complexity. Is beech LLMs ke context windows continuously expand ho rahe hain — ek modern model (likhte waqt) 1-million-token context window support karta hai. Itni capacity ke saath sirf handful "most relevant" documents carefully select karne ki zaroorat kam ho jaati hai — poora knowledge base ya uska bada hissa model ke working context ke andar cache kiya ja sakta hai. Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG) isi ka fayda uthata hai: relevant resources ko advance me preload karke model ke KV cache me daal diya jaata hai, aur query time par retrieval kiye bina model cached context se answers generate karta hai. Isse retrieval latency khatam hoti hai aur system complexity kam hoti hai, phir bhi LLM apne responses ko external knowledge me ground kar pata hai.

RAG me har query ek dynamic search trigger karti hai; CAG me ek baar knowledge docs cache me load ho jaayein, to queries seedha usi cached knowledge se answer hoti hain. Agent design bhi greatly simplify ho jaata hai — RAG component poora hat jaata hai, embeddings, indexes aur vector databases manage karne ki zaroorat nahi rehti. Lekin CAG apni challenges laata hai — bade context windows aur cache management se memory aur compute requirements badh jaate hain, aur CAG serving optimize karne ki techniques (Chapter 7) zaroori ho jaate hain.

RAG vs CAG — competing nahi, alag layers: RAG answer quality improve karta hai — relevant external knowledge retrieve karke prompt context expand karna. CAG serving efficiency improve karta hai — pehle se computed context reuse karke redundant KV-cache computation kam karna. Agar primary concern knowledge grounding aur freshness hai, to RAG se shuru karo; agar latency, throughput aur cost efficiency hai, to CAG introduce karo. Production LLM systems me — khaas taur par agentic workflows me — dono common hain: input enrich karne ke liye RAG, execution optimize karne ke liye CAG.

Agents model serving ko kaise use karte hain

Agents ko kai models aur tools orchestrate karne padte hain: LLMs reasoning, planning aur dialogue ke liye; embedding models retrieval aur semantic matching ke liye; vision ya speech models multimodal perception ke liye; tool-specific models code generation, classification aur summarization ke liye; aur external tools jaise APIs aur databases. Key capability hai tool calling — chaar steps: 1. LLM request aur available tools par reason karta hai; 2. structured output (aksar JSON) generate karta hai jo selected tool ke inputs encode karta hai; 3. agent tool call execute karta hai; 4. results wapas LLM me jaate hain, jo task complete hone tak iterate karta hai. Ye saare models aur tools typically model serving services (HTTP ya gRPC APIs) ke through access hote hain, isliye high-performance, low-latency aur cost-efficient serving kisi bhi agent application ki success ke liye critical hai.

import os
import logging
import numpy as np
from typing import List, Dict, Any, Tuple
from pathlib import Path
import json
from openai import OpenAI
from PyPDF2 import PdfReader
import tiktoken

from config import Config

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class RAGSystem:
    def __init__(self):
        self.config = Config()
        if not self.config.OPENAI_API_KEY:
            raise ValueError("OpenAI API key not found. Please set OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable.")
        
        self.client = OpenAI(api_key=self.config.OPENAI_API_KEY)
        self.encoding = tiktoken.encoding_for_model(self.config.LLM_MODEL)
        
        # In-memory storage for embeddings and documents
        self.documents = []
        self.embeddings = []
        self.metadata = []
        
    def load_pdfs(self, folder_path: str = None) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Load all PDF files from the knowledge folder and split into chunks."""
        if folder_path is None:
            folder_path = self.config.KNOWLEDGE_FOLDER
            
        documents = []
        pdf_files = list(Path(folder_path).glob("*.pdf"))
        
        logger.info(f"Found {len(pdf_files)} PDF files in {folder_path}")
        
        for pdf_file in pdf_files:
            try:
                logger.info(f"Processing {pdf_file.name}")
                
                # Read PDF
                reader = PdfReader(str(pdf_file))
                text_content = ""
                
                for page in reader.pages:
                    text_content += page.extract_text() + "\n"
                
                # Split into chunks
                chunks = self._split_text(text_content)
                
                for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
                    documents.append({
                        "content": chunk,
                        "source": pdf_file.name,
                        "file_path": str(pdf_file),
                        "chunk_id": i
                    })
                
                logger.info(f"Successfully processed {pdf_file.name} into {len(chunks)} chunks")
                
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error(f"Error processing {pdf_file.name}: {str(e)}")
                continue
        
        return documents
    
    def _split_text(self, text: str) -> List[str]:
        """Split text into chunks based on token count."""
        tokens = self.encoding.encode(text)
        chunks = []
        
        for i in range(0, len(tokens), self.config.CHUNK_SIZE - self.config.CHUNK_OVERLAP):
            chunk_tokens = tokens[i:i + self.config.CHUNK_SIZE]
            chunk_text = self.encoding.decode(chunk_tokens)
            if chunk_text.strip():
                chunks.append(chunk_text.strip())
        
        return chunks
    
    def get_embeddings(self, texts: List[str]) -> List[List[float]]:
        """Get embeddings for a list of texts using OpenAI."""
        try:
            response = self.client.embeddings.create(
                model=self.config.EMBEDDING_MODEL,
                input=texts
            )
            return [embedding.embedding for embedding in response.data]
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error getting embeddings: {str(e)}")
            raise
    
    def build_vector_db(self, force_rebuild: bool = False):
        """Build the vector database from PDF documents."""
        if self.documents and not force_rebuild:
            logger.info("Vector database already exists. Use force_rebuild=True to rebuild.")
            return
        
        logger.info("Building vector database...")
        
        # Load documents
        documents = self.load_pdfs()
        if not documents:
            logger.warning("No documents found to process")
            return
        
        # Get embeddings
        texts = [doc["content"] for doc in documents]
        embeddings = self.get_embeddings(texts)
        
        # Store in memory
        self.documents = documents
        self.embeddings = embeddings
        self.metadata = [{"source": doc["source"], "chunk_id": doc["chunk_id"]} for doc in documents]
        
        logger.info(f"Vector database built with {len(documents)} documents")
    
    def cosine_similarity(self, vec1: List[float], vec2: List[float]) -> float:
        """Calculate cosine similarity between two vectors."""
        vec1 = np.array(vec1)
        vec2 = np.array(vec2)
        return np.dot(vec1, vec2) / (np.linalg.norm(vec1) * np.linalg.norm(vec2))
    
    def search(self, query: str, k: int = 5) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Search the vector database for relevant documents."""
        if not self.documents:
            raise ValueError("Vector database not built. Call build_vector_db() first.")
        
        logger.info(f"Searching for query: {query}")
        
        # Get query embedding
        query_embedding = self.get_embeddings([query])[0]
        
        # Calculate similarities
        similarities = []
        for i, doc_embedding in enumerate(self.embeddings):
            similarity = self.cosine_similarity(query_embedding, doc_embedding)
            similarities.append((similarity, i))
        
        # Sort by similarity and get top k
        similarities.sort(reverse=True)
        top_k_indices = [idx for _, idx in similarities[:k]]
        
        # Format results
        results = []
        for i, idx in enumerate(top_k_indices):
            results.append({
                "content": self.documents[idx]["content"],
                "metadata": self.metadata[idx],
                "score": similarities[i][0]
            })
        
        logger.info(f"Found {len(results)} relevant documents")
        return results
    
    def get_context_for_query(self, query: str, k: int = 5) -> str:
        """Get formatted context from search results."""
        results = self.search(query, k)
        
        if not results:
            return "No relevant information found."
        
        context_parts = []
        for i, result in enumerate(results, 1):
            content = result["content"]
            source = result["metadata"]["source"]
            context_parts.append(f"Document {i} (Source: {source}):\n{content}\n")
        
        return "\n".join(context_parts)
    
    # def save_vector_db(self, filepath: str = "vector_db.json"):
    #     """Save vector database to file."""
    #     if not self.documents:
    #         logger.warning("No vector database to save")
    #         return
        
    #     data = {
    #         "documents": self.documents,
    #         "embeddings": self.embeddings,
    #         "metadata": self.metadata
    #     }
        
    #     with open(filepath, 'w') as f:
    #         json.dump(data, f, indent=2)
        
    #     logger.info(f"Vector database saved to {filepath}")
    
    # def load_vector_db(self, filepath: str = "vector_db.json"):
    #     """Load vector database from file."""
    #     if not os.path.exists(filepath):
    #         logger.warning(f"Vector database file {filepath} not found")
    #         return
        
    #     with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
    #         data = json.load(f)
        
    #     self.documents = data["documents"]
    #     self.embeddings = data["embeddings"]

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Simple test cases for the RAG System

This module contains basic tests for the RAG system functionality
using real OpenAI API calls and actual PDF files from knowledge_files folder.
"""

import unittest
import os
from pathlib import Path
from dotenv import load_dotenv

# Load environment variables
load_dotenv(override=True)

# Import the RAG system
from rag_system import RAGSystem
from config import Config


class TestRAGSystemReal(unittest.TestCase):
    """Real test cases for RAGSystem class using actual OpenAI API and PDF files."""
    
    def setUp(self):
        """Set up test fixtures."""
        # Check if OpenAI API key is available
        if not os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'):
            self.skipTest("OpenAI API key not found in environment. Please set OPENAI_API_KEY in .env file.")
        
        # Check if knowledge_files folder exists
        self.knowledge_folder = Path("./knowledge_files")
        if not self.knowledge_folder.exists():
            self.skipTest("knowledge_files folder not found. Please ensure PDF files are in the knowledge_files folder.")
        
        # Initialize RAG system
        try:
            self.rag_system = RAGSystem()
            print("✅ RAG system initialized successfully")
        except Exception as e:
            self.skipTest(f"Failed to initialize RAG system: {e}")
    
    def test_config_loading(self):
        """Test that configuration loads correctly."""
        config = Config()
        
        # Test that required config values exist
        self.assertIsNotNone(config.LLM_MODEL)
        self.assertIsNotNone(config.EMBEDDING_MODEL)
        self.assertIsNotNone(config.KNOWLEDGE_FOLDER)
        self.assertIsNotNone(config.CHUNK_SIZE)
        self.assertIsNotNone(config.CHUNK_OVERLAP)
        
        print(f"✅ Config loaded: LLM={config.LLM_MODEL}, Embedding={config.EMBEDDING_MODEL}")
        print(f"✅ Knowledge folder: {config.KNOWLEDGE_FOLDER}")
        print(f"✅ Chunk size: {config.CHUNK_SIZE}, Overlap: {config.CHUNK_OVERLAP}")
    
    def test_pdf_files_exist(self):
        """Test that PDF files exist in the knowledge_files folder."""
        pdf_files = list(self.knowledge_folder.glob("*.pdf"))
        pdf_files.extend(self.knowledge_folder.glob("*.PDF"))
        
        self.assertGreater(len(pdf_files), 0, "No PDF files found in knowledge_files folder")
        
        print(f"✅ Found {len(pdf_files)} PDF files:")
        for pdf_file in pdf_files:
            print(f"   📄 {pdf_file.name}")
    
    def test_cosine_similarity_calculation(self):
        """Test cosine similarity calculation."""
        # Test identical vectors
        vec1 = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
        vec2 = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
        similarity = self.rag_system.cosine_similarity(vec1, vec2)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(similarity, 1.0, places=5)
        
        # Test orthogonal vectors
        vec3 = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]
        similarity_orthogonal = self.rag_system.cosine_similarity(vec1, vec3)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(similarity_orthogonal, 0.0, places=5)
        
        # Test opposite vectors
        vec4 = [-1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
        similarity_opposite = self.rag_system.cosine_similarity(vec1, vec4)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(similarity_opposite, -1.0, places=5)
        
        print("✅ Cosine similarity calculations work correctly")
    
    def test_text_splitting(self):
        """Test text splitting functionality."""
        test_text = "This is a test document with multiple sentences. It should be split into chunks based on token count."
        
        # Test the actual text splitting method
        chunks = self.rag_system._split_text(test_text)
        
        # Verify chunks were created
        self.assertIsInstance(chunks, list)
        self.assertGreater(len(chunks), 0)
        
        print(f"✅ Text splitting created {len(chunks)} chunks")
        for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
            print(f"   Chunk {i+1}: {chunk[:50]}...")
    
    def test_embedding_generation(self):
        """Test embedding generation with real OpenAI API."""
        test_texts = ["This is a test document about artificial intelligence."]
        
        try:
            embeddings = self.rag_system.get_embeddings(test_texts)
            
            # Verify embeddings were generated
            self.assertIsInstance(embeddings, list)
            self.assertEqual(len(embeddings), 1)
            self.assertIsInstance(embeddings[0], list)
            self.assertGreater(len(embeddings[0]), 0)
            
            print(f"✅ Generated embeddings with {len(embeddings[0])} dimensions")
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.fail(f"Failed to generate embeddings: {e}")
    
    def test_pdf_loading(self):
        """Test loading PDF files from knowledge_files folder."""
        try:
            documents = self.rag_system.load_pdfs()
            
            # Verify documents were loaded
            self.assertGreater(len(documents), 0)
            
            # Verify document structure
            for doc in documents:
                self.assertIn('content', doc)
                self.assertIn('source', doc)
                self.assertIn('file_path', doc)
                self.assertIn('chunk_id', doc)
                self.assertIsInstance(doc['content'], str)
                self.assertIsInstance(doc['source'], str)
                self.assertIsInstance(doc['chunk_id'], int)
            
            print(f"✅ Loaded {len(documents)} document chunks")
            for doc in documents[:3]:  # Show first 3 documents
                print(f"   📄 {doc['source']} (chunk {doc['chunk_id']}): {doc['content'][:50]}...")
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.fail(f"Failed to load PDF files: {e}")
    
    def test_vector_database_building(self):
        """Test building the vector database."""
        try:
            # Build vector database
            self.rag_system.build_vector_db()
            
            # Verify vector database was built
            self.assertGreater(len(self.rag_system.documents), 0)
            self.assertGreater(len(self.rag_system.embeddings), 0)
            self.assertGreater(len(self.rag_system.metadata), 0)
            
            # Verify consistency
            self.assertEqual(len(self.rag_system.documents), len(self.rag_system.embeddings))
            self.assertEqual(len(self.rag_system.documents), len(self.rag_system.metadata))
            
            print(f"✅ Vector database built with {len(self.rag_system.documents)} documents")
            print(f"✅ Generated {len(self.rag_system.embeddings)} embeddings")
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.fail(f"Failed to build vector database: {e}")
    
    def test_search_functionality(self):
        """Test search functionality with real data."""
        # First build the vector database
        self.rag_system.build_vector_db()
        
        # Test search queries
        test_queries = [
            "artificial intelligence",
            "machine learning", 
            "database queries",
            "5-level paging"
        ]
        
        for query in test_queries:
            try:
                results = self.rag_system.search(query, k=3)
                
                # Verify search results
                self.assertIsInstance(results, list)
                self.assertGreater(len(results), 0)
                
                # Verify result structure
                for result in results:
                    self.assertIn('content', result)
                    self.assertIn('metadata', result)
                    self.assertIn('score', result)
                    self.assertIn('source', result['metadata'])
                    self.assertIn('chunk_id', result['metadata'])
                    self.assertIsInstance(result['score'], (int, float))
                
                print(f"✅ Search for '{query}' returned {len(results)} results (top score: {results[0]['score']:.4f})")
                
            except Exception as e:
                self.fail(f"Search failed for query '{query}': {e}")
    
    def test_context_generation(self):
        """Test context generation for queries."""
        # First build the vector database
        self.rag_system.build_vector_db()
        
        test_queries = [
            "What is artificial intelligence?",
            "Explain machine learning concepts",
            "How do database queries work?"
        ]
        
        for query in test_queries:
            try:
                context = self.rag_system.get_context_for_query(query, k=2)
                
                # Verify context
                self.assertIsInstance(context, str)
                self.assertGreater(len(context), 0)
                self.assertIn("Document", context)
                self.assertIn("Source:", context)
                
                print(f"✅ Generated context for '{query[:30]}...' ({len(context)} characters)")
                
            except Exception as e:
                self.fail(f"Context generation failed for query '{query}': {e}")
    
    def test_full_workflow(self):
        """Test the complete RAG workflow end-to-end."""
        try:
            # 1. Load PDFs
            documents = self.rag_system.load_pdfs()
            self.assertGreater(len(documents), 0)
            print(f"✅ Step 1: Loaded {len(documents)} document chunks")
            
            # 2. Build vector database
            self.rag_system.build_vector_db()
            self.assertGreater(len(self.rag_system.documents), 0)
            print(f"✅ Step 2: Built vector database with {len(self.rag_system.documents)} documents")
            
            # 3. Search
            results = self.rag_system.search("artificial intelligence", k=3)
            self.assertGreater(len(results), 0)
            print(f"✅ Step 3: Search returned {len(results)} results")
            
            # 4. Generate context
            context = self.rag_system.get_context_for_query("machine learning")
            self.assertGreater(len(context), 0)
            print(f"✅ Step 4: Generated context ({len(context)} characters)")
            
            print("✅ Full RAG workflow completed successfully!")
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.fail(f"Full workflow failed: {e}")
    
    def test_error_handling(self):
        """Test error handling for edge cases."""
        # Test search without building vector database
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError) as context:
            self.rag_system.search("test query")
        
        self.assertIn("Vector database not built", str(context.exception))
        print("✅ Correctly handles search without vector database")
        
        # Test context generation with no results
        self.rag_system.documents = []
        self.rag_system.embeddings = []
        self.rag_system.metadata = []
        
        context = self.rag_system.get_context_for_query("test query")
        self.assertEqual(context, "No relevant information found.")
        print("✅ Correctly handles context generation with no data")


def run_real_rag_tests():
    """Run real RAG system tests."""
    print("🧪 Running Real RAG System Tests")
    print("=" * 50)
    print("📝 Note: These tests use real OpenAI API calls and require:")
    print("   1. OpenAI API key in .env file")
    print("   2. PDF files in knowledge_files folder")
    print("   3. Internet connection for API calls")
    print("=" * 50)
    
    # Create test suite
    test_suite = unittest.TestSuite()
    
    # Add test cases
    test_suite.addTest(unittest.makeSuite(TestRAGSystemReal))
    
    # Run tests
    runner = unittest.TextTestRunner(verbosity=2)
    result = runner.run(test_suite)
    
    # Print summary
    print(f"\n📊 Test Results: {result.testsRun} tests run")
    print(f"✅ Passed: {result.testsRun - len(result.failures) - len(result.errors)}")
    print(f"❌ Failed: {len(result.failures)}")
    print(f"⚠️  Errors: {len(result.errors)}")
    print(f"⏭️  Skipped: {len(result.skipped) if hasattr(result, 'skipped') else 0}")
    
    if result.failures:
        print("\n❌ Failures:")
        for test, traceback in result.failures:
            print(f"  - {test}: {traceback}")
    
    if result.errors:
        print("\n⚠️  Errors:")
        for test, traceback in result.errors:
            print(f"  - {test}: {traceback}")
    
    return result.wasSuccessful()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    success = run_real_rag_tests()
    exit(0 if success else 1)

04.3Chapter 4 · Model Serving Best Practices

Enterprise LLM serving: layered architecture

Pehle ke chapters ke simplified serving examples se aage badho, to real-world deployment me sirf model host aur execute karna kaafi nahi hota. Scale par providers ko authentication, pricing, resource management, networking, optimization, experimentation, observability aur on-call support jaise requirements bhi address karne padte hain. In business aur operational demands ko meet karne ke liye hundreds ya even thousands of engineers ki multidisciplinary teams chahiye hoti hain. Aisi system architect karna challenging hai: serving platform ko kai teams — har ek ki alag responsibilities — ko ek hi evolving system me contribute karne dena hai, bina bottlenecks ya excessive interdependencies ke, aur fast iteration ko stability ke saath balance karna hai — cost, reliability aur user experience ki constraints ke andar.

Book ek abstract layered architecture present karta hai jo bade providers aur large enterprises ne cloud scale par LLMs deploy karte waqt adopt ki hai. Layered pattern ka fayda ye hai ki har layer ki concerns alag hain — API, orchestration, inference, optimization — aur har layer ki teams independently innovate aur optimize kar sakti hain, phir bhi ek cohesive serving platform me contribute karti hain. Aage field me naye models aur technologies aayenge aur system design badlega, lekin concerns ko separate karne ka ye pattern essential rahega. Layers ko upar se neeche dekhte hain.

1. Public API Layer

Ye primary external interface hai jisse customers, developers aur internal services LLM system se interact karte hain. Ye networking, authentication, pricing, rate limiting aur request routing manage karta hai. Key challenges: high concurrency — millions of simultaneous client connections support karni hain; fair usage aur monetization — quotas enforce karna, abuse rokna aur accurate billing support karna; low-latency global access — geo-routing aur regional caching se nearest region se requests serve karna; aur security — authentication, tenant isolation aur network attacks se protection.

2. Resource Management Layer

Ye layer infrastructure hardware resources (CPU, GPU, memory, disk, networking) manage karti hai jo models, use cases aur customer workloads ko regions ke across serve karne ke liye chahiye hote hain. Budget reviews aur cost allocation bhi aksar yahin integrate hote hain. Challenges: capacity planning — demand forecast karna, bina costly overprovisioning ke; GPU utilization — datacenters ke across heterogeneous GPU pools manage karna aur high utilization maintain karna; aur customer prioritization — critical workloads ke liye quotas aur reservations enforce karna, jabki lower-priority tasks ke liye preemptible scheduling enable karna.

3. Model Selection and Orchestration Layer

Ye layer har request ke liye kaunsa model use hoga, ye decide karti hai — accuracy, latency aur cost ko balance karke. Sirf ek model select karne se aage, ye layer multiple models ko tandem me orchestrate bhi kar sakti hai — jaise speculative decoding apply karna ya model families ke beech routing karna. Speculative decoding me ek chhota "draft" model kai tokens ahead predict karta hai, aur bada "target" model unhe parallel me verify karta hai; draft sahi ho to tokens accept hote hain, warna corrections apply hote hain — isse token-by-token latency kam hoti hai bina quality degrade kiye (detail Chapter 7 me). Challenges: cost–quality trade-offs — har task ko sabse bada model nahi chahiye; aksar default chhota model hota hai aur user explicitly stronger model maangta hai, aur triage ke liye layer ko query samajhni padti hai; load balancing — traffic ko model pools ke across distribute karke bottlenecks rokna; aur latency-sensitive use cases — chhote ya faster models ya speculative decoding jaise optimizations use karna.

4. Distributed Serving Layer

Ye layer LLM model execution ke liye distributed infrastructure set up karti hai — do groups me: distributed model hosting bade models ke liye, aur distributed caching (jaise KV caching, prompt caching, semantic caching) unnecessary computation kam karne ke liye. Challenges: hardware limitations — LLM sizes aksar single-GPU memory se exceed kar jaate hain; multi-GPU aur multi-node coordination — distributed models ko request ka context efficiently share karna padta hai taaki serving SLA maintain rahe; aur caching for efficiency — cache content ke basis par traffic route karna (jaise KV cache-aware routing) aur repeated ya similar inputs ke liye redundant inference kam karna.

5. Core Inference Layer

Yahan models actually execute hote hain. Ye model serving frameworks (jaise vLLM, Triton, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang) ko optimized kernels (FlashAttention, GEMM, PagedAttention) ke saath integrate karke web endpoints ke roop me expose karta hai. Is layer ko Chapter 3 me detail me explore kiya gaya tha.

6. Model Optimization Layer aur 7. Model Layer

Model Optimization Layer har tarah ki model optimization techniques apply karne par focus karta hai — model ki performance aur efficiency improve karna, bina scratch se retrain kiye. In techniques aur unke trade-offs ko Chapters 5, 6, 7 aur 9 me detail me discuss kiya gaya hai. Sabse neeche Model Layer actual trained models provide karta hai: models ko internal training pipelines ya external sources se production me laana, unhe capability (voice, reasoning, video) aur purpose (sandbox, experimentation, production) ke hisaab se organize karna, aur models evolve hote hain to unki tracking aur versioning handle karna.

Yaad rakho: Layered architecture ka point ye nahi ki har company ko saari layers khud banani hain — point ye hai ki concerns separated hon. API team API par, inference team kernels par, optimization team compression par independently kaam kar sake, aur phir bhi system ek cohesive platform ki tarah chale.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 4 — Model Serving Best Practices

04.4Chapter 4 · Model Serving Best Practices

Open source stack se build karna

Enterprise architecture samajh liya — ab use implement kaise karein? Book ek open source stack se poora serving system banane ka practical example deta hai. Goal ek hi solution prescribe karna nahi hai, balki practical design choices illustrate karna aur apna serving platform banane ke liye ek starting point dena hai. Poora design Kubernetes ke upar banta hai — containerized applications ki deployment, scaling aur management automate karne ka open source platform. Kubernetes ke upar ek bada open source ecosystem hai jo metrics, logging, networking, authorization aur hardware management jaise functions cover karta hai — isiliye ye widely adopted hai aur bade cloud providers aur foundation model vendors ki backbone hai. Is design me Kubernetes resource management, networking, traffic routing aur load balancing, service hosting aur scaling, aur service metrics aur monitoring sambhalta hai.

Public API implement karna: FastAPI + Kubernetes

Public API example ke liye FastAPI aur Kubernetes use kiye gaye hain — web API, quota limits, auth aur tenant management implement karne ke liye. Sample web service enterprise-model-api ek chat API (/v1/chat/completions) expose karta hai, aur FastAPI ke dependency injection (Depends) se authorization logic attach ki jaati hai: endpoint pehle require_auth chalata hai, phir tenant ke liye rate limit lagata hai, aur phir model select karke traffic route karta hai. Auth ke liye JWT token ya API key dono options hain — agar dono missing hon to 401 error, aur tenant na mile to 403. Is process me customer metadata bhi retrieve hoti hai, jo downstream steps — quota enforcement, traffic routing, model selection — ke liye essential hai.

Autoscaling ke liye Kubernetes ka HorizontalPodAutoscaler use hota hai: agar service ki average CPU usage 70% se zyada ho jaaye, to Kubernetes 3 se 15 instances tak scale kar deta hai. Rate limiting ke liye Nginx ya Envoy ingress proxies ke roop me sabse common approaches hain — Nginx example me traffic 50 requests per second tak limit hoti hai, burst multiplier 5 aur proxy body size 8 MB ke saath. Dono hi Kubernetes ke saath configuration se seamlessly integrate hote hain — yehi Kubernetes ki strength aur flexibility hai.

Model selection implement karna

Model selection logic public API me, ek separate middleware service me, ya ek static routing config me implement ho sakti hai. Simplified example me ye logic chat endpoint ke andar hi hai: incoming request ke token size ke basis par system ya to request ko directly selected model backend ko forward karta hai, ya speculative decoding use karta hai — jahan ek faster, cheaper model multiple future tokens generate karta hai aur slower lekin zyada accurate model unhe bulk me verify karta hai, jisse redundant step-by-step generation avoid hoti hai aur significant latency improvement milta hai (detail Chapter 7 me). Example rule: agar draft enabled hai aur max_new_tokens > 1024 hai, to speculation use karo, warna simple pass-through stream.

Endpoint-selection logic pehle general preferences apply karti hai — region, cost, load balancing — phir tenant-specific requirements layer karti hai: route config se model ya alias resolve karo, unknown model ho to 404; weighted canary ho to uske weight ki probability se canary URL return karo; tenant override ho to us tenant ke liye specific URL return karo; warna default URL. Speculative decoding ke bhi multiple variations hote hain, jaise per-model adaptive speculative decoding aur multi-draft decoding — sabka foundational idea ek hi hai (chhota, faster model latency kam karta hai), lekin optimization goals ke hisaab se unhe architecture ki alag layers par implement kiya ja sakta hai.

Model serving endpoint: Ray Serve se single aur multi-model hosting

Model hosting layer par single-model aur multi-model serving aati hai — vLLM, NVIDIA Triton, Kubernetes aur FastAPI jaise tools se banayi ja sakti hai. Agar serving instances ki scalability aur networking manage karna heavy lage, to Ray Serve use kar sakte hain — ek scalable, framework-agnostic model serving library jo online inference APIs banane ke liye hai. Single-model example me ek Python class QwenVLLM vLLM ka AsyncLLMEngine initialize karti hai (model Qwen3, tensor parallel size 1, max_num_batched_tokens=4096, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9), phir __call__ JSON body se text, max_new_tokens aur temperature lekar streaming generation chalata hai. @serve.deployment decorator se Ray ko bataya jaata hai ki model ko 3 replicas me serve karo, har replica ko 1 dedicated GPU (aur 0.5 CPU) dekar — deployment par Ray automatically compute resources provision karke service deploy kar deta hai.

Multi-model hosting ke liye Ray Serve model multiplexing deta hai: similar input types wale models ka group shared replicas ke pool se serve hota hai. serve.multiplexed aur serve.get_multiplexed_model_id APIs se single-model service multi-model me extend hoti hai. Farq ye hai: single-model me model __init__ me preload hota hai, multi-model me har request par requested model real time me load hota hai — iska drawback har request par load karne ki latency hai, jise @serve.multiplexed(max_num_models_per_replica=2) se mitigate karte hain (caching + memory constrained hone par LRU eviction se model swapping). Request me ray_serve_multiplexed_model_id header se bataya jaata hai kaunsa model call karna hai — routing aur load balancing Ray backend sambhalta hai.

Yaad rakho: Apna serving stack banana utna mushkil nahi jitna lagta hai — Kubernetes infrastructure ke liye, Ray Serve ya Triton model hosting ke liye, aur vLLM distributed LLM serving aur kernel-level acceleration aur caching jaise optimizations ke liye, saare components production me battle-tested hain. Ek lightweight custom middleware microservice ke saath poora enterprise-grade solution khud assemble karna possible hai.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 4 — Model Serving Best Practices

04.5Chapter 4 · Model Serving Best Practices

Cloud vendor: 6 options + compare, build vs buy

Cloud par model serve karne ke options itne saare hain ki choose karna overwhelming lag sakta hai. Book AWS SageMaker ko example lekar chhe options samjhata hai — fully managed end se lekar sabse customizable end tak. Goal SageMaker step-by-step sikhana nahi hai, balki cloud vendors ke serving options ke peeche ki fundamental logic samjhana hai. Ye options AWS-specific hain, lekin unki functionality general hai — doosre cloud vendors me corresponding components mil jaate hain.

Option 1: Fully Managed Foundation-Model Serving (Bedrock)

Amazon Bedrock foundation models ko simple API se serve karne ki fully managed service hai — chhe options me sabse kam customizable, lekin sabse easy. Aap model train ya host nahi karte — Bedrock ke support kiye hue models me se select karke API calls se predictions lete hain. Price model pay-as-you-go hai (per request ya per output token, per hour nahi), aur AWS scaling aur computing resources internally manage karta hai — zero DevOps overhead. Trade-off: AWS ke diye hue models aur configurations tak limited hain — architecture ya training change nahi kar sakte, sirf moderate fine-tuning ya prompt customization. Use karna teen steps hai: API key banao, catalog se model select karo, client initialize karke API call karo. Limitations: instance type ya container customize nahi kar sakte, aur proprietary ya fine-tuned model jo provided nahi hai, use Bedrock se serve nahi kar sakte. Best hai quick prototype ke liye, jab koi infrastructure manage nahi karna.

Option 2: One-Click Foundation-Model Deployment (JumpStart)

SageMaker JumpStart bhi no-code/low-code hosting hai — pretrained models ka hub (Cohere, Falcon, Llama, Stable Diffusion aur Hugging Face Hub ke models). Bedrock se bada farq: JumpStart models ko aapke apne SageMaker infrastructure par minimal coding se deploy kar deta hai — aksar "one-click deployment" kaha jaata hai. Aap apne account me endpoint host karte hain, to hourly pay karte hain — thoda zyada infrastructure management, lekin server instance types (jaise g5.48xlarge, g6e.48xlarge), instance count aur logging levels configure kar sakte hain. Limitations: customization limited hai — har model fine-tuning support nahi karta, instance choices per model constrained hain, default inference behavior (preprocessing, batching) aur payload schemas customize nahi kar sakte, CUDA/PyTorch version choose nahi kar sakte, aur context length aur batch size JumpStart configure karta hai. Best hai popular pretrained model ko apne AWS environment me jaldi upar laane ke liye.

Option 3: Bring Your Own Model (DLCs)

SageMaker prebuilt serving Docker images — Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) deta hai, jinse bina custom inference code likhe models deploy kar sakte hain (TensorFlow, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, DJL container). Ye "bring-your-own-model" hai, "bring-your-own-code" nahi: trained model artifact serve kar sakte hain, bina serving code ki chinta kiye — DLC ko pata hai us model type ko kaise handle karna hai. JumpStart se farq: yahan aap explicitly choose karte hain kaunsa container use karna hai — isse flexibility milti hai, jaise PyTorch ka exact version specify karna ya aisa model deploy karna jo JumpStart list me nahi hai. Example: PyTorch model ke liye TorchServe DLC search karke S3 model file ke saath model.deploy se endpoint deploy karna; ya Hugging Face se Llama ko Large Model Inference (LMI) containers (DJL + vLLM) se serve karna. Limitations: container internals par control kam hai — frameworks, drivers, CUDA, Python aur OS image tag se pinned hote hain; SageMaker fixed port aur HTTP contract enforce karta hai (port 8080, /invocations POST aur /ping GET, default response timeout jaise 60 seconds); custom preprocessing/postprocessing chahiye to Option 4 chahiye. Best hai jab common framework se trained model hai aur jaldi deploy karna hai, thode customized choices ke saath.

Option 4: Bring Your Own Code (Script Mode)

Customization ladder par agla step hai apna serving code likhna — SageMaker me Script Mode. Aap abhi bhi SageMaker-provided container par rely karte hain, lekin ek entry-point script supply karte hain jo model loading aur prediction ki logic implement karta hai — custom preprocessing/postprocessing, nonstandard input/output formats, aur ek hi container me multiple models. Trade-off: ab code likhna aur maintain karna padta hai. Example: LMI container se LLM host karna — serving.properties me serving engine aur model location define karo, model.py me initialize (model load), run_inference aur handle (execution entry point, empty call par warmup) implement karo, phir code aur weights ko tar karke S3 par upload karo aur deploy karo. Limitations: vendor container se jo inherit karte hain, usi tak limited hain — baked-in frameworks aur versions, aur HTTP interface ya request schema change nahi kar sakte. Best hai jab prebuilt containers ki limitations bottleneck ban jaayein aur per-model serving logic override karni ho bina container scratch se banaye.

Option 5: Bring Your Own Serving Image aur Option 6: Build Your Own Serving Infrastructure

Option 5 sabse zyada customized hai: apna Docker container SageMaker ko laana. SageMaker container ko instances par deploy manage karega aur endpoint URL dega, lekin container ke andar sab kuch aapka hai — koi bhi language, framework, custom inference code, system dependencies. SageMaker container ko black box treat karta hai jo simple contract follow karta hai (HTTP requests andar, responses certain ports/paths par bahar). Drawback: complexity — container khud build, maintain aur update karna, requirements comply karna, aur testing/debugging zyada involved (Dockerfile, ECR push, verbose API calls). Best hai jab provided containers ki constraints bahut limiting ho jaayein. Option 6 me poora platform khud cloud infrastructure par banate hain — jaise cloud-managed Kubernetes par custom serving images, runtime choose karna (Triton, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, KServe, Ray Serve), aur traffic management, autoscaling, security, observability aur cost controls ki ownership lena — saath me AWS primitives (EKS, ALB/NLB, ECR, S3, CloudWatch) aur add-ons (Prometheus/Grafana, Argo CD) use karte hue. Use karo jab runtime ka full control, aggressive cost/performance tuning (spot GPU, MIG/MPS, bin-packing), strict compliance/data isolation, ya cutting-edge hardware aur specialized optimizations chahiye hon.

Options compare karna aur Build vs Buy

Koi one-size-fits-all solution nahi hai. Evaluate karte waqt ease of use vs control ke trade-off se shuru karo, phir cost aur performance se dekho. Decision tree ease of use se shuru hota hai — kitna kam development work aur customization chahiye; jitni zyada managed services leverage karoge, utni jaldi model upar aayega. Lekin development speed sirf ek factor hai — operational aur maintenance costs equally important hain. Kai teams simplest option se idea validate karke shuru karti hain, phir requirements badhne par zyada customized solutions ki taraf shift hoti hain. Book ka cost example: shuru me model Bedrock par $0.10 per input million tokens par chalao; usage badhne par option 2 ya 3 par apne account me host karo, $1.172 per hour server instances ke liye; phir higher throughput aur lower latency chahiye to options 4, 5 ya 6 par jao.

Build vs buy binary nahi hai — ye spectrum hai, switch nahi. Build karna seekhne ka fayda: vendor ke managed options evaluate kar sakte hain, hidden trade-offs spot kar sakte hain, aur kisi bhi moment decide kar sakte hain kitna customize karna hai. Practice me most teams beech me operate karti hain: vendor platforms par chalte hue targeted customizations add karte hain (custom handlers, autoscaling signals, routing logic, cost controls). Full "build your own" usually tab reserve hota hai jab control, large-scale cost efficiency ya strict compliance zaroori ho — jaise vendor lock-in avoid karna. Aur build karna jaanna tab bhi kaam aata hai jab aap build nahi kar rahe: vendor features decode kar sakte hain (kaunsa knob batching, caching, quantization se map hota hai), trade-offs quantify kar sakte hain, 80% paths par vendor defaults rakhkar 20% surgically replace kar sakte hain, aur debugging jaldi kar sakte hain — vendor solutions aksar black boxes ki tarah kaam karte hain, limited documentation aur incomplete logs ke saath.

Selection strategy: vendor managed raho agar SLOs (prediction latency aur throughput) meet ho rahe hon, costs acceptable hon aur feature velocity aur timelines sabse important hon. Hybridize karo jab kuch model endpoints ko special batching, routing ya performance tuning ya per-tenant isolation chahiye. BYO jao jab hardware, runtime ya sovereign networking par control chahiye ya serving cost deep tuning maangta ho. Aur vendor-managed par wapas jao agar volume low rate par stabilize ho jaaye ya system ki complexity pay off na kar rahi ho. Winning strategy dynamic hai: stable API aur shared telemetry rakho, jahan pay off ho wahan customize karo, aur expect karo ki product, traffic aur constraints ke saath aapki position spectrum par badalti rahegi.
Poora code dekho — AWS par serving: Bedrock, DLC, JumpStart (Ch 4)

import boto3
import os

# Set the API key as an environment variable
os.environ['AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK'] = ".. .. .."

# Create the Bedrock client
client = boto3.client(
    service_name="bedrock-runtime",
    region_name="us-west-2"
)

# Define the model and message
model_id = "us.anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620-v1:0"
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Hello! Can you tell me about Amazon Bedrock?"}]}]

# Make the API call
response = client.converse(
    modelId=model_id,
    messages=messages,
)

# Print the response
print(response['output']['message']['content'][0]['text'])

# implement your own model inference logic in model.py file.

%%writefile my-own-llm/model.py
import os
import logging
from djl_python import Input, Output
# ...

PAD_TOKEN_ID = 50256

# initialize model
def initialize(properties):

    model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_id)
    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
    model.to(device)
    model.eval()

model = None
tokenizer = None

# execute model
def run_inference(input_texts, onnx_model, tokenizer):

    max_batch_size = 128
    z = torch.empty([0,768]).to("cuda")
    for i in range(0, len(input_texts), max_batch_size):
        logging.info(f"Start Iteration: {i}")

        start_time = time.time()
        batch_dict = tokenizer(input_texts[i:i+max_batch_size], max_length=512, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors='pt').to("cuda")
        logging.info(f"After Tokenize Latency: {time.time() - start_time}")

        start_time = time.time()
        with torch.no_grad():
            outputs = model(**batch_dict)
        logging.info(f"After Model Inference Latency: {time.time() - start_time}")

        # ... ..

        z = torch.cat((embeddings,z), 0)
        del outputs
        del embeddings
        del batch_dict

    results = [{"embedding": embedding.tolist(), "index": idx} for idx, embedding in enumerate(z)]
    # logging.info(f'Output embeddings: {results}')
    del z
    # return dictonary, which will be json serializable
    return {"embeddings": results}

def average_pool(last_hidden_states: Tensor,
                 attention_mask: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    last_hidden = last_hidden_states.masked_fill(~attention_mask[..., None].bool(), 0.0)
    return last_hidden.sum(dim=1) / attention_mask.sum(dim=1)[..., None]

# model execution entry point
def handle(inputs: Input) -> None:
    logging.info("handle : Handle start...")
    global model, tokenizer
    if not model:
        logging.info("handle : initializing model")
        model,tokenizer = initialize(inputs.get_properties())

    if inputs.is_empty():
        logging.info("handle : inputs is empty")
        # Model server makes an empty call to warmup the model on startup
        return None

    logging.info("handle : Pre-processing start")
    data = inputs.get_as_json()
    logging.info(f"handle : Pre-processing json data {data}")
    input_sentences = data["inputs"]
    logging.info(f"handle : Pre-processing sentences {input_sentences}")
    res = run_inference(input_sentences, model, tokenizer)

    logging.info("handle : Handle End")
    return Output().add_as_json(res)

# package model file
%%sh
tar czvf my-own-llm.tar.gz my-own-llm/

# upload model file to S3

s3_code_prefix = "large-model-lmi/code/my-own-llm" # increment the version
bucket = sess.default_bucket()  # bucket to house artifacts
code_artifact = sess.upload_data("my-own-llm.tar.gz", bucket, s3_code_prefix)

# find the DJL model serving container
image_uri = image_uris.retrieve(
    framework="djl-deepspeed", region=sess.boto_session.region_name, version="0.25.0"
)

# create model object
model = Model(image_uri=image_uri, model_data=code_artifact, role=role)

# deployment model
predictor = model.deploy(initial_instance_count=1,
             instance_type="ml.g5.2xlarge",
             endpoint_name="my-own-llm-128")

04.6Chapter 4 · Model Serving Best Practices

Performance measure karna: latency + throughput

Agentic workflows, layered enterprise architectures aur build-vs-cloud decisions — ye saare design choices aakhir me measurable outcomes se evaluate hote hain. Production systems me architectural elegance kaafi nahi hai — performance feasibility, user experience aur cost-to-serve decide karta hai. Isiliye performance metrics afterthought nahi hain, balki guiding principle hain: agentic systems multistep reasoning chains ke across latency amplify karte hain, enterprise platforms ko scalability aur cost efficiency balance karni hoti hai, aur build-vs-cloud decisions aksar is par depend karte hain ki system SLOs ko budget ke andar meet kar sakta hai ya nahi. Book do critical metrics introduce karta hai jin par production me consistently rely kiya gaya hai: latency (responses process aur generate karne me laga time) aur throughput (per unit time me kitne requests ya tokens process hue).

Latency metrics: E2E, TTFT, ITL/TPOT

LLM prediction execution ki speed measure karne ke liye teen sabse important metrics hain. End-to-end (E2E) latency — model ko request milne se lekar full response generate complete hone tak ka total time. Isme overall serving latency bhi include ho sakti hai — sirf model execution time nahi, balki model serving system me additional delays bhi: request queuing (bade load par), network delays, routing time, scaling overhead aur doosre system-level factors. Time to first token (TTFT) — request milne se lekar pehla token emit hone tak ka time. Chatbot jaise use cases me user ke perspective se ye model ki responsiveness hai — customer ko pehla output token kitni jaldi dikhta hai. Ye Chapter 2 ke prefill phase se correspond karta hai, jahan model input prompt process karta hai, poore context par attend karta hai, use samajhta hai aur output generate karne ki taiyaari karta hai. Inter-token latency (ITL) ya time per output token (TPOT) — pehle token ke baad ke saare subsequent tokens generate karne me laga time. Ye decode phase se correspond karta hai, jahan model tokens ko sequentially generate karta hai, typically relatively steady rate par — autoregressive token generation ki efficiency samajhne ke liye crucial metric hai. Tokenization aur detokenization ka time bhi is picture me aata hai, lekin practice me ye model inference time ke comparison me minimal hota hai aur aksar TTFT aur ITL calculations se ignore kar diya jaata hai.

Formulas — maan lo ITL consistent hai, LLM se generate hue total tokens N hain, aur tokenization/detokenization time ignore kar rahe hain: E2E latency = TTFT + ITL × (N − 1); TTFT = prefill + decode first token; ITL = decode one new token. Priority application par depend karti hai: agentic workflow me jahan downstream ko full output chahiye, E2E latency minimize karna primary objective hai; chatbot me jahan responses real time me stream hote hain, TTFT ka sabse zyada impact hai; aur output bahut lamba ho to ITL bhi critical hai, kyunki high ITL response ko sluggish feel karwata hai. Har technique teeno metrics ko ek saath improve nahi karegi — trade-offs karne padte hain, aur sahi technique use case ki requirements par depend karegi.

Throughput metrics: RPS/RPM aur TPS

Throughput is sawaal ka jawab deta hai: "System time ke saath kitni predictions handle kar sakta hai?" — ye batata hai ki serving system resources ko kitni efficiently use karke scale par results deliver karta hai. Requests per second (RPS) ya requests per minute (RPM) universal throughput metrics hain (ML aur non-ML dono workloads ke liye) — kitne requests model ya poori serving infrastructure ek timeframe me handle kar sakti hai. Lekin LLM serving ke liye RPS/RPM me granularity ki kami hai. Tokens per second (TPS) LLM generation ke liye specific throughput metric hai — model ya LLM serving service per second kitne output tokens generate karti hai. Dhyaan do: TPS sirf generated tokens count karta hai — input tokens ya input + output ka sum nahi.

Dono me se koi bhi perfect standalone measure nahi hai. RPS/RPM request patterns ke prati sensitive hote hain — lambe inputs/outputs aur concurrent users ki sankhya par heavily depend karte hain — isliye alag traffic patterns wale workloads ke beech direct RPS/RPM comparison basically useless hai. TPS manipulate kiya ja sakta hai: input length kam karne se TTFT kam hota hai aur TPS zyada dikhne lagta hai; bade ya optimized batch requests (uniform input/output lengths) bhi GPU utilization improve karke TPS badha sakte hain.

Performance measurement ki best practices

Koi single metric kaafi nahi hai — latency aur throughput ko practical best practices ke saath combine karna padta hai. Latency aur throughput ke beech trade-off pehchano: ek ko improve karna aksar doosre ki cost par hota hai — offline batch processing me throughput sabse important hai (cost kam karta hai), interactive applications me latency critical hai. Use case ke hisaab se acceptable latency goals set karo: chatbot me 1-second response achieve kar liya hai to use 0.5 seconds tak squeeze karne se user experience significantly improve nahi hoga — focus throughput aur cost par shift karo. E2E latency ko TTFT aur ITL me decompose karo — sub-metrics bottlenecks ka sharper view dete hain. Real-world traffic patterns ko closely simulate karo: input/output lengths widely vary karte hain, aur real traffic kabhi uniform nahi hoti; bursts queuing delays ya request failures la sakte hain, isliye simulate karne se pehle traffic pattern carefully analyze karo.

Experiments me consistency maintain karo: ek saath bahut kuch badalne se effects isolate karna impossible ho jaata hai — ek time par ek hi knob turn karo aur request patterns aur configurations ko tests ke across stable rakho. Hardware utilization monitor karo (GPU/CPU usage, memory) taaki pata chale bottlenecks model behavior se hain ya hardware limits se. Metrics ko manipulate ya inflate karne se bacho — inflated metrics production me backfire kar sakte hain. Production me continuously monitor karo aur test suites periodically chalao — regression checks, scalability tests (jaise Black Friday peak loads) aur A/B testing naye optimizations roll out karne se pehle.

Yaad rakho: Meaningful performance measurement ke liye granularity, realism, fairness aur ongoing vigilance ka mix chahiye. In best practices se misleading results avoid hote hain aur aise insights milte hain jo latency, throughput aur cost efficiency me real-world improvements me translate hote hain.

05.1Chapter 5 · Challenges When Serving LLMs

Optimizing kyun zaroori: experience, cost, scalability

Pehle ke chapters me seekha ki ML models ko production me functionally operational aur well-designed kaise banaya jaaye. Ab ek aur crucial aspect hai: model production environment me quickly aur efficiently chale. Ye LLM serving ke liye khaas taur par important hai, kyunki LLMs ko hardware se substantial compute power aur memory chahiye hoti hai. ChatGPT ke late 2022 me rise ke baad se LLMs ne chatbots aur code generation se lekar advanced reasoning aur decision-making tak real-world AI applications transform kar diye hain — lekin unki sheer size, computational demands aur unique serving requirements classic model serving techniques se bahut aage ki challenges laate hain. Is chapter ka kaam bridge banana hai: pehle ke serving concepts aur aane wale chapters ki advanced optimization techniques ke beech. Teen factors se samjho ki optimizing kyun zaroori hai: customer experience, cost efficiency, aur scalability / peak load handling / feasibility.

Customer experience

Customer experience kisi bhi product ki success ke liye key hai aur model response latency se highly correlated ho sakti hai. Imagine karo: ChatGPT me sawaal poochho aur pehla token milne ke liye 20 seconds se zyada wait karna pade — aisi delay unsatisfactory hai aur customers aasani se frustrate ho jaate hain. Agar serving performance optimize karke latency ko 20 seconds se 1 second tak laaya jaaye — same hardware setup aur overall throughput ke saath — to ye product ki success ke liye game-changer hoga. Lekin extremely fast response times hamesha significant benefits nahi dete. Latency aur customer satisfaction ke beech inverse correlation hai — latency high ho to satisfaction significantly drop hokar near zero ho jaati hai; latency kam hone par satisfaction improve hoti hai, lekin jaise-jaise latency aur kam hoti hai, satisfaction me incremental gains bahut kam pronounced ho jaate hain. Example: pehla token milne ka time 0.1 seconds se 0.01 seconds karna human perception me register hi nahi hota — is case me kuch latency trade karke higher throughput lena (0.01 se 0.1 seconds) behtar cost efficiency dega.

Customer experience ka doosra aspect hai generation quality. Same family ya similar families ke models me bade models generally higher-quality responses dete hain — jaise benchmark scores me ek 70-billion-parameter model apne 8-billion-parameter sibling ko outperform karta hai. Bina optimization ke aap latency requirements meet karne ke liye 8-billion-parameter model tak limited reh sakte hain. Lekin poori model serving system ko extensively optimize karne ke baad, same latency aur throughput, same hardware setup par, 32 billion ya even 70 billion parameters wala model leverage kar sakte hain — isse response quality significantly improve hoti hai.

Cost efficiency

Great customer experience deliver karne ke beyond, product ko financially viable bhi hona hai — AI system kitna bhi powerful ho, scale par operate karna bahut costly ho to succeed nahi kar sakta. AI development aur operation ke saare costs me model inference sabse expensive component hai. Ye surprising lag sakta hai, kyunki training dominant cost lagti hai — ek bade LLM ki training cost $50 million se zyada thi. Lekin AI chip revenue projections (2024–2034) dikhate hain ki inference hardware consumption aaj training ko surpass kar chuka hai — aur gap widen hone ki expectation hai. Logic: training primarily upfront investment hai, jabki inference costs continuously scale hoti hain jaise usage badhta hai — har query ongoing expenses incur karti hai.

Shuru me kuch major players foundation-model training dominate karte the; ab AI labs aur open source efforts bhi contribute kar rahe hain, lekin vast majority existing models ko fine-tune karti hai ya RAG jaise techniques se enhance karti hai — foundation model scratch se train karne se significantly kam cost me. Is beech inference ki demand nonstop hai: GenAI applications aur industries me apply hote hain, to production me LLMs ka computational burden skyrocket kar raha hai, aur AI agents aur complex workflows is trend ko amplify karte hain — ek hi workflow me multiple LLM aur embedding model calls. Optimize karke, same hardware aur similar latency par, businesses zyada throughput achieve kar sakti hain (ek saath zyada customers serve karna), jo horizontally scale karte waqt hardware usage kam karta hai aur tremendous money bachata hai. Optimized model lower-grade chip par bhi chal sakta hai, zyada expensive chip ke bajaye, similar latency aur throughput ke saath.

Scalability, peak load handling, aur feasibility

Jab model production me deploy hota hai, to GPU demand customer growth ke saath scale hoti hai. Optimized inference customer experience improve karta hai aur GPU costs kam karta hai — aur ye determine karta hai ki system heavy traffic ke under efficiently scale kar sakta hai ya nahi, khaas taur par jab GPU availability limited ho. Example: LLM-powered sales agent saal bhar stable traffic par smoothly chalta hai, lekin Black Friday par demand 400% ya zyada surge kar sakti hai — kam optimized system ko bottlenecks, degraded latency aur request failures face karne padenge. Optimized models lower-grade chips par deploy ho sakte hain, jo greater flexibility deta hai — high-end GPUs har region me readily available nahi hote, isliye broader hardware range par efficiently chalane ki ability naye markets me expand karne ke liye key enabler hai.

Jaise pehle bataya, optimized models lower-grade chips par deploy ho sakte hain, jo greater flexibility deta hai. Aaj bade cloud providers tak access hone ke bawjood, high-end GPUs har region me readily available nahi hote. Models ko efficiently broader range of hardware par chalane ki ability — specific high-end GPUs tak constrained hone ke bajaye — naye markets me expand karne wale businesses ke liye key enabler ho sakti hai. Ye issue duniya bhar me applications deploy karte waqt frequently encounter hota hai.

Yaad rakho: Optimization sirf speed ke baare me nahi hai. Ye decide karta hai ki aap kitna bada model same hardware par chala sakte hain (quality), kitne customers same cost par serve kar sakte hain (cost), aur peak load par system zinda rehta hai ya fail ho jaata hai (feasibility). Fundamentals samjhe bina optimization tiring trial-and-error ban jaata hai — aapko pata bhi nahi chalta ki aap local optima me stuck hain.
