← Previous04.6 · Performance measure karna: latency + throughput→ Next05.2 · Accelerator chips: GPU specs padhna + compare
05.2Chapter 5 · Challenges When Serving LLMs

Accelerator chips: GPU specs padhna + compare

Optimization kyun zaroori hai, ye samajh liya — ab us hardware ko samjho jo LLMs ko power karta hai. Sahi accelerator setup choose karna aksar LLM serving ke sabse important decisions me se ek hota hai, kyunki system ki hardware constraints uski memory capacity, computational power aur efficiency dictate karti hain. Book NVIDIA GPU par focus karta hai — likhte waqt (early 2026) general-purpose computing on GPUs (GPGPU) ke liye NVIDIA ka solution market dominate karta hai. GPU specs overwhelming lag sakte hain, lekin LLMs ke liye chaar attributes sabse relevant hain: GPU compute power, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, aur interconnects.

GPU specs padhna: H100 SXM vs H100 NVL

Do NVIDIA GPUs ki comparison table se seekhte hain. Compute performance teraFLOPS me measure hoti hai — floating-point operations per second (tera = 1 trillion). Table (pehla number H100 SXM, doosra H100 NVL): FP64 34 vs 30, FP32 67 vs 60, TF32 Tensor Core 989 vs 835, BF16/FP16 Tensor Core 1979 vs 1671, FP8 Tensor Core 3958 vs 3341, INT8 3958 vs 3341 TOPS. H100 SXM FP16 par 1979 × 1012 operations/second kar sakta hai — FP8 model use karo to lagbhag double, kyunki FP8, FP16 se aadha size hai. Horizontally NVL compute me thoda kam hai — lekin kya woh har use case me worse hai? Nahi, aage dekho.

Memory (VRAM) batata hai model load karne ki capacity, aur memory bandwidth GPU computation ke liye data-transfer speed. H100 NVL ke paas zyada memory hai (94 GB vs SXM ke 80 GB) aur zyada bandwidth bhi (3.9 TB/s vs 3.35 TB/s). Choice: SXM faster calculate karta hai (zyada FLOPS), NVL ke paas behtar memory capacity aur bandwidth hai. Book ki analogy: GPU ek pizza kitchen hai — compute power (FLOPS) oven ki speed, memory bandwidth dough supply ki efficiency, aur memory capacity fridge ki capacity. Fridge chhota ho to model load nahi hoga; oven advanced ho lekin dough supply slow ho, to powerful oven khaali chalega; oven weak ho lekin supply fast ho, to bake hone me bahut time lagega. Isliye compute, memory size aur bandwidth ke beech balance dhoondhna zaroori hai.

GPU interconnects: intra-node

Interconnects multiple GPUs ke beech high-speed data transfer enable karte hain — ek node ke andar aur multiple nodes ke across. Pehle ye sirf training ke liye crucial the, lekin ab serving ke liye bhi important ho gaye hain: bade models ke liye ek GPU kaafi nahi hota (weights/layers alag GPUs par load karne padte hain), ya latency-sensitive use case me ek GPU kaafi powerful nahi hota, to multiple GPUs ko milkar faster inference karna padta hai.

Inter-node interconnects aur power

Ek node me GPUs ki sankhya unlimited nahi ho sakti — physical constraints, power supply, cooling aur software support ki wajah se maximum usually 8 GPUs par capped hota hai. LLMs bade hote jaayenge to 8 GPUs bhi insufficient ho sakte hain — tab models ko multiple nodes ke across shard karte hain. Inter-node ke liye best solutions me se ek hai InfiniBand (IB) with GPUDirect RDMA — RDMA ka matlab remote direct memory access, jo nodes ke across GPUs ke beech direct memory access enable karta hai. NDR 400G InfiniBand nodes ke across 50 GB/s achieve kar sakta hai — lekin ye intra-node performance se abhi bhi bahut slower hai. Comparison: intra-node NVLink/NVSwitch 900 GB/s, NVLink Bridge 600 GB/s, PCIe 128 GB/s, aur across node 50 GB/s. Isliye LLM serving me majority deployments abhi bhi single node par 1 se 8 GPUs per model instance (replica) chalate hain, aur traffic badhne par horizontally scale karte hain — same setup ke aur hardware instances add karke — taaki unnecessary inter-node communication minimize ho. Aage ke chapters me tensor parallelism aur pipeline parallelism jaise multi-GPU/multi-node techniques aayenge; prefill aur decode phases ko alag GPUs par separate karna aur MoE models me expert parallelism bhi advanced topics hain.

Aakhri important constraint hai power consumption — GPU chip ki hidden lekin fundamental metric, watts (W) me measure hoti hai, aksar thermal design power (TDP) ke roop me (maximum sustained power, continuous load ke under). Modern datacenter GPUs few hundred watts se 700+ watts per accelerator tak jaate hain — zyada power budget zyada compute density aur bandwidth enable karta hai, lekin cooling aur power delivery par stricter requirements laata hai. General cloud users ke liye power largely abstracted hoti hai (pricing me implicitly reflect hoti hai); cloud providers aur private datacenters ke liye power first-class constraint hai — isliye performance per watt critical metric hai; edge/on-device systems me power poori system ki defining constraint hai (batteries, thermals, form factors).

Popular GPUs compare karna

Specs samajh liye, ab unhe apply karte hain (costs Spring 2026 ke hisaab se): H200 SXM — 141 GB, 1979 teraFLOPS, 4.8 TB/s, FP8 yes, NVLink yes, ~$6.3/hour. H100 SXM — 80 GB, 1979 teraFLOPS, 3.35 TB/s, FP8 yes, NVLink yes, ~$6.2/hour. A100 SXM — 80 GB, 312 teraFLOPS, 1.935 TB/s, FP8 no, NVLink yes, ~$2.7/hour. L40S — 48 GB, 362 teraFLOPS, 0.864 TB/s, FP8 yes, NVLink no, ~$2.25/hour. A10 — 24 GB, 125 teraFLOPS, 0.6 TB/s, FP8 no, NVLink no, <$1.25/hour. General rule: zyada powerful GPU hamesha zyada expensive hota hai. Small model: fine-tuned Llama-3-8B, latency bahut critical nahi — A10 decent choice (kaafi memory, sabse cheap, highly available). Mid-sized model: 14-billion-parameter model — L40S step up karo, khaas taur par FP8 support ke saath (multi-GPU overhead avoid, long context aur high batch size ke liye kaafi memory). Large model: 671-billion-parameter MoE model — NVLink Switch crucial; likely configuration ek machine me 8 H200 GPUs FP8 me. Technology fast change hoti hai — aaj ka hottest chip kal replace ho sakta hai — lekin options weigh karne ke foundational concepts nahi badalte.

Doosre AI accelerators aur trends

Core concepts doosre chips par bhi same hain — AMD MI300X aur Intel Gaudi2 (H100/A100 alternatives), Google TPU aur Amazon Inferentia (mostly apne clouds par), Huawei Ascend NPU, aur startups jaise Groq aur Cerebras. Early 2026 tak NVIDIA ke GPGPU solutions dominate karte hain: kuch offerings specifically inference workloads ke liye tailored hain lekin rapidly evolving model architectures ke saath struggle karte hain; software level par NVIDIA ke paas CUDA ecosystem ka mature support hai, jabki custom chips ko proprietary stacks chahiye hote hain aur switch karna costly hota hai; kuch chips on-chip SRAM se impressive latency achieve karte hain lekin SRAM ki high price ki wajah se rarely cost-effective hote hain; aur NVIDIA ki flexibility edge hai — alag precisions (FP8, FP4), high bandwidth aur advanced interconnects.

Ek badi challenge hai "memory wall" — pichhle 20 saalon me hardware compute FLOPS memory bandwidth aur inter-GPU bandwidth se bahut zyada pace par improve hue hain, aur aaj data-movement limitations compute advancements ko utilize karne me obstacle hain. Do trends: computation ko on-chip SRAM ke closer push karna (parameters aur intermediate data compute units ke paas rakhkar memory-access latency kam karna — expensive, lekin extremely low aur predictable latency, latency-sensitive workloads ke liye attractive) aur tightly coupled multi-GPU systems (CPU layer tak, jaise Grace CPU Blackwell GPUs ke saath high-bandwidth interconnects se integrated — representative example GB200 NVL72: 36 Grace CPUs aur 72 Blackwell GPUs ek bade NVLink domain me). Aise latest setups ke liye strong software–hardware codesign chahiye aur industry me sirf kuch bade players adoption me aage hain.

SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 5 — Challenges When Serving LLMs
← Previous05.1 · Optimizing kyun zaroori: experience, cost, scalability→ Next05.3 · Model loading bottlenecks: size + KV cache estimate
05.3Chapter 5 · Challenges When Serving LLMs

Model loading bottlenecks: size + KV cache estimate

GPU specs samajh liye — ab dekhte hain LLM un specs ke saath kaise interact karta hai. Pehle model loading, phir model execution. Efficient LLM serving ka pehla step hai model weights load karke GPU memory me cache karna. Loading process me model weights pehle CPU memory (system memory) me move hote hain, phir GPU memory me transfer hote hain. Ek baar load hone ke baad weights GPU memory me cached rehte hain, incoming requests serve karne ke liye ready. Isliye kaafi GPU memory hona essential hai taaki model weights hold ho sakein.

Model CPU memory me kyun nahi rakh sakte?

Kuch log soch sakte hain: model ko badi CPU memory me cache kyun na karein, ya requests aane par on-demand load kyun na karein? Jawab hai data transfer speeds: SSD 0.5–14 GB/s, CPU memory 50–200 GB/s, GPU memory 300 GB/s–3 TB/s. CPU memory typically DRAM hoti hai (capacity ke liye optimized), GPU memory HBM hoti hai (massive parallel data movement ke liye optimized). Model weights GPU memory me hi cached hone chahiye — CPU memory me store hon to GPU compute use karne ke liye transfer karna padega, jo serving me unacceptable delay introduce karta hai.

Model size estimate karna

Ek bade AI model ko kitni GPU memory chahiye? Memory footprint calculate karne me do key variables hain: model ka parameter count aur parameters ka data type (precision). Parameter count aksar model ke naam me hi mil jaata hai — jaise Llama-2-7b ka matlab hai lagbhag 7 billion parameters. Data type model ke Hugging Face repository me config.json file me milta hai — torch_dtype attribute batata hai model weights ke liye kaunsi precision use hui hai; jaise value float16 (FP16) ho to model 16-bit floating-point precision use karta hai storage aur computation ke liye. Precision ka matlab hai ek parameter store karne ke liye kitne bits chahiye: FP32 (single precision) 32 bits = 4 bytes, FP16 / BF16 (half precision) 16 bits = 2 bytes, INT8 / FP8 (quarter precision) 8 bits = 1 byte. General rule: precision kam karna — FP32 se FP16, phir INT8 ya FP8 — kuch accuracy ki cost par model size kam karta hai aur serving performance improve karta hai (detail agle chapter me).

Example: Llama-2-7b ke lagbhag 7 billion parameters BF16 format me store hain, har parameter 2 bytes: ~7 billion parameters × 2 bytes/parameter = 14 billion bytes = 14 GB. Model files ko dekhkar ye estimate confirm hota hai — weight files ka sum lagbhag 13 GB aata hai.

KV cache size estimate karna

Ab maan lo aapke paas 16 GB memory wala GPU hai — 14 GB ka model load ho jaayega, aur ek chhoti single request bhi fine chalegi. Lekin sirf model fit karne layak GPU ideal nahi hai. Chapter 2 se yaad karo KV caching — ek optimization technique jo kuch GPU memory space trade karke much faster serving performance deti hai: intermediate results cache karke, model agla token decode karte waqt unhe reuse kar sakta hai bina computation dobara kiye. GPU memory me model weight aur KV cache co-locate hote hain, aur thodi extra memory intermediate computations (activations) ke liye bhi chahiye hoti hai. Agar KV cache ke liye sirf tiny amount bachta hai, to aap bahut limited batch sizes aur short context par constrained ho jaate hain.

Har token ke liye KV cache size estimate karne ka formula hai: KV cache size per token = 2 × number of layers × number of attention heads × head dimension × data type size. Yahan 2 isliye hai kyunki har token ke liye key aur value dono store hote hain. Llama-2-7b basic multi-head attention (MHA) use karta hai: 32 layers, 32 attention heads, head dimension 128 (4096 / 32), half precision (2 bytes). Formula lagao: 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 524,288 bytes = 0.5 MB per token. Ab kitne tokens cache karne hain? Maximum tokens = maximum batch size × maximum sequence length. Max batch size batata hai ek model instance ek time par kitne parallel users/requests process kar sakta hai; max sequence length total input + output length limit karta hai. Isliye zyada requests ek saath process karna ya lambe prompts/lambe generation handle karna KV cache size badha deta hai: Total KV cache = KV cache size per token × (max batch size × max sequence length).

Example: long paragraphs summarize kar rahe hain, max sequence length 4,096, batch size 16: Total KV cache = 0.5 MB/token × 4,096 × 16 = 32 GB — model (14 GB) se bhi bada! Do chips compare karo: A10 (24 GB) — model ke baad 10 GB bachta hai, max batch size 4, ~$2/hour. L40S (48 GB) — 34 GB bachta hai, max batch size 16, ~$3.75/hour. L40S zyada expensive hai, phir bhi zyada cost-efficient — chaar guna zyada parallel requests. Note: theoretical maximum batch size usually achieve nahi hota, kyunki activations ke liye bhi space reserve karni hoti hai.

Yaad rakho: GPU memory usage idling se execution tak badhta hai — execution ke dauraan KV cache size grow karta rehta hai jaise sequence length badhti hai aur zyada tokens cache hote hain. Generation ke end par peak memory usage se beyond kaafi memory honi chahiye, warna out-of-memory (OOM) errors aayenge. General rule of thumb: GPU memory requirements estimate karte waqt model size ka lagbhag double GPU memory lena shuru karo — taaki behtar parallelism achieve ho aur GPU performance poori tarah unleash ho. Prefix caching jaise techniques (Chapter 6) ko aur zyada space chahiye ho sakti hai, kyunki woh faster TTFT ke liye zyada cache rakhna chahti hain.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 5 — Challenges When Serving LLMs
← Previous05.2 · Accelerator chips: GPU specs padhna + compare→ Next05.4 · Model execution bottlenecks: arithmetic intensity
05.4Chapter 5 · Challenges When Serving LLMs

Model execution bottlenecks: arithmetic intensity

Model load ho gaya aur GPU memory me ready hai — ab asli sawaal: model serving GPU compute FLOPS se bounded hai ya GPU memory bandwidth se? Pizza kitchen analogy me wapas: kya humein faster bake karne wala bada oven chahiye, ya ingredients aur dough faster supply karne ki zaroorat hai? Inme se kaunsa hamare model serving workload ka bottleneck hai? Iska analysis karne ke liye ek concept chahiye: arithmetic intensity — algorithm ke operations ka ratio, data movement ke saath. Ye basically compute (FLOPS) ko compute unit tak data movement se divide karta hai, FLOPS per byte me: arithmetic intensity = number of FLOPS / data movement. Agar workload ko bahut kam computation chahiye lekin bahut data read/write karna hai, to uski arithmetic intensity low hai. Ulta, agar workload kam data read/write karke us par bahut computation karta hai, to arithmetic intensity high hai.

Data movement kya hai?

Data movement ko model loading se confuse mat karo. Data movement execution time par hota hai, jab weights pehle se GPU memory me hain: off-chip HBM se, on-chip SRAM (L2/L1 cache, shared memory) ke through, register tak — jahan actual compute hota hai. SRAM HBM se chhota aur expensive hai, lekin bahut faster aur compute ke paas hai — SRAM capacity/cost ko speed ke liye trade karta hai, HBM speed ko capacity ke liye. Serving me weights GPU memory se constantly read hote hain, saath me intermediate outputs — aur GPU memory sabse slow hai, isliye GPU memory bandwidth hi data movement ka number hai.

Roofline model: L40S example

Sirf GPU specs dekhkar chip ki theoretical arithmetic intensity calculate kar sakte hain. L40S: bandwidth 864 GB/s, FP16 Tensor Core 362 TFLOPS — 362 / 864 ≈ 419 FLOPS/B. Isse roofline model draw kar sakte hain (x-axis arithmetic intensity, y-axis teraFLOPS): intensity 419 se kam ho to GPU ke saare 362 TFLOPS use nahi kar sakte. Example: ~210 FLOPS/B wala workload memory bandwidth-bound hai; 1,000 FLOPS/B wala compute-bound hai — chahe kitna bhi data read karo, chip se isse fast calculate nahi ho sakta.

Matrix multiplication ki arithmetic intensity

LLM serving workload compute-bound hai ya memory bandwidth-bound, ye jaanne ke liye LLM architecture ke andar alag layers ki arithmetic intensity calculate karni padti hai. Chapter 2 se yaad karo: LLM mostly Transformer blocks se bana hota hai — andar do main components hain, self-attention layers aur feedforward layers — aur dono me vast majority computations matrix multiplications (matmul) hain. Doosri layers (element-wise operations, reduction operations) typically low arithmetic intensity rakhti hain, kyunki har loaded data point par computation matmul jitna high nahi hota — lekin ye overall computation ka chhota portion represent karti hain. Matmul me input matrix [M, K] weight matrix [K, N] se multiply hokar output matrix [M, N] banata hai. Operations ki sankhya: 2 × M × N × K (M × N × K multiplications + M × N × (K − 1) additions, simplify karke). Data movement (half precision, 2 bytes each): 2 × (M × K + K × N + M × N) — input matrices read + output matrix write. Isliye arithmetic intensity = M × N × K / (M × K + K × N + M × N).

M = N = K maan kar values dekho: size 64 → 21 FLOPS/B, 512 → 170 (dono L40S par memory bandwidth-bound), 4096 → 1365 (compute-bound, crossover 419 se well over). Matlab matrices kaafi badi hon to operation compute-bound push ho sakta hai — lekin LLM serving me matrices hamesha badi nahi hoti, khaas taur par jab batch size 1 ho (batching Chapter 6 me).

Prefill vs decode: arithmetic intensity ka farq

Input tensor three-dimensional hota hai: [batch size, sequence length, model hidden dimension]. Batch size ek saath process hone wale requests ki sankhya hai, sequence length input prompt me tokens ki sankhya hai (user ke hisaab se highly variable — "Hello" jaise chhote phrase se lekar million tokens tak), aur model hidden dimension har token ke vector me values ki sankhya hai. Batch size 1 ho to 3D input tensor 2D matrix ban jaata hai: [sequence length, model hidden dimension]. Prefill aur decode phases revisit karo: prefill initial processing stage hai — model input prompt encode karta hai, Transformer layers se saare input tokens par attention compute karta hai aur pehle KV cache entries generate karke store karta hai. Decode me model pehle se computed KV cache use karke ek-ek token generate karta hai.

Matmul me M, N, K ki jagah h (hidden dimension, prefill aur decode me same) aur s (sequence length) aate hain: prefill me saare tokens ek saath process hote hain, isliye s badi hoti hai; decode me tokens ek-ek karke generate hote hain, isliye s sirf 1 hota hai. Numbers (hidden dim 4096, L40S crossover 419): seq length 64 → prefill 31, decode 0.5; 512 → prefill 240, decode 0.5; 4096 → prefill 1365, decode 0.5 (prefill compute-bound, decode hamesha memory bandwidth-bound).

Yaad rakho: Prefill vs decode jaise alag components aur model ki alag layers — sabki arithmetic intensity bahut alag ho sakti hai. Sequence length (aur batch size, jise abhi intentionally skip kiya gaya hai) bhi isse affect karta hai. Is analysis se intuition banta hai ki alag phases me bottleneck kya hai, taaki baad me samajh aaye ki alag optimization techniques kyun kaam karti hain aur unhe kaise select karna hai. Rule: workload compute-bound ho to mathematical computations optimize karo aur FLOPS kam karo; memory bandwidth-bound ho to unnecessary data movement minimize karo. Batch size 1 par LLM bahut memory bandwidth-bound ho sakta hai — khaas taur par decode me ya jab input sequence kaafi lambi na ho — aur is case me GPU compute apni full potential tak saturate nahi hota.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 5 — Challenges When Serving LLMs
← Previous05.3 · Model loading bottlenecks: size + KV cache estimate→ Next06.1 · Batching & scheduling: dynamic, continuous, chunked prefill
06.1Chapter 6 · Essential LLM Optimization Techniques

Batching & scheduling: dynamic, continuous, chunked prefill

Pehle ke chapters me seekha ki LLM serving ko optimize karna kyun zaroori hai aur bottlenecks kahan hain. Ab is chapter me essential optimization techniques ek-ek karke dive karte hain — taaki aap decide kar sakein kab, kaise aur kyun koi technique apni serving needs ke liye use karni hai. Is chapter me chaar cheezein hain: request batching aur scheduling, attention optimization, model compression, aur prefix caching. Pehle batching.

Batching ki zaroorat kyun? Prefill vs decode

Chapter 2 se yaad karo: serving offline aur real-time online me divide hoti hai. Offline serving me requests pehle se available hoti hain, isliye unhe ek saath batch karke ek badi tensor input ki tarah model ko feed kiya ja sakta hai, ek-ek karke bhejne ke bajaye. Real-time online serving me requests user ke bhejte hi aati hain. Requests ko serving ke dauraan group karne se higher throughput achieve hota hai, bhale hi responses thode slower hon. Kyun? Chapter 5 ki arithmetic intensity se samjho. Prefill phase me model input prompt ko samajhta hai — input prompt ke tokens parallel me process hote hain aur high arithmetic intensity achieve hoti hai, jo compute-bound workload banata hai. Decode phase me LLM ek time par ek token generate karta hai — autoregressive nature ki wajah se decode memory bandwidth-bound hai: model ko sirf ek token generate karne ke liye apne billion-level parameters se guzarna padta hai, jo GPU memory bandwidth ke hisaab se bahut inefficient hai.

GPU compute ko fully utilize karne ke liye batching se zyada requests add karo: max batch size 3 maan lo — teen prompts batch karke bhejo, to decode ek iteration me teen naye tokens generate karta hai (har request ke liye ek). Arithmetic intensity artificially badhti hai: model weights ek baar read ho rahe hain, lekin zyada calculations aur zyada tokens generate ho rahe hain. Summary: batching khaas taur par decode phase me effective hai (throughput aur GPU FLOPS utilization badhta hai). Prefill me benefits limited hain — model pehle se saare input tokens parallel me process karta hai; jab tak prompt bahut chhota na ho (1,024 tokens se kam), prefill akele hi GPU compute saturate kar leta hai.

Dynamic batching

Offline batching common aur straightforward hai, lekin online inference me requests beforehand available nahi hoti — to batching kaise achieve karein? Client-side batching (client requests accumulate karke preset batch size par ek saath bhejta hai) aur server-side static batching (server preset batch size bharne tak wait karta hai) offline ke liye achhe hain, online ke liye ideal nahi — real-world requests random aati hain aur unke beech bade time gaps ho sakte hain. Example: batch size 10 ho, pehle 9 requests ek second me aa jaayein, 10th 5 minutes baad aaye — pehle 9 requests 5 minutes wait karengi.

Solution hai dynamic batching — inference time par requests ko defined logic se group karna, latency aur throughput balance karne ke liye. Do key parameters: batch size (max batch size / max number of sequences) aur max delay time (existing requests max kitna wait kar sakti hain, batch bharne ke liye). Pending count max batch size tak pahunche ya max delay time reach ho, to batch turant bhej diya jaata hai — bhale hi usme sirf ek request ho.

Analogy: ferry-boat business — har boat 10 logon ko paar kara sakti hai. Bina batching ke har aadmi par ek boat (great experience, horribly inefficient). Static batching me boat 10 log poore hone tak wait karegi (efficient, lekin pehle aane wale ko bahut der wait karna padega). Dynamic batching beech ka rasta hai: max batch size 10 + max delay time 5 minutes — 5 minutes me 8 log aayein to boat nikal jaati hai, 10 log pehle aa jaayein to turant bhej di jaati hai.

Do parameters tune karna latency aur throughput requirements ke basis par hota hai: jitna high batch size ho sake, utna achieve karo, jab tak latency SLA meet ho rahi ho. Batch size badhane se processing latency aur memory usage badhti hai (memory khatam hone tak). Max delay time bhi tune karo: bahut lamba delay pehle se aayi requests ko bahut wait karwayega; bahut chhota delay batch ko time par bharne se rok dega.

Continuous batching

Dynamic batching most models aur kai traditional ML serving settings ke liye kaafi achha kaam karta hai aur widely adopted hai. Lekin LLMs ek bada unique challenge rakhte hain: LLM serving me varying input aur output lengths hoti hain, jisse ek batch me requests ko process karne me vastly alag time lagta hai. Dynamic batching me batch finish hone ka total time sabse lambi aur slowest request determine karti hai, kyunki result tab return hota hai jab batch ki saari requests complete ho jaayein. Example: teen requests me ek bahut lambi hai — requests 1 aur 2 jaldi finish ho jaati hain, lekin request 3 ka wait karte hue bahut GPU idle time banta hai. Ferry analogy me: boat ko logon ko seedha unke ghar drop karna hai nadi ke doosri taraf — trip times alag honge, ghar ki distance ke hisaab se — boat ko sabse door wale ko drop karne ke baad hi dock wapas aana hai, isliye capacity kam hoti jaati hai.

Is challenge ko mitigate karne ke liye continuous batching (inflight/iterative batching) introduce hui: requests ko backend model me on the fly add kiya jaata hai, bina fixed batch size ya time window ka wait kiye — jaise hi ek running request finish hoti hai, queued request turant batch me add ho jaati hai. Dynamic batching me nayi requests sabse lambi request ke finish hone ka wait karti thin; continuous me aisa nahi hota. Ferry analogy me: ek 10-person boat ki jagah 10 chhoti boats — jaise hi koi aata hai, ek boat turant nikal jaati hai, koi waste nahi.

Continuous batching me max delay time set karne ki zaroorat nahi hoti; max batch size sirf upper bound ke roop me rehta hai. Kai modern frameworks me ek aur parameter hai: max number of batched tokens — max batch size request level par control karta hai, batched tokens token level par granular control deta hai (input lengths bahut vary karti hain: 20 tokens wali 10 requests vs 100,000 tokens wali 2 requests bilkul alag workload hain). Dono constraints meet karne hote hain: prefill me key constraint maximum token count, decode me maximum batch size. Max tokens kaafi high set karo, warna prefill me GPU compute saturate nahi hoga. vLLM example: vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 128.

Continuous batching with chunked prefill

Continuous batching alag lengths ki problem solve karta hai, lekin prefill aur decode do alag workloads hain — ab tak ke diagrams me unhe abstract kiya gaya tha. Happy-path me sab line up hota hai (same lengths, same start), lekin real world me lengths random hain aur start times alag hain. Sawaal: pehli request decode me ho aur doosri prefill start karna chahe, to kis ko prioritize karein — decode ya prefill? Kya unhe same iteration me batch kar sakte hain?

Agar prefill aur decode ko ek saath batch na karein, to requests 2 aur 3 aane par decide karna hai prefill prioritize karein ya decode — usually prefill choose karte hain, kyunki prefill TTFT determine karta hai. Lekin tab request 1 poori tarah idle wait karti hai, aur lambe prompts ho to uski end-to-end latency aur ITL hurt hoti hai. Dono ko combine karke batch karne se bhi zyada madad nahi milti, kyunki ek token decode karna long prompt ka prefill finish karne se bahut faster ho sakta hai.

Iska solution hai chunked prefill — long input prompt ko chhote chunks me split karna, jinka size ideally decode boxes ke similar hota hai. Jab requests 2 aur 3 batched iteration me join karti hain, to request 1 decode continue karti hai jabki doosri requests apna chhota chunked prefill start karti hain; request 2 phir seamlessly decode me transition kar jaati hai. Benefit: decode boxes lambe prefill ke blocked hokar wait nahi karte — ITL improve hoti hai. Lekin ye prefill performance ki cost par milta hai (multiple chhote prefill steps ka overhead TTFT lamba banata hai), aur end-to-end latency really improve nahi hoti. Throughput usually improve hoti hai, kyunki idle gaps fill hokar GPU behtar utilize hota hai. Chunk size bhi tune karni hai (max number of batched tokens ka hissa): bahut bada chunk matlab chunking hi nahi; bahut chhota chunk matlab zyada overhead aur low GPU utilization — beech ki value dhoondho.

Yaad rakho: Continuous batching production-level LLM serving me kuch saalon se industry standard hai. Chunked prefill aur uske variations bhi bahut popular hain, khaas taur par long context workloads handle karne ke liye. Ek aur advanced technique — prefill–decode disaggregation — prefill aur decode jobs ko completely alag GPUs aur even alag nodes par tod deti hai; woh Chapter 7 me aayegi.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 6 — Essential LLM Optimization Techniques
← Previous05.4 · Model execution bottlenecks: arithmetic intensity→ Next06.2 · Attention scaling + kernel fusion
06.2Chapter 6 · Essential LLM Optimization Techniques

Attention scaling + kernel fusion

Chapter 2 se yaad karo: LLM serving ke dauraan Transformer block ke do major components hain — attention aur feedforward layers (FFN/MLP). Is section me attention ko scale karne par focus karte hain: pehle KV cache size kam karna, phir custom GPU kernels se attention computation aur memory access improve karna. Attention hi LLMs ke breakthrough ki key hai — lekin original multi-head attention ab scale par queries, keys aur values leverage karne ka eklauta ya sabse efficient tareeka nahi raha.

Scalable attention mechanisms: MHA, MQA, GQA, MLA

KV cache size kam karna LLM serving performance improve karne ka ek key tareeka hai. Decode phase ke dauraan KV cache har decode iteration me HBM se on-chip registers aur shared memory me constantly transfer hota hai — chhota KV cache GPU memory bandwidth par pressure kam karta hai (Chapter 5 se). Ek aur benefit: chhota KV cache GPU memory me kam space leta hai, isliye zyada requests parallel me higher batch sizes ke saath run kar sakte hain (zyada throughput) aur limited GPU memory space me pehle se zyada lamba context serve kar sakte hain. Multi-head attention (MHA) original version hai jo kai pehle ke models ko underpin karta hai — lekin is setup me har query ke liye attention calculate karne ke liye ek distinct key aur value head chahiye hota hai, isliye is architecture ka KV cache sabse bada aur sabse kam efficient hota hai.

Performance improve karne ke liye multi-query attention (MQA) aayi — saari queries ek hi key aur value head share karti hain. 7B model me 32 aur 70B me 64 attention heads hote hain — MHA me 32/64 KVs honge, MQA me sirf ek — KV cache size 32–64 guna kam ho sakti hai. Lekin MQA accuracy significantly degrade karti hai. Isliye grouped-query attention (GQA) aayi — query heads ko groups me baantna, har group ka same key aur value — MHA aur MQA ke beech good middle ground, ab kai architectures me use hoti hai.

Kaise pata karein model kaunsa use kar raha hai? config.json dekho: purane model me num_attention_heads: 32 aur num_key_value_heads: 32 — barabar, matlab MHA. Naye model me num_attention_heads: 32 lekin num_key_value_heads: 8 — matlab GQA (32 / 8 = 4 attention heads per KV head). Ek aur advancement hai multi-head latent attention (MLA) — KV counts kam karne ke bajaye unhe compress karne ka clever tareeka; ek paper claim karta hai iska KV cache "GQA with only 2.25 groups ke barabar hai, lekin performance MHA se stronger hai." Ye choices model architecture level par hoti hain — kaunsa model family aapke use case ke liye best hai, ye holistic decision hai.

Ye saare advancements model architecture level par ho rahe hain — isliye attention mechanism ka choice usually is par bhi depend karta hai ki kaunsa model family ya specific model aapke use case ke liye best kaam karta hai. Ye ek holistic decision hai. Ye advancements model development me ek important shift mark karte hain: focus ab sirf model quality improve karne par nahi hai, balki increasingly models ko productize karne par hai — LLMs AI systems ka integral part ban rahe hain, to success ki key aisi architectures design karna hai jo na sirf powerful hon, balki real-world systems me serve karne ke liye practical, scalable aur cost-efficient bhi hon.

Kernel fusion aur custom attention kernels

Ab dekhte hain attention computation ko specialized GPU kernels se aur faster kaise banaya jaaye. Kernels chhote, specialized programs hain jo GPU par execute hokar computations perform karte hain — jaise matrix multiplications, softmax aur LLMs ke liye doosre crucial operations. Model architecture, hardware aur LLM workload ke basis par properly optimized aur specialized GPU kernels use karne se GPU utilization, inference speed aur throughput significantly improve ho sakte hain. Kernel optimization me ek key technique hai kernel fusion — multiple individual operations (jaise multiplication operation aur addition operation) ko ek single operation me merge karna, taaki memory aur compute ke beech data-movement overhead minimize ho. Is tareeke se register ya shared memory me pehle se pada data reuse hota hai, bina GPU global memory me wapas likhne aur dobara load karne ke round trip ke. Kernel fusion bina wale setup me shapes convert karne ke beech me memory me likhna aur load karna padta hai; fusion ke saath conversion ek go me ho jaata hai.

FlashAttention

Attention kernels me ek major advancement hai FlashAttention: attention GPU memory bandwidth se bottlenecked hota hai (frequent reads/writes), isliye algorithm ko hardware-aware banakar I/O kam karna memory limitation combat karta hai. HBM hierarchy me sabse badi lekin sabse slow memory hai — FlashAttention badi matrices ko HBM me materialize karne se bachkar unhe chhote pieces me todta hai (tiling/blocking), taaki saari computation faster memory (SRAM/registers) me ho aur sirf final output HBM me save ho. Ye saare attention operations fuse bhi karta hai (jaise online softmax). FlashAttention 2 aur 3 ne GEMM calculation ko softmax ke saath overlap karke GPU utilization aur improve kiya (khaas taur par H100 jaise naye GPUs me).

Practical takeaway: LLMs serve karte waqt efficient kernels leverage karna important hai — doosre optimized kernels hain FlashInfer, xFormers aur Triton (Triton Inference Server se confuse mat karo). Example: vLLM me FlashInfer kernel ke liye VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER jaise env vars set karo; SGLang me --attention-backend flag se choose karo. SGLang non-Hopper machines (A100, A40) par FlashInfer aur Hopper GPUs (H100, H200, H20) par FlashAttention3 default karta hai. Pehle recommended kernel se shuru karo, phir additional gain ke liye experiment karo.

PagedAttention

Attention improve karne ka ek aakhri important tareeka hai KV cache memory ko efficiently manage karna. Model serving ke dauraan system constantly naya KV cache create aur store kar raha hai aur purana cache evict kar raha hai. KV cache size badi hoti jaati hai jaise modern LLMs lambi context lengths support karne lagte hain. Is bade KV cache ko schedule karna kabhi easy nahi hota, kyunki LLM serving me input length har request ke hisaab se vary karti hai aur output length predetermined nahi hoti. In unique challenges ki wajah se GPU memory me bahut inefficiency ho sakti hai — traditional methods memory space preallocate karte hain jo usually fully use nahi hoti, jisse significant memory fragmentation aur real-world memory space ka low usage hota hai.

Is problem ko combat karne ke liye advancement hai PagedAttention, saath me vLLM framework jo iske upar banta hai. Ye operating systems ki paging technique se inspired hai — memory ko fixed-size blocks (pages) me divide karna, taaki scattered free spaces allocate karna easy ho. PagedAttention KV cache ko fixed-sized blocks me partition karta hai, phir block table (lookup table) se query keys ko specific blocks se map karta hai — KV cache contiguous memory me store karne ki zaroorat nahi. Example: prompt + completion teen alag blocks me store hote hain (block 7, 1, 3), har block me max 4 tokens, aakhri me sirf 2 (abhi generate ho raha hai).

Yaad rakho: PagedAttention par ek paper kehta hai ki bina PagedAttention ke "KV cache memory ka sirf 20.4%–38.2% actual token states store karne ke liye use hota hai", lekin PagedAttention ke saath ye "KV cache memory me near-zero waste" achieve karta hai. Memory fragmentation kam karne ke is great improvement ki wajah se PagedAttention aur uske variants LLM serving me basic feature ban gaye hain — continuous batching ki tarah, lagbhag saare usages ke liye enabled rehte hain.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 6 — Essential LLM Optimization Techniques
← Previous06.1 · Batching & scheduling: dynamic, continuous, chunked prefill→ Next06.3 · Model compression: quantization, distillation, pruning
06.3Chapter 6 · Essential LLM Optimization Techniques

Model compression: quantization, distillation, pruning

LLMs ne astonishing capabilities unlock ki hain, lekin unki sheer size real-world production me bahut problems laati hai — high-performance GPUs acquire karna costly aur challenging hai. Inhe smartly shrink karna padta hai — yahin model compression techniques aati hain: quantization (parameters ki precision high-bit se low-bit karna), distillation (bade "teacher" ka knowledge chhote "student" me transfer karna), aur pruning (redundant weights/attention heads remove karna). Inme quantization practicality me standout hai — fast, effective, aur training pipeline me little ya no modification — isliye production me LLMs compress aur accelerate karne ki go-to choice hai.

Quantization: errors aur number formats

Quantization model ke parameters (weights, activations, KV cache) ki precision kam karta hai — FP32/FP16/BF16 se FP8/INT8 ya FP4/INT4 tak — lower accuracy ko behtar serving performance se trade karke. Do errors: rounding errors (number exactly represent nahi ho sakta, nearest value tak round hota hai — jaise 7.6 → 8, error 0.4) aur clamping errors (number range se bahar ho to max/min value par clamp hota hai — jaise 1,000 → FP8 max 448; 4,096 → 448 severe distortion hai). Modern techniques hard clamping avoid karke scaling strategies (symmetric/asymmetric) use karti hain, taaki relative magnitude preserve ho.

Numbers store kaise hote hain? Floating-point (FP) format: total bits = 1 sign bit + mantissa bits + exponent bits — sign bit positive/negative batata hai, mantissa precision control karta hai, exponent scale control karta hai. FP32 — 32 bits (1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa), range ±1038 — training ka standard. FP16 — 16 bits (1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa). BF16 — 16 bits (1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa), range ±1038 — FP16 se zyada exponent bits (range ke liye) aur kam mantissa (precision trade-off); BF16 aur FP32 ki exponent bits same (8) hain, isliye FP32→BF16 conversion me clamping ka risk nahi, sirf precision loss hota hai. Aaj most checkpoints FP16 ya BF16 me hote hain.

Quantized number formats do tarah ke hote hain: integer-based (INT8, INT4) aur floating-point-based (FP8, FP4 — likhte waqt ye aur popular ho rahe hain). Key difference hai data points ka distribution: integer-based format me data distribution completely uniform hoti hai — data points poori value range me evenly spaced hote hain aur number precision change nahi hoti. Floating-point me nonuniform distribution hoti hai — zero ke aas-paas zyada data points aur extremely large ya small numbers par kam data points. Ye isliye hai kyunki FP number values logarithmic hote hain: FP8 format me value = (−1)sign × (1 + mantissa) × 2exponent − bias. Jaise exponent badhta hai, representable numbers ke beech ki distance bhi badhti hai — 1.0 aur 2.0 ke beech kai values represent kar sakte hain (1.01, 1.001, etc.), lekin 1,000,000 aur 2,000,000 ke beech smallest step size bahut bada ho jaata hai (128 ya zyada). Model ke parameters ke data distribution (weights aur activation values) ke hisaab se best accuracy retain karne ke liye ek format doosre se choose karna chahiye.

Quantization serving me kaise madad karta hai?

Pehla reason hai data size: 7B model FP16 me 14 GB hai, INT8 me quantize karo to 7 GB — huge win jab GPU memory kaafi na ho; bade model ek machine/node me fit ho sakta hai, aur freed space KV cache ke liye use hoti hai (zyada concurrent requests, higher throughput). Chapter 5 se: decode phase me GPU memory bandwidth key hai — model chhota karne se data movement kam hoti hai, latency kam hoti hai. Aakhir me lower precision = faster computation: H100 par FP16/BF16 1979 teraFLOPS, FP8/INT8 3958 — bits aadhe karo to FLOPS typically double. Short me: quantization size, data movement aur compute time — teeno kam karta hai.

Weight-only vs weight-and-activation quantization

Do sabse common quantization strategies hain: sirf model weight quantize karna, aur weight + activation dono quantize karna. Aapne W4A16 aur W8A8 jaise notations dekhe honge — W model weights ki bit width aur A activation parameters (model ke middle-step inputs aur outputs) ki bit width batata hai. Example: W4A16 matlab 4-bit weights aur 16-bit activations; W8A8 matlab 8-bit weights aur 8-bit activations. Weight-only quantization me sirf weights quantize hote hain, activations nahi — size aur data movement ka benefit milta hai, lekin execution me lower-bit values ko wapas high-bit me dequantize karna padta hai (thoda overhead, faster computation nahi). Isse bachne ke liye mixed-precision kernels hain — Ampere GPUs ke liye Marlin, Hopper ke liye Machete — jo INT4 aur FP16 matrices ke beech multiplication ek pass me kar sakte hain, bina dequantization ke; kai log weight-only LLMs serve karte waqt inhe default on kar dete hain.

Weight-and-activation quantization size aur data movement kam karne ke saath compute-bound workload me higher FLOPS bhi deta hai, lekin activate karna zyada complex hai (activation har time change hoti hai). Scaling kab karni hai: dynamic scaling (factor inference me on the fly calculate — behtar accuracy, kam performant) ya static scaling (factor calibration dataset se pehle precalculate — zyada performant). Production me weight-only ke liye sabse common hai W4A16 (GPTQ/AWQ), weight-and-activation ke liye W8A8 (pehle INT8, ab FP8). Comparison: W4A16 size reduction 75%, FLOPS no change, prefill no change, decode improved (low batch par behtar) — best for long generation, latency sensitive, low batch. W8A8 size reduction 50%, FLOPS 2×, prefill aur decode improved (high batch par behtar) — best for long context, high throughput, high batch. Rule: single GPU/machine me fit karne ke liye 4× compression chahiye to W4A16; W8A8 se SLA meet ho jaaye to higher batch aur throughput push karo.

Data format par wapas: pehle W8A8 mostly INT8 me hoti thi (weights aur activations fixed ±127 range me clamp), ab bahut models FP8 variants (E4M3 aur E5M2) me deploy ho rahe hain — FP8E4M3 FP16 ke comparison me minimal accuracy loss ke saath performance improve karta hai, bina calibration ke. E4M3 inference ke liye zyada common hai (E5M2 se zyada precision; E4M3: 1 sign, 4 exponent, 3 mantissa; E5M2: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 2 mantissa). Lekin FP8 hamesha applicable nahi — NVIDIA me sirf Hopper aur Blackwell FP8 support karte hain; A100 ya older GPUs par expected gain nahi milega.

Hands-on: quantized models benchmark karna

Book ke notebook example me Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ko teen variations me vLLM server me host karke benchmark kiya gaya — original, GPTQ W4A16, aur W8A8 — TTFT, TPOT/ITL aur throughput record karke. Quantized models aksar seedha Hugging Face par mil jaate hain; khud quantize karna ho to GPTQModel, AutoAWQ aur LLMCompressor jaise libraries hain. Results: low-concurrency me GPTQ W4A16 best — original se latency aur throughput me lagbhag 300% gain; FP8 W8A8 lagbhag 150% gain deta hai (low batch me bottleneck GPU memory bandwidth hai, aur INT4 weight chaar guna chhota hai). High-batch me picture badal jaati hai: GPTQ W4A16 original se bhi slower ho jaata hai (computation abhi bhi 16-bit + dequantization overhead), jabki FP8 W8A8 behtar perform karta hai (activations bhi FP8). Agar W8A8 latency SLA satisfy kare, to zyada batches push karke cost bachao.

Doosri quantization methods aur accuracy trade-offs

Ab tak quantization mostly feedforward layers (FFN) par focus thi — KV cache quantization bhi certain cases me apply hoti hai: KV cache significant GPU memory le sakta hai, use quantize karne se memory free hoti hai, batch size badhta hai, aur prefix caching ko benefit milta hai. Lekin latency significantly kam nahi hoti — attention calculation abhi bhi high-precision me hoti hai, aur quantized KV cache ko dequantize karna padta hai — poora benefit lene ke liye quantized attention kernels ke saath combine karo. Aam taur par FP8 weight + activation se shuru karo, phir long context ya decode-heavy workload ke liye FP8 KV cache quantization add karo. GGUF quantization alag type hai — local, portable, low-resource deployments ke liye, CPU/Apple Silicon par LLMs chalane par focus karta hai.

Quantization ka sabse bada trade-off hai accuracy vs serving performance: agar quantized model original ki accuracy maintain nahi kar sakta, to saara performance gain bekaar hai. Fortunately, GPTQ W4A16, AWQ aur FP8 ne real-world accuracy metrics me minimal loss dikhaya hai — aur quantization se kabhi-kabhi bade model ka quantized version chalaya ja sakta hai (jaise FP16 8B ke bajaye FP8 12B — comparable latency, higher throughput, behtar accuracy). Patterns: model jitna bada, accuracy weight aur KV cache quantization ke prati utni sensitive; KV cache quantization accuracy me kam intrusive hai lekin performance gain bhi kam deta hai. Quantization ke baad accuracy LM Eval jaise tools se evaluate karo. Current research FP4, FP6 aur W4A8 ki taraf badh rahi hai (Blackwell GPUs ke saath) — per-tensor/per-channel scaling aur outlier-aware clipping ke saath ye lower-bit options near future me production me aayenge.

Quantization-aware training (QAT) vs post-training quantization (PTQ)

Accuracy issues mitigate karne ka ek powerful lekin complex tareeka hai quantization-aware training (QAT). Ab tak describe ki gayi saari techniques post-training quantization (PTQ) par focus thi — training pipeline tak access ki bilkul zaroorat nahi hoti, isliye aap foundation aur custom-trained models ko quantize kar sakte hain jinhe aapne necessarily train nahi kiya. Isliye practice me PTQ, QAT se bahut zyada popular hai — use karna easy hai aur phir bhi decently accurate hai. QAT training/fine-tuning phase me fake quantization perform karta hai, taaki model weights adjust karke precision loss compensate kar sake — isliye aggressive compression (jaise 4-bit) ke liye often eklauta reliable choice hai, jahan simple post-training rounding fail karwa dega. Comparison: PTQ training ke baad static weights par, difficulty much lower, higher bits (8+) par accuracy good, lower bits (4 aur neeche) par usually acceptable nahi, flexibility high. QAT training ke dauraan, difficulty much higher (extra compute), higher bits par good, lower bits par behtar aur acceptable, flexibility kam (scheme se tied).

QAT ka real-world example hai ek bade model provider ki open source model family — FP4 QAT se model size aggressively shrink kiya gaya: 120-billion-parameter wala model single 80 GB GPU par chalta hai (117B × 0.5 bytes = 58.5 GB), 20-billion-parameter wala 16 GB edge devices par (21B × 0.5 = 10.5 GB). Quantization sirf MoE layers par hoti hai (Chapter 7), lekin 90%+ parameters MoE me hain, isliye estimate valid hai. Trade-off: hardware aur inference stack ko woh FP4 format natively execute karna aana chahiye — Blackwell GPUs dedicated 4-bit support laate hain, Hopper FP8 Tensor Cores par based hai (mixed precision kernels se usable), aur sirf Ampere ya older GPUs hon to alag architecture choose karke apni quantization karna behtar ho sakta hai.

Distillation aur pruning

Model distillation teeno techniques me sabse bada potential rakhta hai — original model ka size kam karne ke bajaye ye naya chhota model train karta hai: bade "teacher" ka knowledge chhote "student" me transfer hota hai. Teacher ke outputs (sirf output token nahi, logits aur losses bhi) se student train hota hai — isliye teacher model tak full access chahiye, sirf API calls kaafi nahi. Example: 671-billion-parameter MoE model se 1.5B–70B tak distilled models — serving me 10 guna ya zyada size reduction. Benchmarks (original 671B vs distilled 70B): MATH-500 97.3 vs 94.5, GPQA Diamond 71.5 vs 65.2, LiveCodeBench 65.9 vs 57.5. Quantization vs distillation: accuracy drop quantization me low (usually ≤3%), distillation me much higher; speed gain quantization me 1.5×–3×, distillation me much more; ease — PTQ bahut easy, distillation costly (training cost original ka 10% tak). Guidance: distilled model available ho to pehle evaluate karo; na ho to quantization pehla step hona chahiye.

Model pruning aakhri compression idea hai aur sabse kam popular — production ke liye abhi aur research chahiye. Core idea: models overparameterized hote hain — redundancies prune karne se behtar compression aur serving performance mil sakti hai. Structured pruning model ke sections poori tarah remove karti hai, unstructured pruning individual weights remove karti hai; beech me 2:4 semi-structured sparsity hai — har 4 elements me se 2 prune (50% sparsity), aur Ampere/Hopper ke sparse Tensor Cores isse matrix multiplication me double speed de sakte hain. Ek sparse model example claim karta hai sparsity alone se 98% accuracy recovery, 30% higher throughput aur 20% lower latency.

import time
import requests


def check_vllm_status():
  max_retries = 100  # e.g. wait up to 60 seconds (30 x 2s)
  wait_time = 10

  print("⏳ Waiting for vLLM server to become healthy...")

  for i in range(max_retries):
      try:
          r = requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:8000/health")
          if r.ok:
              print("✅ vLLM server is healthy and ready!")
              break
      except Exception as e:
          print(f"Attempt {i+1}: Not ready yet...")

      time.sleep(wait_time)
  else:
      print("❌ Timed out waiting for vLLM server to start.")
  return
check_vllm_status()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import json

# Load the JSON lines from a local json saved containing benchmark results
with open("vllm_bench.json", "r") as f:
    data = [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import json
import numpy as np

# Parse raw data
#raw_data = """<...your data here...>"""  # keep the full string as before
#data = [json.loads(line) for line in raw_data.strip().split('\n')]

# Organize by rate (max_concurrency)
grouped = {}
for entry in data:
    rate = entry["max_concurrency"]
    model = entry["model_id"]
    ttft = entry["median_ttft_ms"]
    if rate not in grouped:
        grouped[rate] = {}
    grouped[rate][model] = ttft

# Sort the group keys (rates) for consistent display
sorted_rates = sorted(grouped.keys())

# Unique models across all groups
all_models = sorted(set(model for group in grouped.values() for model in group))

# Prepare bar positions and heights
bar_width = 0.2
x = np.arange(len(sorted_rates))
offsets = np.linspace(-bar_width*(len(all_models)-1)/2, bar_width*(len(all_models)-1)/2, len(all_models))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

for i, model in enumerate(all_models):
    ttft_values = [grouped[rate].get(model, 0) for rate in sorted_rates]
    bar_positions = x + offsets[i]
    bars = plt.bar(bar_positions, ttft_values, bar_width, label=model.split("/")[-1])

    # Add text labels above each bar
    for pos, val in zip(bar_positions, ttft_values):
        if val > 0:
            plt.text(pos, val + 10, f"{val:.1f}", ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8)


plt.xlabel("Max Concurrency")
plt.ylabel("Median TTFT (ms)")
plt.title("Median TTFT by Concurrency and Model ID")
plt.xticks(x, sorted_rates)
plt.grid(True, axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
plt.legend(title="Model")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

06.4Chapter 6 · Essential LLM Optimization Techniques

Prefix caching: RadixAttention, use cases, best practices

Software engineering me caching common technique hai — frequently accessed data ko fast, temporary storage me store karna, latency kam karne ke liye. ML me same requests ke prediction outputs cache karna production me common hai (client side, server side, ya dono). Example: Triton Inference Server har request (model name, version, inputs) ko hash karke output ke saath cache karta hai; hash mile to output seedha cache se milta hai. Caching kaam isliye karti hai kyunki storage compute se cheaper hai. Lekin LLM serving me general request-caching ka gain chhota hota hai — free-form text ki wajah se naive request hashing ki hit rate bahut low hoti hai.

Prefix caching kya hai?

LLM serving me widely used, proven, powerful caching technique hai prefix caching: poore prompt ko match karne ke bajaye, prompt ke "prefix" ko pehle process kiye gaye prompts se match kiya jaata hai — match mile to prefix part ka KV cache dobara compute nahi hota, cached data retrieve ho jaata hai (simple cases me seedha GPU memory se). KV cache CPU, local SSD, distributed GPUs ya external storage par bhi offload ho sakta hai (complex design Chapter 7 me). Prefix caching enabled na ho to har request ke baad uska KV cache GPU memory se remove ho jaata hai; enabled ho to caches space available rehne tak rakhe jaate hain, aur LRU mechanism se evict hote hain jab memory kaafi na ho.

RadixAttention

Prominent prefix-caching solutions me se ek hai RadixAttention, jo SGLang serving framework ke saath introduce hui. Ye ek radix tree (trie/prefix tree jaisi data structure) leverage karti hai, jo KV caches ke prefix strings ka track rakhta hai. Jab tree bahut bada ho jaata hai, to LRU mechanism se KV cache evict kiya jaata hai, recursively leaf nodes par. Example: do requests same head node share karti hain ("You are a helpful assistant") aur phir branch ho jaati hain — RadixAttention tree me corresponding nodes dhoondhkar (CPU memory me store) unke KV cache (GPU memory me store) ko bina recomputation ke reuse kar sakta hai.

Use cases: multiturn chat aur long context

Ab dekhte hain kin cases me prefix cache kaam karta hai. Teen prompts lo: Prompt 1 — "Hi, what is the weather like today?", Prompt 2 — "Hi, what is the weather like now?", Prompt 3 — "What is the weather like today?". Prompt 2, Prompt 1 ke prefix KV cache ko "Hi, what is the weather like…?" tak reuse kar sakta hai. Lekin Prompt 3, kyunki usme "Hi" prefix nahi hai, ko poora fresh recalculation chahiye hoga. Aap soch sakte hain — kya ye really powerful nahi hai? Lekin real-world LLM production me ye already bahut helpful prove ho raha hai. Do major scenarios jahan prefix caching best kaam karta hai: Scenario 1: Multiturn chat. User LLM ke saath multiple baar interact karta hai — prior chat history naye prompt ke saath concatenate karke rakhi jaati hai. Example: user poochhta hai "What is the weather like today?", LLM jawab deta hai "The weather is 70F, but with a likelihood of rain." Doosra sawaal "Could you tell me the actual possibility?" sirf akele nahi bheja jaata — prior interactions context ke roop me di jaati hain, taaki LLM samjhe user aaj baarish ki possibility pooch raha hai. Bina prefix caching ke, LLM doosra sawaal par pehli do lines ka prefill dobara karta; prefix caching ke saath woh lines KV cache me rakhi rehti hain aur reuse hoti hain. Jaise context lamba hota hai, bina caching ke wait times badhte jaate hain — khaas taur par TTFT, jo chatbots me customer experience dominate karta hai.

Scenario 2: Long context serving. LLMs ka context size badhta ja raha hai — 4,000 se 128,000 aur even 1 million tak — users input prompt me bahut relevant information feed kar sakte hain, bina hamesha RAG par rely kiye. Lekin lamba context prefill phase me TTFT ko intolerably lamba bana sakta hai — prefix caching KV cache save karke recomputation avoid karta hai, jab tak user prompt carefully reconstruct kare taaki prefixes vary na hon. Prefix caching ab lagbhag saare scenarios ke liye default enabled hai — modern serving engines minimal ya zero overhead achieve kar sakte hain, isliye lagbhag koi drawback nahi hai: cache hit rate sirf 5% ho, to bhi us 5% ki blazing TTFT speed worthwhile hai.

Best practices: cache hit rate badhana

Prefix caching ko best utilize karne ke liye aapka key target hona chahiye cache hit rate improve karna. Sabse pehla tareeka: prompts ko carefully structure karo — static parts (prefix hit ko prompt ke front par target karte hain) ko dynamic parts (suffix me user input) se cleanly separate karo. Template: <system> You are a helpful assistant. <context> Document: {relevant static context} <user> {dynamic questions}. Sirf "Document" ko "Documents" me badalna — ek extra letter — cache miss de sakta hai. Isliye prompt ko programmatically aur consistently assemble karna bahut important hai.

Yahi baat RAG use cases ke liye bhi sahi hai: high cache hit rate chahiye aur hit jitna lamba ho sake. Context aisa shape hona chahiye — "Document 1: <chunk_1> Document 2: <chunk_2> Document 3: <chunk_5> Document 4: <chunk_7>" — clean formatting aur sorted chunks ke saath. Pehli do lines me extra spaces omit karna ("Document1:" ya "Document 2:<...>") ya chunks ko galat order me rakhna cache miss cause kar sakta hai. Har baar same formatting aur structure maintain karo; consistent ranking aur proper deduplication longest prefix hits achieve karne me help karte hain — full context ka hit na mile, to bhi "...Document 3:" tak ka hit ek win hai.

Scaling prefix cache: routing aur multi-tenant isolation

Jaise traffic badhti hai, setup ko scale karna inevitable hai. Single instance me GPU me common prefixes cache karne ke liye kaafi space reserve karna important hai (doosre storage methods Chapter 7 me). Horizontally scale karne par smart routing layer important ho jaati hai: common techniques round robin, least connection, ya custom metrics (GPU utilization) hain — lekin prefix caching ke saath cache-aware routing chahiye, jo consistent hashing ki tarah prefixes aur instances ke beech affinity create karti hai, taaki requests us instance ko route hon jiske paas prefix KV cache pehle se hai. Isse saare instances ko saare prefixes cache karne ki zaroorat nahi hoti — GPU memory kam lagti hai aur evictions/recomputation avoid hote hain. Prefixes bahut lambe hon ya GPU memory kaafi na ho, to KV cache CPU/SSD par offload kiya ja sakta hai (Chapter 7).

Aakhir me, LLMs usually multi-tenant hote hain — alag customers same endpoint aur instance share karte hain (har customer ke liye alag instance bahut expensive hoga, aur batching se GPU utilization improve aur cost save hoti hai). Lekin prefix caching ke saath customer A ke prefixes accident se customer B jaise ho sakte hain, aur customer A latency observe karke doosre customer ka data infer kar sakta hai. Isolate karne ka tareeka: prompt me har customer ke liye unique ID inject karna — system prompt aur context ke beech user/session ID add karo, taaki alag customers sirf system prompt ko prefix share kar sakein, koi context share na ho.

Yaad rakho: Prefix caching storage ko compute se trade karta hai — pehle se computed KV cache reuse karke recomputation bachata hai aur TTFT ko lightning-fast banata hai. Ye multiturn chat aur long-context scenarios me excel karta hai, jo modern LLM applications me aur essential hote ja rahe hain. Cache hit rate hi king hai — prompt structure consistent rakho, static parts aage, dynamic parts peeche, aur routing ko cache-aware banao.

07.1Chapter 7 · Advanced LLM Optimization Techniques

Speculative decoding

Decode phase ko do ya teen guna tez karne wali ek technique hai — speculative decoding. Idea simple hai: ek chhota, tez model pehle agle tokens ka andaza lagata hai, aur bada target model unhe ek saath verify karta hai. Agar andaza sahi nikla, to ek forward pass me ek se zyada tokens mil jaate hain, aur inter-token latency (ITL) gir jaati hai. Ye khaas taur par lambi, reasoning-heavy generation ke liye useful hai, jahan decode hi bottleneck hota hai.

Kaam kaise karta hai — draft aur verify

Ye wahi pattern hai jo bade ML systems me pehle se chalta hai: pehle ek chhota model candidates ko filter karta hai, phir bada model sirf bache hue candidates par final result deta hai. Speculative decoding yehi kaam token level par karti hai. Ek iteration me chaar steps hote hain: pehle draft model K tokens speculate karta hai — K woh number hai jo aap tune karte ho. Phir target model ek hi forward pass me un K tokens ko verify karta hai.

Verification probability se hoti hai. Maan lo draft model kehta hai agla token "States" hoga, probability 0.6 ke saath. Agar target model us token ko 0.8 probable manta hai — draft se zyada — to token accept ho jaata hai. Agar target model use sirf 0.4 probable manta hai, to acceptance probabilistic hoti hai: 0.4 ko 0.6 se divide karke accept karne ka chance nikalta hai. Jaise hi ek token reject hota hai, uske baad ke saare draft tokens discard kar diye jaate hain, kyunki generation autoregressive hai — galat token ke baad ke tokens ka koi matlab nahi rehta. Reject hone par target model khud ek sahi token sample karta hai, apni modified distribution se, jisme rejected token ko exclude kar diya gaya hota hai.

Yaad rakho: speculative decoding accuracy ko compromise nahi karti. Verification step ki wajah se final output wahi hota hai jo bina speculation ke autoregressive model deta — reject hone par target model khud correct token daal kar wahi se restart karta hai.

Draft model kaise chunein

Performance ki kunji hai ek aisa chhota model jo tez bhi ho aur jiska acceptance rate bhi high ho. Target model ki same family ka model chunna madad karta hai, kyunki tokenizer aur pretraining same hone se acceptance rate badhta hai. Draft model ko aggressively quantize karna bhi safe hai, kyunki peeche target model fallback ke roop me hai hi. Agar aap training kar sakte ho, to target model se ek chhota draft model distill karna aam taur par kisi existing chhote model ko chunne se behtar hota hai — distillation se drafter aur target ke beech ka mismatch kam hota hai, acceptance rate badhta hai, aur technique zyada robust ho jaati hai.

Self-drafting: Medusa aur EAGLE

Alag draft model rakhne ke bajaye model khud apne future tokens ka andaza laga sakta hai — ise self-drafting kehte hain. Isse GPU memory bachti hai, deployment simple hota hai, aur target model ke saath alignment achha rehta hai. Medusa target model me halke prediction heads jodta hai: ek forward pass me original model pehla token deta hai, aur har Medusa head parallel me doosra, teesra aur chauthe token ke candidates generate karta hai. In candidates se kai candidate sequences banti hain, aur sabse lambi accepted sequence chuni jaati hai — ek forward pass me teen tokens mil sakte hain ("It is difficult") jabki bina speculation ke sirf ek milta ("It").

EAGLE tokens ko seedha draft nahi karta — woh future ke hidden states predict karta hai. Ek chhota auxiliary module target model ke future internal hidden states ka andaza lagata hai, aur target model un hidden states se tokens generate karta hai. Isse predictions zyada stable aur accurate hoti hain. EAGLE-2 ne dynamic draft tree joda, jo speculation ki length ko is hisaab se badalta hai ki current text kitna predictable hai, aur EAGLE-3 ne multiple layers ke features ko fuse karke accuracy aur badhai. Book likhte waqt EAGLE sabse high-performing self-drafting techniques me se ek tha — lekin iske liye extra training aur tuning chahiye hoti hai.

N-gram: sabse halka tareeka

Teesra option hai n-gram — na koi chhota model, na koi extra module. Ye pehle ke hisse se n adjacent tokens ki sequence uthata hai, use n-gram table me save karta hai, aur matching se agle token ka proposal deta hai. Example: "a quick brown fox" se trigram table me "quick brown" ke baad "fox" aata hai, to model "fox" propose karta hai aur target model use verify karta hai. Iska computational overhead bahut kam hai, aur ye do scenarios me khaas taur par powerful hai: structured outputs jaise JSON ya SQL, jahan generation highly deterministic aur repetitive hoti hai; aur jab LLM ko kisi preset template ko bharna ho ya likha hua text improve karna ho, jahan prompt se hi kai n-gram sequences reuse ho jaati hain. Overhead itna kam hai ki acceptance rate low ho to bhi net gain mil sakta hai — isliye book ise pehli speculative method ke roop me try karne ki salah deti hai.

K ko tune karna

K — maximum draft tokens — doosra crucial knob hai. K bada ho to speedup ka ceiling high hota hai, lekin acceptance rate low ho to bahut se draft tokens waste hote hain. K chhota ho to performance predictable rehti hai, lekin speculative decoding ka poora fayda nahi milta. Aam taur par best K 4 se 8 ke beech hota hai; bahut predictable generation jaise structured outputs ya agent function calling me K 16 ya 32 tak bhi ja sakta hai. Chhota K jaise 2 ya 4 ek decent, stable baseline hai, jahan se aap increment kar sakte ho. Frameworks me aap har position ka acceptance rate dekh sakte ho — jaise K = 6 par [0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.10, 0.02] ka matlab hai pehla token 80% accept hota hai, lekin paanchva aur chhatha 10% se bhi kam — to K kam karna samajhdari hai. N-gram ka overhead kam hai, isliye woh low acceptance rate ko bhi tolerate kar leta hai.

Limitations aur kab use karein

Speculative decoding sirf decode stage me madad karti hai. Acceptance rate low ho to extra computation waste hoti hai. Agar input context lamba hai aur prefill stage pehle se compute-bound hai, to ye kaam nahi karegi. Bade batches bhi bottleneck ko memory-bound se compute-bound me badal dete hain — tab bhi latency sudhar sakti hai, lekin extra computation throughput ko nuksan pahunchata hai. Do models ko ek shared GPU par efficiently chalana bhi mushkil hai, isliye recent focus self-drafting aur n-gram par zyada hai. Best scenario: workload latency-sensitive ho, prefill:decode token ratio low ho, real-world batches chhote hon aur GPU memory-bound bottleneck ho — tab aap thodi throughput ya TTFT trade karke behtar ITL aur overall latency pa sakte ho.

Hands-on: vLLM me results

Book ke lab me Qwen3-32B par chaar setups compare kiye gaye: vanilla vLLM, n-gram, improved n-gram, aur EAGLE-3. Concurrency 1 par improved n-gram ne vanilla se lagbhag 16% ka gain diya, aur EAGLE-3 ne throughput lagbhag double kar di (56.5 tokens/s vs 28.9 tokens/s). Concurrency 16 par dono n-gram variants vanilla se worse ho gaye — propose aur verify ka overhead high concurrency par CPU aur GPU load badha deta hai — jabki EAGLE-3 ab bhi aage tha, lekin gain chhota tha. EAGLE-3 ki TTFT vanilla se significantly lambi thi, extra speculative heads ke overhead ki wajah se. Matlab trade-off hai: TTFT prioritize karein ya ITL — ye aapke SLA/SLO par depend karta hai. Real world me setup dataset par bahut depend karta hai, isliye acceptance rate samajh kar multiple runs se decode method aur K chunna chahiye.

from openai import OpenAI


# Modify OpenAI's API key and API base to use vLLM's API server.
openai_api_key = "EMPTY"
openai_api_base = "http://localhost:8000/v1"
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=openai_api_key,
    base_url=openai_api_base,
)
model_id="Qwen/Qwen3-32B"

def run_vllm_bench_spec(
    *,
    base_url: str = "http://localhost:8000",
    model: str = "Qwen/Qwen3-32B",
    num_prompts: int = 16,
    spec_bench_output_len: int = 512,
    spec_bench_category: str | None = None,
    dataset_path: str = "Spec-Bench/data/spec_bench/question.jsonl",
    max_concurrency: int = 1,
    request_rate: float | None = None,
    burstiness: float | None = None,
    seed: int | None = None,
    result_filename: str = "spec_bench_decode.json",
    save_result: bool = True,
    append_result: bool = True,
):
    cmd_parts = [
        "vllm", "bench", "serve",
        "--backend", "vllm",
        "--base-url", base_url,
        "--endpoint", "/v1/completions",
        "--dataset-name", "spec_bench",
        "--num-prompts", str(num_prompts),
        "--model", model,
        "--max-concurrency", str(max_concurrency),
        "--spec-bench-output-len", str(spec_bench_output_len),
    ]

    if dataset_path is None:
        raise ValueError("Spec Bench needs --dataset-path pointing to the Spec-Bench file")

    cmd_parts += ["--dataset-path", dataset_path]

    if spec_bench_category:
        cmd_parts += ["--spec-bench-category", spec_bench_category]
    if request_rate is not None:
        cmd_parts += ["--request-rate", str(request_rate)]
    if burstiness is not None:
        cmd_parts += ["--burstiness", str(burstiness)]
    if seed is not None:
        cmd_parts += ["--seed", str(seed)]
    if save_result:
        cmd_parts.append("--save-result")
    if append_result:
        cmd_parts.append("--append-result")
    if result_filename:
        cmd_parts += ["--result-filename", result_filename]

    print("Running command:\n", " ".join(cmd_parts))

    import subprocess, shlex
    process = subprocess.Popen(
        cmd_parts,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
        text=True,
        bufsize=1,
    )
    try:
        assert process.stdout is not None
        for line in process.stdout:
            print(line, end="")
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("Interrupted by user, terminating benchmark...")
        process.terminate()
    process.wait()
    print(f"\nBenchmark finished with exit code {process.returncode}")
    return process.returncode

import time
import requests
from collections import deque

def tail_log(filename, n=2):
    """Read and print the last n lines of a log file."""
    try:
        with open(filename, 'r') as f:
            last_lines = deque(f, maxlen=n)
        print(f"\n📜 Last {n} lines from {filename}:")
        for line in last_lines:
            print(line.rstrip())
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"⚠️ Log file {filename} not found.")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"⚠️ Error reading log file: {e}")

def check_vllm_status():
    max_retries = 100
    wait_time = 10  # seconds

    print("⏳ Waiting for vLLM server to become healthy...")

    for i in range(max_retries):
        try:
            r = requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:8000/health")
            if r.ok:
                print("✅ vLLM server is healthy and ready!")
                tail_log("vllm.log", n=2)
                break
        except Exception:
            print(f"Attempt {i+1}: Not ready yet...")

        # Always print the last two lines of the log each iteration
        tail_log("vllm.log", n=2)

        time.sleep(wait_time)
    else:
        print("❌ Timed out waiting for vLLM server to start.")
        tail_log("vllm.log", n=2)

check_vllm_status()
run_vllm_bench_spec(max_concurrency = 1)
run_vllm_bench_spec(max_concurrency = 16)

import json
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ----- Load data -----
with open("spec_bench_decode.json", "r") as f:
    data = [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]

# ----- Variants & assumed ordering -----
# Assumes file order: [v0@c1, v0@c16, v1@c1, v1@c16, v2@c1, v2@c16, v3@c1, v3@c16]
variant_labels = ['vanilla vllm', 'n-gram', 'improved n-gram', 'eagle3']

if len(data) != 2 * len(variant_labels):
    raise ValueError(f"Expected {2*len(variant_labels)} rows, got {len(data)}")

# ----- Detect concurrencies -----
concs = sorted({d["max_concurrency"] for d in data})
if len(concs) != 2:
    raise ValueError(f"Expected exactly 2 concurrencies in data, found {concs}")
c1, c2 = concs  # e.g., 1 and 16

# ----- Build per-variant records for each concurrency -----
# records[(variant_idx, concurrency)] = dict
records = {}
for i, d in enumerate(data):
    v_idx = i // 2
    records[(v_idx, d["max_concurrency"])] = d

def metric_by_concurrency(key, scale=1.0):
    """Return arrays shaped (num_concurrencies=2, num_variants)."""
    vals_c1 = [records[(i, c1)][key] / scale for i in range(len(variant_labels))]
    vals_c2 = [records[(i, c2)][key] / scale for i in range(len(variant_labels))]
    return np.array([vals_c1, vals_c2])  # shape (2, V)

# ----- Extract metrics -----
total_tput = metric_by_concurrency("total_token_throughput")        # (2, V)
output_tput = metric_by_concurrency("output_throughput")            # (2, V)
durations   = metric_by_concurrency("duration")                     # (2, V)
mean_ttft   = metric_by_concurrency("mean_ttft_ms")                 # (2, V)
mean_tpot   = metric_by_concurrency("mean_tpot_ms")                 # (2, V)

# ----- Plot helper: x-axis = concurrencies, bars grouped by variant -----
def grouped_bars_by_variant(ax, values, title, ylabel, variants, concurrencies):
    """
    values: shape (num_concurrencies, num_variants)
    x-axis: concurrencies
    inside each concurrency bucket: one bar per variant
    """
    num_conc, num_vars = values.shape
    assert num_conc == 2, "This helper expects exactly 2 concurrencies."
    x = np.arange(num_conc)  # [0,1] -> [c1,c2]
    group_width = 0.85
    bar_width = group_width / num_vars
    # center the bars around each x
    offsets = (np.arange(num_vars) - (num_vars - 1) / 2.0) * bar_width

    for v_idx in range(num_vars):
        ax.bar(x + offsets[v_idx], values[:, v_idx], width=bar_width, label=variants[v_idx])

        # value labels
        for xi, val in zip(x + offsets[v_idx], values[:, v_idx]):
            ax.text(xi, val * 1.02, f"{val:.1f}", ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8)

    ax.set_xticks(x)
    ax.set_xticklabels([str(c) for c in concurrencies])
    ax.set_xlabel("Concurrency")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
    ax.legend(ncols=min(len(variants), 4), fontsize=9)

# =====================================================
# Plot 1: Total Token Throughput (tokens/s)
# =====================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
grouped_bars_by_variant(
    ax,
    total_tput,
    title="Total Token Throughput by Concurrency (grouped by variant)",
    ylabel="Tokens / s",
    variants=variant_labels,
    concurrencies=[c1, c2],
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# =====================================================
# Plot 2: Output Throughput (tokens/s)
# =====================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
grouped_bars_by_variant(
    ax,
    output_tput,
    title="Output Throughput by Concurrency (grouped by variant)",
    ylabel="Tokens / s",
    variants=variant_labels,
    concurrencies=[c1, c2],
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# =====================================================
# Plot 3: Duration (s)
# =====================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
grouped_bars_by_variant(
    ax,
    durations,
    title="Execution Duration by Concurrency (grouped by variant)",
    ylabel="Seconds",
    variants=variant_labels,
    concurrencies=[c1, c2],
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# =====================================================
# Plot 4: Latency (Mean TTFT vs Mean TPOT) — concurrency = 16
# =====================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

x = np.arange(len(variant_labels))
bar_width = 0.35

# Use index [1, :] for concurrency = 16
ttft_vals = mean_ttft[1, :]
tpot_vals = mean_tpot[1, :]

plt.bar(x - bar_width/2, ttft_vals, width=bar_width, label='Mean TTFT (ms)', color='steelblue')
plt.bar(x + bar_width/2, tpot_vals, width=bar_width, label='Mean ITL (ms)', color='darkorange')

# Add numeric labels
for pos, val in zip(x - bar_width/2, ttft_vals):
    plt.text(pos, val * 1.02, f"{val:.1f}", ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8)
for pos, val in zip(x + bar_width/2, tpot_vals):
    plt.text(pos, val * 1.02, f"{val:.1f}", ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8)

plt.xticks(x, variant_labels)
plt.ylabel("Latency (ms)")
plt.title("Mean TTFT vs Mean ITL (Concurrency = 16, grouped by variant)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
