07.2Chapter 7 · Advanced LLM Optimization Techniques

Multi-GPU/multi-node: data, tensor, pipeline, expert parallelism

100 billion parameters se bade models aam taur par ek GPU ki memory me fit hi nahi hote — aur fit ho bhi jaayein to latency SLA poori nahi hoti. Tab model ko multiple GPUs ya multiple nodes par baantna padta hai. Is section me chaar parallelism techniques hain: data parallelism (DP) throughput badhane ke liye, tensor parallelism (TP) aur pipeline parallelism (PP) bade models ko fit karne ke liye, aur expert parallelism (EP) mixture-of-experts (MoE) models ke liye.

Data parallelism: replicas aur routing

DP sabse pehchanane wala tareeka hai: model ki multiple copies (replicas) alag GPUs ya nodes par chalti hain, aur ek load balancer/router requests ko unme baant deta hai. Example: nau requests aayein to teen instances ko teen-teen mil jaati hain. Agar ek instance down ho jaaye, router uski taraf traffic bhejna band kar deta hai aur baaki do par bhejta hai — isse high availability milti hai. DP production traffic me har jagah use hota hai.

Routing strategies: round robin sabse simple hai — requests fixed order me baanti jaati hain, lekin kuch requests lambi hoti hain to load uneven ho jaata hai. Least connections us instance ko request bhejta hai jiske active connections sabse kam hon — ye workload ko dhyan me rakhta hai, lekin request ki complexity ya length ko nahi. Latency-based routing har instance ki real-time latency monitor karke sabse tez instance ko request bhejta hai, jisse tail latency kam hoti hai. Cache-aware routing prefix caching se judi hai: same prefix wali requests usi instance par bheji jaati hain jiske paas woh KV cache pehle se hai, taaki cache hit rate high rahe.

Modern LLM routing sirf rule-based nahi raha — ye real-time signals use karta hai: KV cache locality, KV cache hit percentage, instance ki KV cache space usage, raw input length, queued requests ki sankhya, processing me pending requests, already generate ho chuke tokens, aur request ka SLA/SLO latency budget. Aise smart routers ke examples hain KV Router aur llm-d router, jo prefill/decode worker routing aur KV offloading bhi support karte hain.

Tensor parallelism vs pipeline parallelism

Jab database ek machine me fit nahi hota to use shard karte hain — waise hi bada model ek GPU me fit nahi hota to use baant te hain. TP model ko width me kaat ta hai: har layer ka weight tensor tukdon me alag GPUs par jaata hai, har GPU partial computation karta hai, aur results combine karke poora layer output banta hai. PP model ko depth me kaat ta hai: layers ke contiguous blocks alag GPUs par jaate hain — jaise chaar layers hon aur PP = 2 ho to layers 1–2 ek GPU par aur layers 3–4 doosre GPU par. Data assembly line ki tarah sequentially behta hai.

Farq communication me hai: TP ko har layer par GPUs ke beech communication chahiye hoti hai, jabki PP ko sirf tab jab ek stage khatam ho kar agle par jaata hai. Isliye PP inter-GPU communication minimize karta hai — lekin iski apni problem hai: pipeline bubble. Agar ek stage slow ho jaaye, to aage ke stages wait karte hain aur GPUs idle rehti hain. Example: layer 2 slow ho to layers 3–4 wait karenge — ek GPU full utilization par aur doosri mostly idle.

Decision flowchart: pehle ek GPU hi kaafi hai?

Sabse pehla sawaal: kya multi-GPU chahiye hi? H100 GPU memory se compute core tak lagbhag 3 TB/s transfer karta hai, jabki NVLink se GPUs ke beech sirf lagbhag 900 GB/s — lagbhag teen guna slow. Isliye agar workload ek GPU me reh sakta hai, to wahi behtar hai — communication overhead se bachein. GPUs jodne se performance linearly nahi badhti: ek GPU jodne se memory aur FLOPS double hote hain, lekin interconnect bottleneck ki wajah se performance double nahi hoti. Kai baar ek higher-end, badi-memory wala GPU lena multiple lower-end GPUs se behtar hota hai. Aur yaad rakho: agar model memory me fit nahi ho raha, to pehle quantization try karo — FP8 quantization model size ko FP16/BF16 se aadha kar deti hai, aur W4A16 use quarter tak le ja sakta hai, agar accuracy allow kare.

Agar quantization ke baad bhi model fit nahi hota ya latency SLA nahi milti, to multiple interconnected GPUs wala node lo. Example: ek AWS P5.48xlarge node me aath H100 GPUs NVLink se jude hote hain, jabki aath alag P5.4xlarge nodes ke GPUs InfiniBand se baat karte hain, jo NVLink se kai guna slow hai. Node ke andar TP ideal hai jab NVLink ho — jaise aath GPUs par bada LLM chalana ek common setup hai. NVLink na ho aur sirf PCIe ho (jo device-to-host traffic ke liye bana hai, GPU-to-GPU ke liye nahi), to TP ke liye transfer speed bahut slow hoti hai — tab PP try karo ya alag instance lo, aur TP ko zero ya bahut chhota rakho.

Hyperscale setup me model ek node ke aath GPUs me bhi fit nahi hota — tab multi-node serving aati hai. Aam pattern: node ke andar TP (NVLink ki tez intra-node speed ke liye) aur nodes ke beech PP (kyunki inter-node communication slow hai aur PP data transfer minimize karta hai). Example: chaar-layer model ko TP = 8 aur PP = 2 ke saath do nodes par sharding, har node me aath GPUs. vLLM me ek node par ye simple hai: --tensor-parallel-size 4 --pipeline-parallel-size 2. Multi-node ke liye Ray ke saath vLLM use kar sakte ho, jo distributed execution manage karta hai.

Expert parallelism: MoE models ke liye

Modern LLMs me MoE layers hoti hain jo tokens ko dynamically alag experts ki taraf route karti hain — jaise Mixtral 8x7B, DeepSeek-V3 aur GPT-OSS family. MoE har token ke liye sirf kuch experts activate karke serving latency aur cost kam karta hai, lekin total parameters itne bade ho jaate hain ki ek GPU me fit nahi hote. EP experts ko multiple GPUs par baant deta hai: har incoming token sirf unhi GPUs par bheja jaata hai jahan uske selected experts loaded hain — inactive experts par unnecessary computation nahi hoti. EP = 2 ka matlab chaar experts wale model me experts do GPUs par bante hain. Practice me EP, TP aur PP ke saath combine karke best performance deta hai.

Yaad rakho: DP throughput aur availability ke liye hai (model replicate karo), TP/PP model ko fit karne ke liye hain (model baanto), aur EP MoE experts ko baantne ke liye hai. Teenon ko aksar ek saath use karna padta hai — aur hamesha pehle check karo ki quantization ya bada single GPU kaam kar jaaye ya nahi.

07.3Chapter 7 · Advanced LLM Optimization Techniques

Prefill-decode disaggregation

Prefill aur decode do bilkul alag kaam hain: prefill poora input sequence parallel me process karta hai aur compute-intensive hota hai, decode tokens ek-ek karke generate karta hai aur memory-bandwidth-bound hota hai. Ab tak dono ek hi GPU par chalte the, jahan ek phase doosre ka wait karta tha. Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation in dono ko alag GPUs par alag kar deti hai — taaki har phase ko independently optimize aur scale kiya ja sake.

Kyun alag karna? Chaar fayde

1. TTFT aur ITL ko independently optimize karo: alag use cases me input/output token ratio bahut alag hota hai. Input-heavy, interactive workload me TTFT key hai — PD disaggregation se aap prefill ke liye zyada resources laga kar lambi prompts ko tez process kar sakte ho. Decode ke liye bhi aisa hi kar sakte ho. Aur kyunki dono phases ek hi resource par interfere nahi karte, ITL zyada stable aur predictable hoti hai.

2. Workloads ko independently optimize karo: compute-heavy prefill ab memory-bound decode ka wait nahi karta, aur vice versa. Dono ke batch sizes bhi alag ho sakte hain: prefill me batch size itna bada rakho ki matrix multiplications GPU tensor cores ko saturate kar dein; decode me batch size itna bada rakho ki workload memory-bandwidth-bound na rahe, lekin ITL requirements bhi balance me rahein. Aap prefill aur decode par alag-alag parallel strategy bhi laga sakte ho — jaise TP aur PP ko ek stage ke liye alag tareeke se tune karna, doosre ko affect kiye bina.

3. Hardware ke zyada options: prefill compute-optimized GPUs par chal sakta hai (zyada FLOPS per cost), decode memory-optimized GPUs par (high memory bandwidth per cost). Example: H200 aur H100 ke FLOPS specs same hain, lekin H200 me zyada memory (141 GB vs 80 GB) aur zyada memory bandwidth (4.8 TB/s vs 3.35 TB/s) hai. To H100 prefill ke liye cost-effective hai, H200 decode ke liye behtar. Agar decode ke liye itni performance chahiye hi nahi, to L40S use karo — decent GPU memory, bahut kam cost. H100 prefill + L40S decode se optimal TTFT aur satisfactory ITL mil sakti hai, aur significant paise bachte hain.

4. Independent aur asymmetric scaling: prefill entry point hai, isliye burst-driven hota hai aur aggressive scaling strategy ke saath pair ho sakta hai; decode lambi अवधि tak tokens generate karta hai, zyada predictable aur stable hota hai. Dono ko apni demand ke hisaab se alag scale kiya ja sakta hai.

Architecture aur KV cache transfer

Architecture simple hai: saari incoming requests pehle controller par aati hain routing ke liye, phir prefill instances par jaati hain. Prefill instances KV cache banati hain, jo turant decode instances ko transfer kar di jati hai, aur wahi tokens generate karke request complete karti hain. Traditional aggregated serving me GPU instances dono phases karte hain; disaggregated serving me instances do groups me bante hain — dedicated prefill instances computation maximize karte hain, dedicated decode instances memory-bandwidth issues tackle karte hain.

Iska sabse critical step hai KV cache transfer — PD disaggregation ka fayda is transfer ke overhead se zyada hona chahiye. KV cache bahut bada ho sakta hai: ek aam 8-billion-parameter model, 1,024 input tokens ke saath, lagbhag 0.1–0.15 GB KV cache banata hai. Continuous batching me ek GPU ek second me dason requests process karta hai, aur real-world input length 1,024 ka multiple hoti hai — 10x length ka matlab per request 1–1.5 GB, aur 16 requests per second par lagbhag 25 GB per second transfer karna padta hai. NVLink intra-node bandwidth 900 GB/s ya zyada deta hai, InfiniBand inter-node 50–100 GB/s, aur bina RDMA ke PCIe sirf lagbhag 10 GB/s. To 25 GB/s NVLink par aaram se aur InfiniBand par theek hai, lekin PCIe par practical limits se zyada hai — isliye aise setup me prefill aur decode instances ko same server node ke andar rakhna zaroori hai, taaki communication NVLink se ho.

Transfer overhead kaise kam karein

Intra-node placement ki restriction ideal nahi hai — ye dono phases ko same hardware par force karti hai aur model parallelism limit karti hai. Inter-node setup me overhead kam karne ke liye RDMA to must hai hi, aur upar se ye optimizations hain: chunked transfer — poora KV cache ek saath bhejne ke bajaye chhote blocks me bhejo, jaise streaming video; block size tune kar sakte ho. Asynchronous, nonblocking transfer — compute aur communication overlap karein, taaki prefill GPU compute karte waqt transfer peeche se chalta rahe aur decode GPU jaldi shuru kar sake. Layer-by-layer transfer — KV cache per layer local hota hai, to jaise hi prefill ek layer ka compute khatam kare, uska KV cache transfer ho jaaye, aur decode us par kaam shuru kar de. Compression — KV cache ka size kam karo. In sab optimizations aur behtar scheduling ke saath PD disaggregation ka overhead per-request latency ke 1% se bhi kam tak laaya ja sakta hai.

Yaad rakho: PD disaggregation default nahi hai. Ise sirf bade models, heavy load, aur advanced TTFT/ITL tuning ki zaroorat ho tabhi use karo. Chhote models ke liye simple aggregated setup hi behtar hai — complexity aur transfer overhead fayde se zyada ho jaata hai.

07.4Chapter 7 · Advanced LLM Optimization Techniques

Advanced KV caching: long-context, LMCache hands-on

Coding copilots ko hazaaron lines ka source code yaad rakhna hota hai, conversational agents ko lambi interaction history, aur enterprise platforms ko bade document collections — sab ke liye long-context serving chahiye. Is section me KV cache ek implementation detail se badh kar serving stack ka first-class citizen ban jaata hai: use store, schedule, move aur evict karna — bilkul model weights ya input data ki tarah. Isi ke liye LMCache jaise systems bane hain.

RAG vs long-context CAG

RAG har query par relevant documents retrieve karke prompt me daalta hai — isse context length aur TTFT manageable rehte hain, aur responses fresh, tenant-specific knowledge se grounded hoti hain. Cache-augmented generation (CAG) iske ulta relevant context ko KV cache ke roop me cache karke reuse karta hai. Prefix caching ko CAG ka naive implementation samjho: saara relevant knowledge static prefix banao, dynamic prompt ko suffix ke roop me jodo, aur LLM prefix caching se KV cache reuse karke bahut low TTFT achieve kare.

Do shifts ne long-context CAG ko plausible banaya hai. Pehla: long-context models — context windows 100k se 1M tokens tak pahunch gayi hain, to tenant ka poora context seedha model me load ho sakta hai, bina baar-baar retrieval ke. Ye models "lost in the middle" problem ko bhi solve kar rahe hain — pehle LLMs context ke shuru aur ant ki information ko beech se zyada importance dete the. Doosra: efficient KV cache management — CPU memory, SSD, ya remote storage par offloading, aur cross-replica routing — se bade amounts ka knowledge KV cache ke roop me rakhna aur reuse karna possible ho gaya hai. Isse retrieval pipeline ki complexity kam hoti hai, bade input par reasoning smooth hota hai, aur kai baar responses bhi behtar aati hain.

Cost aur latency ka hisaab

Book ka example: system prompt 500 tokens ka hai, jo aasani se cache ho jaata hai. RAG me har user prompt par 10 chunks (500 tokens har ek) dynamically aate hain, jo vary karte hain, isliye KV cache hit rate bahut low hoti hai. Non-cached prefill: 5,000 (chunks) + 500 (user prompt) = 5,500 tokens. Long-context CAG me system prompt aur 100,000 tokens ka static context dono cache se aate hain — sirf user prompt dynamic hai. Non-cached prefill: sirf 500 tokens. Matlab CAG prefill me sirf 1/10th input leta hai, aur TTFT bhi usi hisaab se girta hai — RAG par TTFT 5 seconds ho to CAG par lagbhag 0.5 seconds. Isme RAG ka embedding aur vector-search time bhi nahi joda — real world me savings aur bhi badi hoti.

Lekin cost ka hisaab ulta bhi ho sakta hai. Late 2025 ke vendor prices: cached input regular input ka lagbhag 10%–25% hota hai (example: ek vendor par regular $1.25 per 1M tokens, cached $0.125; doosre par regular $3, cached $0.30). Ussi example me RAG ka cost lagbhag $0.007 per request, aur CAG ka lagbhag $0.013 per request — lagbhag double, kyunki CAG me 100,000 cached tokens hain, RAG me sirf 5,000. RAG ki offline indexing aur retrieval ki cost isme nahi jodi, lekin woh aam taur par LLM calls se bahut kam hoti hai — to is hypothetical scenario me RAG sasta rehta hai, bhale TTFT slow ho. Matlab: CAG TTFT jeetta hai, RAG cost jeet sakta hai — decision workload par depend karta hai.

Self-hosting: tiered offloading, compression, blending

Self-hosted models ke liye teen techniques hain. KV cache offloading: GPU memory se CPU memory par offload karne se lagbhag 3x KV cache space milti hai, SSD se 50x tak! Matlab 50 guna zyada long-context documents cache kar sakte ho, ya ek instance me multiple tenants ke documents. Aur ye extra space literally free hai agar aap pehle se usi instance par self-serve kar rahe ho. Redis ya S3 jaise distributed storage se aur bhi space mil sakti hai. Example: prefix caching me koi single instance ek se zyada long-context KV cache hold nahi kar sakta, to multiple replicas aur routing layer chahiye; CPU offloading se ek hi instance chaaron long-context KV caches rakh kar GPU aur CPU ke beech efficiently swap kar sakta hai — agar ek long context ya tenant ek instance ko saturate nahi karta, to ye 4x cost savings deta hai, saal me millions of dollars.

KV cache compression: traditional KV cache quantization, ya CacheGen jaise advanced tareeke jo KV cache ko uski distribution ke hisaab se compact bitstream me encode karte hain — size significantly kam hota hai, quality high rehti hai, aur transfer tez hota hai, bina decompression me zyada GPU overhead ke. Isse GPU memory me zyada batch aur zyada context cache ho pata hai. KV cache blending (CacheBlend): RAG ke liye — alag RAG chunks ke KV caches ko merge karna. LLMs sirf prefixes match kar sakte hain, to alag chunks ya alag order me same chunks se KV cache miss hota hai aur full recomputation hoti hai. Naive concatenation kaam nahi karti, kyunki self-attention ko cross-token interactions chahiye hoti hain — baad wale tokens ko poori prior history attend karni hoti hai. CacheBlend sirf KV cache ka chhota subset selectively recompute karta hai (default 15%, blend_recompute_ratios se tune kar sakte ho) — full recomputation ka cost bachta hai, aur quality me bahut minimal drop aata hai.

Hands-on: LMCache vLLM ke saath

Lab me Qwen3-14B ko do setups me host kiya gaya: vanilla vLLM (default prefix caching) aur vLLM + LMCache (local CPU offloading, 150 GB CPU memory). Enable karna simple hai: environment variables set karo (LMCACHE_USE_EXPERIMENTAL=True, LMCACHE_LOCAL_CPU=True, LMCACHE_MAX_LOCAL_CPU_SIZE=150.0) aur vLLM ko --kv-transfer-config me LMCacheConnectorV1 aur kv_both role ke saath start karo. SSD offloading bhi available hai (LMCACHE_LOCAL_DISK aur max disk size se).

Benchmark 1: 30 sequential requests, har ek unique prefix ke saath, phir wahi 30 reverse order me. Cold start me — zero KV cache hits — LMCache hamesha vanilla se slow tha, KV cache handling ke overhead ki wajah se. Matlab: agar workload me KV cache hits zyada expected nahi hain, to LMCache ke bina vLLM behtar hai, aur short prefixes ya bahut random requests ke liye wahi default hona chahiye. Warm-up ke baad, pehle nau requests dono setups me barabar the (sab GPU memory me the), lekin dasve request ke baad vanilla vLLM ki latency cold-processing level par wapas chadh gayi — purana cache LRU eviction se nikal gaya tha — jabki LMCache CPU memory se cache retrieve karne laga. CPU se retrieval GPU se slow hoti hai, lekin full prefill se bahut tez: 1 second vs 6–7 seconds.

Benchmark 2: 20 alag long-context requests, teen waves me — pehle cold sequential, phir wahi 20 dobara, phir 5 concurrent requests ke saath. Vanilla vLLM 20 prefixes store nahi kar saka, to uska median TTFT LMCache se bahut zyada tha; concurrent load par gap aur bada ho gaya, kyunki same GPU memory ko KV cache aur paanch concurrent requests ke activations dono sambhalne the. Throughput me LMCache ne vanilla ko lagbhag 16x peeche chhoda — vanilla lagbhag 4,700 tokens/s par bottleneck ho gaya tha.

Yaad rakho: modern LLM serving ek hierarchical stack hai — neeche CUDA/Triton kernels, uske upar execution engine (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM), phir cache-management layer (vLLM KV manager, LMCache), aur sabse upar routing aur orchestration layer (jaise Dynamo aur llm-d) jo request ko sahi prefill/decode worker aur optimal instance par bhejta hai. Bottleneck kisi bhi layer par ho sakta hai — isliye tuning saare layers me concert me karni padti hai.

import time
import requests
from collections import deque

def tail_log(filename, n=2):
    """Read and print the last n lines of a log file."""
    try:
        with open(filename, 'r') as f:
            last_lines = deque(f, maxlen=n)
        print(f"\n📜 Last {n} lines from {filename}:")
        for line in last_lines:
            print(line.rstrip())
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"⚠️ Log file {filename} not found.")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"⚠️ Error reading log file: {e}")

def check_vllm_status():
    max_retries = 100
    wait_time = 10  # seconds

    print("⏳ Waiting for vLLM server to become healthy...")

    for i in range(max_retries):
        try:
            r = requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:8000/health")
            if r.ok:
                print("✅ vLLM server is healthy and ready!")
                tail_log("vllm.log", n=2)
                break
        except Exception:
            print(f"Attempt {i+1}: Not ready yet...")

        # Always print the last two lines of the log each iteration
        tail_log("vllm.log", n=2)

        time.sleep(wait_time)
    else:
        print("❌ Timed out waiting for vLLM server to start.")
        tail_log("vllm.log", n=2)

check_vllm_status()

def print_output_online(
    client,
    prompt: list[str],
    sampling_params: SamplingParams,
    req_str: str,
):
    # Should be able to see logs like the following:
    # `LMCache INFO: Storing KV cache for 6006 out of 6006 tokens for request 0`
    # This indicates that the KV cache has been stored in LMCache.
    start = time.time()
    completion = client.completions.create(model=model_id,
                                              prompt=prompt)
    print("Completion result:", completion)
    print("-" * 50)
    # for output in outputs:
    #     generated_text = output.outputs[0].text
    #     print(f"Generated text: {generated_text!r}")
    time_elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Generation took {time_elapsed:.2f} seconds, "
          f"{req_str} request done.")
    print("-" * 50)
    return time_elapsed

time_cold_lmcache = []
for i in range(30)[::-1]:
    print('First time', i)
    shared_prompt = f"Hello this is now a brand new prompt, how are you? {i}"
    auto_prompt = shared_prompt*2000 + "Hello, my name is"

    time_cold_lmcache.append(print_output_online(client, auto_prompt, sampling_params, "auto"))

time_warm_lmcache = []
for i in range(30):

def run_vllm_bench(
    base_url="http://localhost:8000",
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-14B",
    num_prompts=20,
    num_prefixes=20,
    prefix_len=40000,
    suffix_len=10,
    output_len=20,
    max_concurrency=1,
    result_filename="longctx_40k.json",
    request_rate=None,
    burstiness=None,
    seed=None,
):
    """
    Run vLLM benchmark with real-time streaming of stdout/stderr.
    """

    cmd = f"""
    vllm bench serve \
      --backend vllm \
      --base-url {base_url} \
      --endpoint /v1/completions \
      --dataset-name prefix_repetition \
      --prefix-repetition-num-prefixes {num_prefixes} \
      --prefix-repetition-prefix-len {prefix_len} \
      --prefix-repetition-suffix-len {suffix_len} \
      --prefix-repetition-output-len {output_len} \
      --num-prompts {num_prompts} \
      --save-result \
      --append-result \
      --result-filename {result_filename} \
      --model {model} \
      --max-concurrency {max_concurrency}
    """

    if request_rate is not None:
        cmd += f" --request-rate {request_rate}"
    if burstiness is not None:
        cmd += f" --burstiness {burstiness}"
    if seed is not None:
        cmd += f" --seed {seed}"

    print("Running command:\n", cmd)

    # Stream stdout/stderr line-by-line in real time
    process = subprocess.Popen(
        shlex.split(cmd),
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
        text=True,
        bufsize=1,
    )

    try:
        for line in process.stdout:
            print(line, end="")  # print without double newlines
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("Interrupted by user, terminating benchmark...")
        process.terminate()

    process.wait()
    print(f"\nBenchmark finished with exit code {process.returncode}")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import json
import numpy as np

with open("longctx_40k.json", "r") as f:
    data = [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]

# Order in file is assumed:
# 0: lmcache cold, 1: lmcache warm, 2: lmcache warm concurrent,
# 3: vllm cold,    4: vllm warm,    5: vllm warm concurrent

# Extract metrics (TTFT -> seconds)
median_ttft = [entry["median_ttft_ms"] / 1000 for entry in data]
p99_ttft = [entry["p99_ttft_ms"] / 1000 for entry in data]
total_token_throughput = [entry["total_token_throughput"] for entry in data]

# Keep only WARM / WARM CONCURRENT (drop cold)
group_labels = ["Warm", "Warm Concurrent"]
lmcache_median = [median_ttft[1], median_ttft[2]]
vllm_median    = [median_ttft[4], median_ttft[5]]

lmcache_p99 = [p99_ttft[1], p99_ttft[2]]
vllm_p99    = [p99_ttft[4], p99_ttft[5]]

lmcache_tput = [total_token_throughput[1], total_token_throughput[2]]
vllm_tput    = [total_token_throughput[4], total_token_throughput[5]]

def plot_comparison(lm_vals, vllm_vals, metric_name, ylabel):
    x = np.arange(len(group_labels))
    bar_width = 0.35

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    plt.bar(x - bar_width/2, lm_vals, bar_width, label='LMCache')
    plt.bar(x + bar_width/2, vllm_vals, bar_width, label='vLLM')

    # Labels
    for pos, val in zip(x - bar_width/2, lm_vals):
        plt.text(pos, val * 1.01 if val >= 0 else val - abs(val)*0.05,
                 f"{val:.2f}", ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8)
    for pos, val in zip(x + bar_width/2, vllm_vals):
        plt.text(pos, val * 1.01 if val >= 0 else val - abs(val)*0.05,
                 f"{val:.2f}", ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8, color='gray')

    plt.xlabel("Execution Mode")
    plt.ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.title(f"{metric_name} Comparison (LMCache vs vLLM)")
    plt.xticks(x, group_labels)
    plt.grid(True, axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
    plt.legend()
    plt.ylim(bottom=0)  # start y-axis at 0
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# Plots
plot_comparison(lmcache_median, vllm_median, "Median TTFT", "Median TTFT (s)")
plot_comparison(lmcache_p99,    vllm_p99,    "P99 TTFT",    "P99 TTFT (s)")
plot_comparison(lmcache_tput,   vllm_tput,   "Total Token Throughput", "Total Token Throughput (tokens/s)")

08.1Chapter 8 · LLM Serving Frameworks

Specialized frameworks kyun chahiye

LLM era se pehle bhi model serving frameworks the — jaise TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, aur NVIDIA Triton. Lekin woh image recognition aur structured data inference jaise workloads ke liye bane the: chhote inputs, fixed-shape tensors, predictable latency, aur batch processing hi main optimization. LLM serving fundamentally alag hai — isliye ek nayi class ke specialized LLM serving frameworks aaye: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, aur llama.cpp.

LLM serving ki paanch nayi challenges

  • Autoregressive generation: LLM ek-ek token generate karta hai. Image model ke ulta, ek inference session seconds ya minutes tak khula reh sakta hai.
  • Context length explosion: prompts kuch tokens se lekar hundreds of thousands ya ek million tokens tak ho sakte hain. KV cache memory management critical bottleneck ban jaata hai.
  • Continuous batching: input aur output lengths requests ke beech bahut vary karti hain — static batching GPUs ko underutilize karta hai.
  • Streaming requirements: users ko hundreds of milliseconds me time to first token (TTFT) chahiye, aur uske baad continuous token streaming.
  • Resource utilization: GPUs mehenge hain. Fragmentation ya idle tokens ki wajah se GPU FLOPS waste karna scale par acceptable nahi hai.

Ek aur farq ye hai ki traditional frameworks me model ek request ko ek baar me process karke result deta tha — fixed input, fixed output. LLM me input aur output dono variable hain, aur generation ke dauraan KV cache har naye token ke saath badhta hai. Isliye memory management ko request ke lifetime ke saath dynamically manage karna padta hai, na ki ek baar allocate karke bhool jaana. Specialized frameworks isi liye paged attention jaise ideas laaye — KV cache ko blocks me baant kar waste kam karna — aur chunked prefill jaise ideas, taaki lambi prompt decode ko block na kare. Ye optimizations general-purpose stack me add-on ke roop me nahi, framework ke core design me hain.

Is chapter me chaar widely adopted open source frameworks cover hote hain: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, aur llama.cpp. Har ek ki apni philosophy, hardware footprint aur battle-tested technology hai, aur sabke peeche active communities aur badhti hui production usage hai.

Ye chapter pehle ye samjhata hai ki specialized frameworks kyun zaroori hain, phir vLLM ka deep dive karta hai — architecture, initialization aur request-handling pipeline, request aur token-level scheduling, aur layered optimization strategy — taaki aapko intuition mile ki LLM frameworks andar se kaise kaam karte hain aur doosre frameworks ke trade-offs evaluate karna aasan ho. Aakhir me baaki frameworks ke concise, decision-oriented overviews aur framework compare karne ka evaluation method diya gaya hai.

Yaad rakho: general-purpose serving stack me LLM daalna kaam to karega, lekin token-level scheduling, KV-cache management, long-context memory handling aur streaming-first execution ke bina woh GPU ka poora fayda nahi utha payega — aur scale par yehi farq cost aur latency tay karta hai.

08.2Chapter 8 · LLM Serving Frameworks

vLLM deep dive: architecture, workflows, scheduler

vLLM sabse popular open source LLM serving frameworks me se ek hai — iski adoption open source communities aur enterprise teams dono me tezi se badhi hai, kyunki ye scale par LLMs chalane ke pain points solve karta hai: lambe prompts, high memory demands, aur ek saath kai users serve karna. Iska core hai paged KV caching + continuous batching, aur upar se quantization, speculative decoding, streaming, aur multi-GPU/distributed execution. Log ise pasand karte hain kyunki ye "just works" — battle-tested hai, open source aur self-fine-tuned models ke saath integrate karna aasan hai, aur bina deep system-level tuning ke GPU efficiency maximize karta hai.

Do tareeke: LLM class aur API Server

vLLM ek single model service setup ke liye optimized hai — har instance startup par ek model initialize karta hai. Use karne ke do primary tareeke hain: LLM class (in-process library) — pure-Python local interface, offline inference ke liye, bina alag server ya web API ke; existing service ya batch workflow me plug karne ke liye ideal, tight control aur low overhead ke saath. API Server — standalone HTTP server, multi-client aur production use ke liye, streaming ke saath, OpenAI-compatible Chat/Completions API se easy integration. Example: llm = LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen3-7B-Instruct", dtype="float16", max_model_len=32768, gpu_memory_utilization=0.8) aur phir llm.generate(prompts, sampling); server ke liye vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-7B-Instruct --dtype bfloat16 --max-model-len 32768 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8, aur curl se http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions par call.

Architecture: LLMEngine, EngineCore, Scheduler, ModelExecutor

LLMEngine high-level interface aur main entry point hai — public API jisse users interact karte hain, aur jo saare components ko coordinate karta hai, request lifecycle, request queue aur configuration manage karta hai. EngineCore central orchestrator hai — "inner loop" jo model executor, output processor aur scheduler ko integrate karta hai aur poora request-processing pipeline manage karta hai.

Scheduler poori inference pipeline ka "traffic controller" hai — limited compute resources (GPU memory, KV cache blocks, processing capacity) ko competing requests me efficiently allocate karta hai, throughput maximize karte hue fairness banaye rakhta hai. Ye system-wide, model-agnostic optimizations ka zimmedar hai: token-level scheduling, dynamic batching, prefix caching, chunked prefill. Model-specific optimizations ModelExecutor aur GPUWorker ke andar hoti hain. Scheduler apna execution plan SchedulerOutput naam ki data structure me pack karta hai — ModelExecutor ke liye "work order": kaunsi requests ka batch, har ek ko kitne tokens, input data, parameters, allocated memory blocks, aur special processing requirements. ModelExecutor isse actual GPU batch taiyaar karta hai (flattened input IDs, attention metadata, KV cache blocks), forward pass chalata hai, aur results scheduler ko wapas deta hai.

ModelExecutor, GPUWorker, GPUModelRunner layered architecture hai: ModelExecutor multiple worker processes orchestrate aur manage karta hai; GPUWorker har worker process me chalne wala interface hai, device/model lifecycle manage karta hai; GPUModelRunner asal me neural network execute karta hai. Ye separation har component ko apni zimmedari par focus karne deta hai, clean interfaces ke saath.

Model initialization workflow (multi-process)

Production me sabse common setup multi-process hai — chaar steps: 1. LLM() instance banate hi main process me saare major components initialize hote hain — LLMEngine, Scheduler, KVCacheManager, MultiProcessExecutor — aur configuration distribute hoti hai. Example me Qwen model, tensor_parallel_size=4, distributed_executor_backend="mp" (single-node multi-GPU ke liye; cross-machine ke liye "ray" backend). 2. MultiProcessExecutor chaar worker processes spawn karta hai aur rpc_broadcast_mq message queue setup karta hai signals aur commands ke liye. 3. Har worker process me GPUWorker CUDA device setup karta hai, cross-process communication establish karta hai, aur model load/initialize karta hai; results wapas bhejne ke liye worker_response_mq hoti hai. 4. GPUModelRunner model registry se sahi implementation dhoondhta hai (example me Qwen3NextForCausalLM) aur weights GPU par load karta hai.

Generation-request execution workflow

llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params) ke andar paanch steps hote hain: 1. Processor raw inputs ko validate aur preprocess karke Request object banata hai, prompts tokenize karke. 2. LLMEngine execution loop me EngineCore ko repeatedly call karta hai; Scheduler decide karta hai agla batch kaunsa ho aur kitne tokens process hon — yahi paged attention aur continuous batching apply hoti hai. 3. EngineCore scheduled tokens (SchedulerOutput) MultiProcessExecutor ko deta hai. 4. MultiProcessExecutor request ko worker process ko deta hai aur GPU worker model forward pass chalata hai — yahi asal model execution hoti hai. 5. EngineCore model output ko output processor ko deta hai, jo final response banata hai. Dhyaan do: asal model execution aur model-specific optimization GPUWorker ke paas hai, jabki general planning aur optimization Scheduler orchestrate karta hai.

Scheduler deep dive: token-level scheduling

Scheduler request ka poora lifecycle manage karta hai — arrival se completion tak — WAITING aur RUNNING queues me organize karke, GPU memory, KV cache blocks aur token budgets ke hisaab se dynamic decisions leta hai. Iski sabse badi strength hai unified token-based scheduling: request-based scheduler request ko poora unit manta hai, lekin vLLM ka Scheduler token-by-token kaam karta hai. Har scheduling step me woh decide karta hai har request kitne tokens process kar sakti hai, global constraints (max batch size, GPU memory limits) ka samman karte hue. Isse finer-grained control milta hai: token budgets allocate karna, attention states ke liye KV cache blocks manage karna, aur multimodal models me encoder inputs support karna.

Scheduler ek optimization integration hub bhi hai: prefix caching, speculative decoding, chunked prefill aur distributed KV cache transfers ko coordinate karta hai — aur adaptive decisions leta hai ki kab aur kaise ye optimizations apply karni hain, request characteristics, resource availability aur system state ke hisaab se. Scheduling cycle ki shuruaat schedule state banane se hoti hai — nayi requests, resume karni hain paused requests, running requests, preempted requests — aur available resources ka hisaab (kitne decoding tokens bache, multimodal ke liye kitni encoder capacity bachi). Phir do prioritized waves: pehle running requests (kyunki woh KV cache blocks occupy kar chuke hain), phir waiting queue — jo bachi hui token aur encoder budgets me fit ho, woh activate hoti hain. Resources constrained hon to scheduler lower-priority work ko preempt kar sakta hai. Aakhir me post-processing phase — kaunse LoRA adapters active hone chahiye, multimodal ke liye encoder inputs taiyaar karna, speculative decoding ke draft-token predictions finalize karna — aur phir SchedulerOutput assemble hota hai.

Implementation level par Scheduler num_computed_tokens (already processed tokens) aur num_tokens_with_spec (prompt + output + speculative tokens, total process karne hain) ke beech ka gap minimize karne ki koshish karta hai — aur yehi gap optimization strategies ki chain ko drive karta hai. Important separation: request queues order tay karti hain, aur token-level comparison batata hai har request ko kitne tokens execute karne ki permission hai. Isse fairness aur efficiency ek saath milti hain. Examples: chunked prefill me naye tokens long_prefill_token_threshold se zyada nahi hote; prefix caching me scheduler pehle local cached blocks dhoondhta hai (kv_cache_manager.get_computed_blocks), phir external connector se matched tokens.

Layered optimization strategy

vLLM ki optimization philosophy hai: optimization sahi level par honi chahiye. LLMs tezi se evolve karte hain — naye architectures, attention mechanisms, hardware tricks har mahine aate hain — to vLLM ek model family ya hardware ke liye optimizations hardcode nahi kar sakta. Isliye chaar levels hain: Scheduler — system-wide, model-agnostic (fairness, efficiency, scalability); ModelExecutor — model architecture-specific (jaise Transformer models ke liye fused attention kernels, multimodal encoders ke liye specialized operators); Model layer — component-specific (attention layer aur feedforward block par KV cache reuse, flash attention, layer-wise operator fusion); CustomOp — hardware-specific (CUDA kernels, tensor-core acceleration, quantized operators). Isse Scheduler model-specific details se clutter nahi hota, aur naya architecture ya hardware aane par optimization sahi layer me slot ho jaati hai, bina poora system redesign kiye.

import sglang as sgl

from sglang.utils import async_stream_and_merge, stream_and_merge

llm = sgl.Engine(model_path="Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ")

prompts = [
    "Hello, my name is",
    "The president of the United States is",
    "The capital of France is",
    "The future of AI is",
]

sampling_params = {"temperature": 0.8, "top_p": 0.95}

outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params)
for prompt, output in zip(prompts, outputs):
    print("===============================")
    print(f"Prompt: {prompt}\nGenerated text: {output['text']}")

prompts = [
    "Write a short, neutral self-introduction for a fictional character. Hello, my name is",
    "Provide a concise factual statement about France’s capital city. The capital of France is",
    "Explain possible future trends in artificial intelligence. The future of AI is",
]

sampling_params = {
    "temperature": 0.2,
    "top_p": 0.9,
}

print("\n=== Testing synchronous streaming generation with overlap removal ===\n")

for prompt in prompts:
    print(f"Prompt: {prompt}")
    merged_output = stream_and_merge(llm, prompt, sampling_params)
    print("Generated text:", merged_output)
    print()

08.3Chapter 8 · LLM Serving Frameworks

TensorRT-LLM + SGLang + llama.cpp

vLLM ke alawa teen aur widely used open source frameworks hain, har ek alag philosophy ke saath: TensorRT-LLM NVIDIA GPUs par peak efficiency ke liye, SGLang structured generation aur agent applications ke liye, aur llama.cpp "runs anywhere" — laptops se edge devices tak — ke liye.

TensorRT-LLM: NVIDIA par maximum performance

TensorRT-LLM NVIDIA ki open source library hai high-performance LLM inference ke liye, sirf NVIDIA GPUs par. Model checkpoint se ye highly tuned TensorRT (TRT) engines build karta hai, aur Python/C++ runtimes deta hai modern serving capabilities ke saath: in-flight batching (TensorRT-LLM ka continuous batching), paged KV cache, speculative decoding, multi-precision quantization (FP8/FP4/INT4/INT8), aur tensor/pipeline parallelism. Ye NVIDIA serving ecosystem se tightly integrate hota hai — khaas taur par Dynamo aur Triton ke saath. High-level LLM API ka example simple hai: llm = LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen3-7B"), phir SamplingParams(temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95) ke saath llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params).

Iska core objective hai NVIDIA GPUs ki maximum practical performance dikhana aur Tensor Cores aur CUDA kernels ko poori tarah exploit karna. Ye best hai un organizations ke liye jo NVIDIA hardware aur serving stack par standardized hain aur production me best-in-class efficiency aur throughput chahte hain. Trade-off clear hai: peak efficiency NVIDIA par, lekin hardware lock-in.

SGLang: structured generation aur agents ke liye

SGLang naya entrant hai, jo structured-generation aur agent applications ko target karta hai. Ye open source, high-performance serving framework hai LLMs aur vision-language models (VLMs) ke liye. Ye fast backend runtime (kernels, caching, scheduling) ko flexible frontend language aur API (OpenAI-compatible aur native) ke saath co-design karta hai, taaki generation tez aur zyada controllable ho.

Headline features: RadixAttention (calls ke across prefix/KV reuse), continuous batching, paged attention/KV, speculative decoding (EAGLE-2/3), chunked prefill, structured outputs (JSON/regex/EBNF), multi-LoRA batching, aur parallelism modes (tensor/pipeline/expert/data). Example: llm = sgl.Engine(model_path="Qwen/Qwen3-7B") aur phir llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params). TensorRT-LLM se alag, SGLang broader hardware range target karta hai — official docs me NVIDIA (H100/Blackwell), AMD Instinct, CPU, TPU, Jetson Orin, aur Ascend deployments cover hote hain — jo multi-vendor fleets ke liye attractive hai.

Functionally SGLang vLLM ka peer hai: infrastructure portability, broad open-model support, aggressive performance optimizations, scale-out routing, aur agentic, multistep prompts ke liye strong support. Practice me iski performance competitive hai — kuch workloads par kabhi behtar — jabki vLLM ki open source community aur ecosystem abhi badi hai.

llama.cpp: runs anywhere

llama.cpp ek lean, open source C/C++ inference stack hai jo modern open-weight LLMs ko lagbhag kisi bhi machine par efficiently chalata hai — laptops aur workstations se lekar on-prem servers aur edge devices tak. Models GGUF format me package hote hain (aam taur par Hugging Face checkpoints se repo ke scripts se convert karke). Built-in OpenAI-compatible HTTP server se serve kar sakte ho, ya experiments aur benchmarking ke liye chhote CLI tools use kar sakte ho.

Iska focus: minimal dependencies, fast startup, aggressive integer quantization (8/6/5/4-bit), aur portable CPU/GPU backends (SIMD wala CPU, plus optional accelerators jaise Metal, CUDA/ROCm, ya Vulkan). Baaki teen frameworks datacenter GPUs par high-throughput, low-latency serving optimize karte hain — multi-tenant batching, advanced scheduling, large-scale deployment features. llama.cpp iske ulta portability, simplicity aur cost efficiency ko peak throughput se upar rakhta hai. Example: Llama.from_pretrained(repo_id="Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF", filename="*Q8_0.gguf") se CPU par model load karke llm("Q: Name the planets...") chalao, ya create_chat_completion se chat API use karo.

Ye teen scenarios me strong adoption dekhta hai: local development (apni machine par built-in server, existing clients reuse karo — jaise RAG aur search systems); private aur on-prem assistants (saara data apne VPC ya device boundary ke andar); edge inference (laptops, desktops, Apple Silicon, chhote servers — 2- to 8-bit quantization aur portable backends se). Agar llama.cpp ko REST API se expose karna ho, to Ollama use kar sakte ho — ek higher-level framework jo llama.cpp (aur kabhi-kabhi doosre backends) ko wrap karke local LLM use ko simple aur developer-friendly banata hai.

Yaad rakho: har LLM application ko high-throughput serving nahi chahiye. Local inference me goals badal jaate hain — fleet-wide tokens per second nahi, latency aur responsiveness; low concurrency (aksar ek user) me bade batching aur complex schedulers ki value kam; footprint aur cost (memory, compute, power) primary constraints; aur privacy aur offline reliability first-class requirements. Is profile ke liye llama.cpp super-low-cost, low-ops option hai — bina per-token cloud charges ke aur bina data device se bahar bheje.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 8 — LLM Serving Frameworks
← Previous08.2 · vLLM deep dive: architecture, workflows, scheduler→ Next08.4 · Framework choose kaise karein
08.4Chapter 8 · LLM Serving Frameworks

Framework choose kaise karein

Framework chunne ka general idea hai: workload first, not hype — apne service-level objectives (SLOs), hardware aur operational reality se match karne wala framework chuno, flashiest benchmark wala nahi. Book ek six-step evaluation approach recommend karti hai, aur phir har framework ke liye clear recommendation deti hai.

Evaluation approach: chhah steps

1. SLOs se shuru karo, features se nahi. Apne targets likho: latency (TTFT, p95/p99), throughput (TPS/QPS), cost per token, quality constraints (structured JSON, safety), aur availability. 2. Apne use case ke real prompts analyze karo: prefill-heavy hai ya decode-heavy? Context length kya hai? Tool calls ya multi-turn chains hain? 3. Apples-to-apples comparison karo: saare contenders par same model, dtype/quantization, max sequence, batch/concurrency aur streaming settings use karo. 4. Operability measure karo: cold-start time, observability, autoscaling behavior, multi-tenancy fairness, upgrade friction, aur failure modes. 5. Hardware aur vendor lock-in ko account me lo: agar multiple vendors use karte ho (NVIDIA/AMD/CPU/TPU/edge), to portability ka weight bahut zyada hota hai. 6. Change ke liye plan karo: model swaps aur naye decoding tricks har hafte aate hain, to aisa framework chuno jise bina major surgery ke update kar sako.

Recommendations: kaunsa kab

  • vLLM — fastest path to production: broad model coverage aur Python-native workflow chahiye to vLLM chuno. Strong baseline performance, continuous batching, aur bada community aur ecosystem.
  • SGLang — agentic ya multistep workflows: strict JSON/regex (grammar-constrained) outputs aur multi-vendor portability ho to SGLang lo. Prefix/KV reuse, speculative decoding, aur scale-out clusters ke liye router milta hai.
  • TensorRT-LLM — all-in on NVIDIA: NVIDIA stack par peak tokens per dollar chahiye to TensorRT-LLM se shuru karo. First-class Triton aur Dynamo integration aur deep CUDA/Tensor Core optimizations ise NVIDIA hardware par efficiency leader banati hain.
  • llama.cpp — local, on-prem, ya edge: tiny footprint, low cost aur privacy by default chahiye to llama.cpp use karo. GGUF quantization (2- to 8-bit) aur portable CPU/GPU backends ise laptops, desktops aur chhote servers ke liye ideal banate hain.

Core takeaway: framework choice contextual hai. Kai teams online serving ke liye vLLM aur local development ke liye llama.cpp se shuru karti hain, lekin specific requirements — edge deployment, NVIDIA-centric optimization, strict JSON/grammar outputs, ya agent pipelines — aapko TensorRT-LLM ya SGLang ki taraf le ja sakti hain.

Yaad rakho: LLM serving tezi se evolve hota hai — naye architectures, kernels, schedulers, quantization schemes aur runtime features har mahine aate hain. Book ke authors har teen se chhah mahine me frameworks ko re-evaluate karte hain aur current SLOs aur hardware reality ke hisaab se best option chunte hain. Isliye ek framework abstraction layer banao aur clear exit plan rakho, taaki apps rewrite kiye bina frameworks swap kar sako. Goal permanent winner crown karna nahi hai — flexible rehna hai, taaki system agle wave par sawaar ho sake, usme doob na jaaye.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 8 — LLM Serving Frameworks

09.1Chapter 9 · LLM Optimization in Practice

Optimization plan

Optimization ek moving target hai: alag environments me "best" strategy badal jaati hai, aur resources limited hain, isliye har option ko brute-force nahi kar sakte. Is chapter me book Qwen3-14B model aur vLLM ko running example bana kar ek practical optimization process dikhati hai — pehle ek concise plan, phir use step by step execute karna, aur aakhir me battle-tested takeaways aur trade-offs. Lab code book ke code repository ke ch09 folder me hai, aur ek Jupyter notebook me complete lab code ke saath har step ke captured outputs bhi hain — taaki bina high-end GPU ke bhi process follow kar sako.

Goal: throughput maximize karo, latency acceptable rakho

Is exercise ka goal hai Qwen3-14B ki token throughput maximize karna ek single model instance par, online serving environment me — given time frame me jitne zyada tokens process kar sako. Higher token throughput seedha lower serving cost me translate hoti hai, kyunki processed tokens hi most LLM pricing models ka basis hote hain. Lekin ek trade-off yaad rakho: peak throughput aur minimal latency aksar conflicting goals hain. Higher throughput aksar batching ya queuing par depend karta hai, jo waiting time badha kar per-request latency badhata hai. Aur sirf lowest latency optimize karne ka matlab hai requests aate hi process karna, kam parallelism ke saath — resources underutilized, throughput low. Practice me aam taur par throughput improvement prioritize karte hain, latency ko acceptable range me rakhte hue — efficiency ka fayda, user experience compromise kiye bina. Is chapter me focus throughput par hai, lekin distributed serving jaise techniques bhi discuss hote hain jo responsiveness ko efficiency se zyada priority dete hain.

Aath steps ka plan

1. Hardware examine karo: GPU specifications review karo jo serving performance ko sabse zyada influence karte hain — GPU memory size, bandwidth, compute capability, aur NVLink interconnects. Ye benchmark results ko sahi tareeke se interpret karne me madad karta hai.

2. Benchmark traffic generate karo: representative benchmark traffic design karo jo real-world request patterns simulate kare — input data ke types, request length distribution, aur repetition settings (caching evaluation ke liye).

3. Evaluation metrics define karo: benchmarks chalane se pehle primary metrics tay karo — token throughput (TPS), time to first token (TTFT), aur end-to-end latency. Clear metrics se saare optimization setups par consistent evaluation hoti hai.

4. Model serving service setup karo: vLLM se model serving service start karo — environment taiyaar karo, GPU availability, memory consumption aur KV cache size verify karo, aur confirm karo model successfully load hua.

5. Qwen3 model ko vLLM par benchmark karo: default setup se baseline banao — throughput aur latency results collect aur analyze karo.

6. Quantized Qwen3 model ko benchmark karo: wahi benchmark quantized version (Qwen3-14B-AWQ) par repeat karo, aur baseline se compare karke dekho quantization ka GPU memory usage aur throughput par kya impact hai.

7. Additional optimization techniques apply karo: chunked prefill, speculative decoding, advanced caching, aur batching adjustments jaise strategies discuss karo — aur yahi benchmarking process se unke effects khud measure karo.

8. Distributed serving par benchmark karo: multiple GPUs aur alag GPU types par experiments karke samjho distributed serving kab beneficial hoti hai aur multi-GPU servers ko scalability ke liye kaise best utilize karein.

Yaad rakho: optimization universal "best" configuration dhoondhne ke baare me nahi hai — ye apne system ka dominant bottleneck samajhne aur sahi technique sahi level par apply karne ke baare me hai: hardware, model, ya scheduling. Pehle apna scenario samjho — business use case, traffic pattern, aur performance target — phir tune karo.
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 9 — LLM Optimization in Practice
← Previous08.4 · Framework choose kaise karein→ Next09.2 · Qwen3-14B end-to-end optimization (8 steps)
09.2Chapter 9 · LLM Optimization in Practice

Qwen3-14B end-to-end optimization (8 steps)

Ab plan ko execute karte hain — Qwen3-14B, vLLM, aur ek AWS EC2 g6e.2xlarge instance par single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Har step ke saath actual numbers hain, taaki aapko intuition mile ki har factor serving performance ko kaise affect karta hai.

Step 1: GPU hardware check karo (nvidia-smi)

nvidia-smi (NVIDIA System Management Interface) aam taur par pehla command hota hai jo aap NVIDIA GPU par chalate ho — GPU recognized hai, sahi configure hai, aur use se pehle idle hai ya nahi, ye check karne ke liye. Isse available GPUs, memory, temperature, GPU utilization, running processes, driver aur CUDA versions dekh sakte ho, aur performance bottlenecks diagnose kar sakte ho. Lab me key information: CUDA aur GPU driver version (serving framework ke saath compatible hone chahiye); performance state — P8 ka matlab GPU idle hai, active serving me P0 ya P1 dikhega (full-speed operation); power usage aur GPU utilization — load ke neeche low utilization ka matlab batching ya scheduling inefficiency, high power lekin low throughput ka matlab memory bottleneck ya kernel inefficiency; memory usage — 0MiB/46068MiB ka matlab total memory lagbhag 46 GB hai aur abhi occupied nahi hai. Specific attributes ke liye flags use kar sakte ho: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,compute_cap,memory.free,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv — output: NVIDIA L40S, compute capability 8.9, 45469 MiB free, 0 MiB used, 46068 MiB total.

Step 2: Benchmark traffic — ShareGPT aur Prefix Repetition

Dataset selection critical hai: optimization poori tarah se specific traffic types ke liye tune hoti hai. Long input contexts (prefill-heavy) wale workloads ko long outputs (decode-heavy) wale workloads se alag strategies chahiye hoti hain — isliye benchmark dataset ko deployed model ke expected usage patterns ko accurately reflect karna chahiye. Lab chatbot aur conversational scenarios target karta hai, jahan input aur output token lengths relatively balanced hain aur users repetitive ya follow-up questions poochte hain. Isliye do complementary datasets: ShareGPT — real conversational data, diverse dialogue structures aur linguistic styles, real end-user traffic ka realistic approximation, interactive serving performance aur user experience evaluate karne ke liye ideal. Prefix Repetition — synthetic benchmark jahan har prompt common prefixes se shuru hota hai, phir repeated ya similar suffixes aate hain; repetition bias aur cache utilization test karne ke liye design kiya gaya, aur prefix length, suffix length aur unique prefixes ki sankhya precisely control ki ja sakti hai — kam prefixes ka matlab input prompts me zyada repetition, stronger cache-reuse traffic pattern.

Helper script se 100 ShareGPT samples ke statistics: prompt length min 5, max 817, mean 232.60, median 141.50; output length min 4, max 771, mean 220.61, median 164.50. Traffic generate karne ke liye vLLM benchmark CLI (vllm bench serve) use hoti hai — total prompts, request rate, traffic ramp-up, max concurrent requests configure kar sakte ho, aur latency aur throughput metrics automatically collect hoti hain. Example: 2,000 ShareGPT prompts, 10 requests per second, max concurrency 10, local vLLM server par.

Step 3: Metrics — TPS, TTFT, ITL

Book ki metrics table me categories hain: throughput (total token throughput, output token throughput, request throughput), latency (TTFT, TPOT, ITL — mean + P99), resource utilization (GPU utilization, memory usage), workload profile (input/output token ratio, concurrency, request rate), reliability/cost (error rate, cost efficiency). Lab simplicity ke liye chaar metrics par focus karta hai: total token throughput (TPS) — input + output tokens per second, system efficiency ka high-level indicator; output token throughput (TPS) — output tokens per second, decoding performance ka core metric (LLM cost ka main driver); mean TTFT (ms) — request start ke baad pehla token aane ka average time, prefill efficiency capture karta hai (model loading, tokenization, scheduling delay se influenced); mean ITL (ms) — consecutive output tokens ke beech ka average delay, real-time streaming quality ke liye critical (chat aur interactive agents).

Step 4–5: Baseline — model load aur ShareGPT benchmark

Baseline ke liye default settings se vLLM server start kiya: vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-14B. Server log se pata chalta hai: model loading me 27.5185 GiB lage, available KV cache memory 11.00 GiB, GPU KV cache size 72,064 tokens, aur 40,960 tokens per request par maximum concurrency 1.76x. Kul mila kar vLLM 46 GB me se 38.5 GiB occupy karta hai — model 27.5 GB se zyada (total GPU memory ka 65% se zyada), KV cache sirf 11 GB. KV cache capacity seedha batching aur concurrency limit karti hai: cache constrained ho to server ko ya batch size kam karna padta hai ya cache entries zyada frequently evict karni padti hain — zyada recomputation, kam GPU utilization, kam token throughput.

Baseline results (2,000 ShareGPT prompts, 10 RPS): total throughput 474 TPS, output token throughput 227.64 TPS, request throughput 1.10 req/s, mean TTFT 104.15 ms, mean ITL 43.24 ms, median ITL 42.43 ms, P99 ITL 72.15 ms. Benchmark ke dauran nvidia-smi par GPU utilization 97% thi — GPU highly saturated. Prefix Repetition traffic (1,000 prompts, 5 RPS) par total throughput 1,123 TPS mili — ShareGPT se zyada double — jabki TTFT aur ITL lagbhag same rahe (104.64 ms / 43.95 ms). Iska reason: repetitive traffic par vLLM automatically prefix caching, continuous batching aur memory block sharing apply karta hai, jo similar input prompts ke across computation reuse karta hai.

Step 6: Quantization — AWQ 4-bit, 2.7x throughput

Quantized model Qwen3-14B-AWQ (4-bit) sirf 9.6 GB GPU memory occupy karta hai, original 27.5 GB ke mukable — 17 GB memory free hoti hai caching ke liye. Available KV cache memory 11.00 GiB se badh kar 29.15 GiB, GPU KV cache size 72,064 se badh kar 191,056 tokens, aur 40,960 tokens per request par maximum concurrency 1.76x se badh kar 4.66x. ShareGPT par total throughput 474 TPS se badh kar 1,280 TPS — 2.7x, aur average TTFT lagbhag 42% improve hoke 103.61 ms se 59.29 ms. Prefix Repetition dataset par bhi similar improvement dikhi. AWQ ke results primarily dikhate hain ki weight quantization CPU-GPU data movement aur overall memory usage kam karti hai; activation quantization jaise compute bhi kam karne wali techniques ke liye book Chapter 6 refer karti hai.

Step 7: Aur optimization — workload ke hisaab se

Quantized model default configuration par bhi strong performance deta hai, lekin specific workload ya GPU ke liye aur push kar sakte ho. Long-context, prefill-heavy workloads ke liye LMCache enable karo — repeated prefixes ke liye pehle compute kiye gaye KV pairs reuse hote hain (multi-turn chat ya RAG jaise prompts me bahut efficient). Decode-heavy workloads (lambe outputs) ke liye speculative decoding zyada effective hai — chhota draft model multiple tokens ahead predict karta hai, decoding iterations kam hoti hain, throughput badhta hai. Dono ke hands-on examples Chapter 7 me hain.

vLLM bahut se knobs expose karta hai: KV cache size aur block management ke liye --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9, --max-model-len 4096, --block-size 16 (chhote blocks = behtar cache utilization); batching ke liye --max-num-seqs 512, --max-num-batched-tokens 16384, --max-paddings 256. Ek typical fine-tuned startup script: Qwen3-14B-AWQ, --quantization awq --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 --max-model-len 1024 --block-size 16 --enable-prefix-caching --max-num-seqs 8 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --enable-chunked-prefill. Lekin savdhaan: over-tune mat karo. Ek GPU type ya workload pattern ke liye perfectly tuned configuration doosre hardware ya varied traffic par kharab perform kar sakti hai ya fail bhi ho sakti hai. Modern frameworks startup par hardware aur environment ke hisaab se achhi settings automatically infer karne lage hain — practice me zyada effort ye identify karne me lagta hai ki kaunsi optimization technique apply karni hai, perfect configuration dhoondhne me nahi.

Step 8: Distributed serving — NVLink hi farq banata hai

Experiments single-node multi-GPU par focus karte hain (sabse common practical scenario; multi-node ke liye PD disaggregation recommend ki jaati hai). Qwen3-14B-AWQ ko do EC2 instances par test kiya gaya: g6e.12xlarge (chaar NVIDIA L40S GPUs) aur p4d.24xlarge (aath NVIDIA A100 GPUs). vLLM me distributed hosting straightforward hai: vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --tensor-parallel-size 2 — vLLM automatically distributed-serving group initialize karta hai, communication aur model partitioning internally handle karta hai.

Results ulta nikle: g6e par single-GPU setup best tha — highest throughput aur lowest TTFT, 2-GPU aur 4-GPU configurations se behtar. p4d par multi-GPU behtar tha — 4-GPU setup ne best overall throughput aur lowest latency di. Reason GPU interconnect hai: p4d ke A100 GPUs NVLink se jude hain — high-speed, low-latency communication, to tensor parallelism efficiently split aur synchronize kar pata hai. g6e ke L40S GPUs me NVLink nahi hai — sirf PCIe, significantly kam bandwidth aur zyada latency — to multi-GPU setups inter-GPU communication overhead se suffer karte hain aur single GPU tez rehta hai. Halaanki L40S aam taur par single-GPU inference me A100 se behtar hai, distributed me interconnect hi decide karta hai.

Ek aur surprising result: p4d par 4-GPU distributed setup best tha, lekin chaar independent model instances (har GPU par ek) lagbhag teen guna total throughput dete hain (9,816 TPS vs 3,926 TPS) — chaar GPUs ko ek distributed model ke liye use karne ke mukable. Distributed serving ka asli fayda vertical scaling me hai: latency kam karna aur model size ki limitation overcome karna. p4d par TTFT 1 GPU se 4 GPU jaane par lagbhag 50% gir gayi (66 ms se 33 ms) — ye improvement horizontal scaling se kabhi nahi milegi, kyunki zyada replicas jodne se per-request latency kam nahi hoti.

Yaad rakho: distributed serving hamesha behtar performance ki guarantee nahi deti — ye ek common misconception hai. Single GPU kabhi-kabhi multi-GPU setups ko throughput aur latency dono me hara deta hai. Distributed tabhi use karo jab model (quantization ke baad bhi) single GPU ki memory me fit na ho, ya low latency priority ho.

python — ch09/model_optimization_in_practice.ipynb — notebook code cells, outputs skipped (GitHub: https://github.com/orca3/llm-model-serving/blob/main/ch09/model_optimization_in_practice.ipynb)
import subprocess
import os
import time
import requests
import json
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def start_vllm_serve(
    model: str = "Qwen/Qwen3-14B",
    extra_args: str = "",
    log_file: str = "vllm.log"
):
    """
    Launch vllm serve as a non-blocking background process from a notebook cell.

    Args:
        model (str): The model to load (passed as --model), down load from huggingface.
        extra_args (str): Any extra arguments to pass to vllm serve.
        log_file (str): File to write vllm's stdout/stderr logs.
    Returns:
        subprocess.Popen: The process object for the launched server, or None if an error occurs.
    Example:
        proc = start_vllm_serve(model="Qwen/Qwen3-14B", extra_args="--port 8000")
    """
    cmd = [
        "vllm", "serve",
        "--model", model
    ]
    # Split extra_args by spaces if given
    if extra_args:
        # Support both string or list input
        if isinstance(extra_args, str):
            cmd += extra_args.split()
        elif isinstance(extra_args, list):
            cmd += extra_args

    # Clean up any old log files if desired (could help avoid confusion)
    try:
        if os.path.isfile(log_file):
            os.remove(log_file)
    except Exception as log_exc:
        print(f"Warning: Could not remove existing log file {log_file}: {log_exc}")

    try:
        with open(log_file, "a") as f:
            proc = subprocess.Popen(
                cmd,
                stdout=f,
                stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
                start_new_session=True  # Avoid killing if notebook restarts kernel
            )
        print(f"Started vllm serve with PID {proc.pid}, logging to {log_file}")
        print("If you see an exception shortly after this step, please check the last 50 lines of the log file with:\n")
        print(f"!tail -50 {log_file}")
        return proc
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ Failed to start vllm serve! Exception: {e}")
        print(f"Check for more details in the log file: {log_file}")
        return None

# Example usage:
# proc = start_vllm_serve(model="Qwen/Qwen3-14B")
# !pkill -f "vllm serve"

def check_vllm_status():
  """ Check vLLM server status
  """
    
  max_retries = 100  # e.g. wait up to 60 seconds (30 x 2s)
  wait_time = 10

  print("⏳ Waiting for vLLM server to become healthy...")

  for i in range(max_retries):
      try:
          r = requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:8000/health")
          if r.ok:
              print("✅ vLLM server is healthy and ready!")
              break
      except Exception as e:
          print(f"Attempt {i+1}: Not ready yet...")

      time.sleep(wait_time)
  else:
      print("❌ Timed out waiting for vLLM server to start.")
  return


def plot_vllm_bench_metrics(
    raw_results,
    metrics=None,
    cols = 3,
    title="Qwen3-14B Model Optimization Comparison"
):
    """
    Visualize and compare vllm bench serve results on a set of metrics.

    Args:
        raw_results (str): Newline-separated JSON lines, each line a benchmark result.
        metrics (list[tuple], optional): Each tuple: (label, json_key, ylabel, invert_is_better)
        title (str, optional): Figure title.
    """
    # Default metrics list
    if metrics is None:
        metrics = [
            ("Total Token Throughput (tok/s)", "total_token_throughput", "", False),
            ("Output Token Throughput (tok/s)", "output_throughput", "", False),
            # ("Peak Concurrent Requests", "max_concurrent_requests", "", False),
            ("Mean TTFT (ms)", "mean_ttft_ms", "ms", True),    # invert: lower is better
            ("Mean ITL (ms)", "mean_itl_ms", "ms", True),      # invert: lower is better
            ("Total Input Tokens", "total_input_tokens", "", False),
            ("Total Generated Tokens", "total_output_tokens", "", False)
        ]
    # Parse results
    results = [json.loads(line) for line in raw_results.strip().split('\n') if line.strip()]
    if not results:
        print("No valid results parsed!")
        return

    # Legend labels
    labels = [r.get("setup") or r.get("label") or r.get("model_id", f"run {i}") for i, r in enumerate(results)]

    bar_width = 0.35
    n_metrics = len(metrics)
    x = np.arange(len(labels))

    ncols = cols
    nrows = (n_metrics + ncols - 1) // ncols
    fig_width = 16
    fig_height = 4 * nrows  # shorter height to avoid tall figure
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=nrows, ncols=ncols, figsize=(fig_width, fig_height))

    # axes could be non-array or 1d, flatten for uniform indexing
    if n_metrics == 1:
        axes = np.array([axes])
    axes = np.array(axes).reshape(-1)
    colors = ['#4C72B0', '#55A868']

    for idx, (mtitle, key, unit, invert) in enumerate(metrics):
        ax = axes[idx]
        try:
            vals = [float(r[key]) for r in results]
        except KeyError as e:
            ax.set_title(f"{mtitle} (missing key: {e})")
            continue

        if invert:
            # lower is better (greener)
            bar_colors = [colors[1] if v == min(vals) else colors[0] for v in vals]
        else:
            # higher is better (greener)
            bar_colors = [colors[1] if v == max(vals) else colors[0] for v in vals]

        ax.bar(x, vals, bar_width, color=bar_colors)
        ax.set_xticks(x)
        ax.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=20)
        ax.set_title(mtitle, fontsize=12)
        if unit:
            ax.set_ylabel(unit, fontsize=10)
        for i, v in enumerate(vals):
            ax.text(i, v*1.01 if v != 0 else 0.01, f'{v:,.2f}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=9)
    # Remove any unused subplots
    for j in range(len(metrics), len(axes)):
        fig.delaxes(axes[j])

    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.0, w_pad=2.5)
    plt.suptitle(title, fontsize=16, y=1.05)
    plt.show()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Inspect the benchmark datasets used by `vllm bench serve`.

This helper loads a dataset with the very same code path that
`vllm bench serve` uses (``vllm.benchmarks.datasets``), then reports the
prompt/output length distributions, prints a few sample prompts and draws a
simple ASCII histogram. It is meant to answer "what traffic am I actually
sending to the server?" before a benchmark run.

Copy this file into the root of your local `vllm` repository (see README.md)
and run, for example:

    python3 inspect_dataset.py \
        --dataset-name sharegpt \
        --dataset-path ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json \
        --model Qwen/Qwen3-14B \
        --num-prompts 100 \
        --save-samples

    python3 inspect_dataset.py \
        --dataset-name prefix_repetition \
        --model Qwen/Qwen3-14B \
        --num-prompts 50 \
        --prefix-repetition-prefix-len 256 \
        --prefix-repetition-suffix-len 256 \
        --prefix-repetition-num-prefixes 5 \
        --prefix-repetition-output-len 128 \
        --save-samples
"""

import argparse
import json

import numpy as np

from vllm.benchmarks.datasets import (
    PrefixRepetitionRandomDataset,
    RandomDataset,
    ShareGPTDataset,
)
try:
    # vLLM >= 0.12: tokenizer helpers live in their own package.
    from vllm.tokenizers import get_tokenizer
except ImportError:
    from vllm.transformers_utils.tokenizer import get_tokenizer

# Number of buckets in the ASCII histogram.
NUM_HISTOGRAM_BINS = 9
# Prompts longer than this are truncated when printed.
MAX_PROMPT_CHARS = 200
# How many sample prompts to print.
NUM_SAMPLES_TO_SHOW = 5


def build_dataset(args, tokenizer):
    """Sample `args.num_prompts` requests from the requested dataset."""
    if args.dataset_name == "sharegpt":
        if not args.dataset_path:
            raise ValueError("--dataset-path is required for the sharegpt dataset")
        dataset = ShareGPTDataset(
            dataset_path=args.dataset_path,
            random_seed=args.seed,
        )
        return dataset.sample(
            tokenizer=tokenizer,
            num_requests=args.num_prompts,
            output_len=args.sharegpt_output_len,
            request_id_prefix=args.request_id_prefix,
        )

    if args.dataset_name == "prefix_repetition":
        dataset = PrefixRepetitionRandomDataset(random_seed=args.seed)
        return dataset.sample(
            tokenizer=tokenizer,
            num_requests=args.num_prompts,
            prefix_len=args.prefix_repetition_prefix_len,
            suffix_len=args.prefix_repetition_suffix_len,
            num_prefixes=args.prefix_repetition_num_prefixes,
            output_len=args.prefix_repetition_output_len,
            request_id_prefix=args.request_id_prefix,
        )

    if args.dataset_name == "random":
        dataset = RandomDataset(random_seed=args.seed)
        return dataset.sample(
            tokenizer=tokenizer,
            num_requests=args.num_prompts,
            prefix_len=args.random_prefix_len,
            input_len=args.random_input_len,
            output_len=args.random_output_len,
            range_ratio=args.random_range_ratio,
            request_id_prefix=args.request_id_prefix,
        )

    raise ValueError(f"Unknown dataset name: {args.dataset_name}")


def print_distribution(name, values):
    """Print min/max/mean/median/std for one length distribution."""
    print(f"\n=== {name} Length Distribution ===")
    print(f"Min {name.lower()} length: {int(np.min(values))}")
    print(f"Max {name.lower()} length: {int(np.max(values))}")
    print(f"Mean {name.lower()} length: {np.mean(values):.2f}")
    print(f"Median {name.lower()} length: {np.median(values):.2f}")
    print(f"Std {name.lower()} length: {np.std(values):.2f}")


def print_samples(requests, num_samples):
    """Print the first few requests with their prompt truncated."""
    print("\n=== Sample Prompts ===")
    for i, request in enumerate(requests[:num_samples]):
        prompt = request.prompt
        if not isinstance(prompt, str):
            prompt = str(prompt)
        if len(prompt) > MAX_PROMPT_CHARS:
            prompt = prompt[:MAX_PROMPT_CHARS] + "..."
        print(f"\n--- Sample {i + 1} ---")
        print(f"Prompt length: {request.prompt_len}")
        print(f"Output length: {request.expected_output_len}")
        print(f"Request ID: {getattr(request, 'request_id', None)}")
        print(f"Prompt: {prompt}")


def print_histogram(prompt_lens, num_bins=NUM_HISTOGRAM_BINS):
    """Draw an ASCII histogram of the prompt length distribution."""
    print("\n=== Prompt Length Histogram ===")
    min_len = int(np.min(prompt_lens))
    max_len = int(np.max(prompt_lens))

    if min_len == max_len:
        # Every prompt has the same length (the usual case for the synthetic
        # datasets): a histogram of empty bins would be noise, so print one row.
        print(f"{min_len:4d} tokens: {'*' * len(prompt_lens)}")
        return

    bin_width = (max_len - min_len) / num_bins
    counts = [0] * num_bins
    for length in prompt_lens:
        index = min(int((length - min_len) / bin_width), num_bins - 1)
        counts[index] += 1

    for i, count in enumerate(counts):
        low = int(min_len + i * bin_width)
        high = int(min_len + (i + 1) * bin_width)
        print(f"{low:4d}-{high:4d} tokens: {'*' * count}")


def save_samples(requests, filename):
    """Dump the sampled requests to JSON for offline inspection."""
    samples = [
        {
            "request_id": getattr(request, "request_id", None),
            "prompt": request.prompt,
            "prompt_len": request.prompt_len,
            "expected_output_len": request.expected_output_len,
            "has_multimodal": bool(getattr(request, "multi_modal_data", None)),
        }
        for request in requests
    ]
    with open(filename, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(samples, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
    print(f"\nSaved {len(samples)} samples to {filename}")


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Inspect a vLLM benchmark dataset before running a benchmark."
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--dataset-name",
        type=str,
        default="sharegpt",
        choices=["sharegpt", "prefix_repetition", "random"],
        help="Which benchmark dataset to load.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--dataset-path",
        type=str,
        default=None,
        help="Path to the dataset file (required for sharegpt).",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--model",
        type=str,
        required=True,
        help="Model name or path used to load the tokenizer.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--tokenizer",
        type=str,
        default=None,
        help="Tokenizer name or path (defaults to --model).",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--trust-remote-code",
        action="store_true",
        help="Trust remote code when loading the tokenizer.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--num-prompts",
        type=int,
        default=100,
        help="Number of prompts to sample from the dataset.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--seed",
        type=int,
        default=0,
        help="Random seed used when sampling the dataset.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--request-id-prefix",
        type=str,
        default="",
        help="Prefix prepended to generated request IDs.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--num-samples-to-show",
        type=int,
        default=NUM_SAMPLES_TO_SHOW,
        help="How many sample prompts to print.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--save-samples",
        action="store_true",
        help="Save the sampled requests to a JSON file.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--samples-filename",
        type=str,
        default=None,
        help="Output file for --save-samples "
        "(defaults to <dataset-name>_samples.json).",
    )

    # ShareGPT specific.
    parser.add_argument(
        "--sharegpt-output-len",
        type=int,
        default=None,
        help="Override the output length of every ShareGPT request.",
    )

    # Prefix repetition specific.
    parser.add_argument("--prefix-repetition-prefix-len", type=int, default=256)
    parser.add_argument("--prefix-repetition-suffix-len", type=int, default=256)
    parser.add_argument("--prefix-repetition-num-prefixes", type=int, default=10)
    parser.add_argument("--prefix-repetition-output-len", type=int, default=128)

    # Random dataset specific.
    parser.add_argument("--random-input-len", type=int, default=1024)
    parser.add_argument("--random-output-len", type=int, default=128)
    parser.add_argument("--random-prefix-len", type=int, default=0)
    parser.add_argument("--random-range-ratio", type=float, default=0.0)

    return parser.parse_args()


def main():
    args = parse_args()

    tokenizer = get_tokenizer(
        args.tokenizer or args.model,
        trust_remote_code=args.trust_remote_code,
    )

    print(f"Loading dataset: {args.dataset_name}")
    requests = build_dataset(args, tokenizer)

    print("\n=== Dataset Overview ===")
    print(f"Total samples: {len(requests)}")
    if not requests:
        return

    prompt_lens = [r.prompt_len for r in requests]
    output_lens = [r.expected_output_len for r in requests]

    print_distribution("Prompt", prompt_lens)
    print_distribution("Output", output_lens)
    print_samples(requests, args.num_samples_to_show)
    print_histogram(prompt_lens)

    if args.save_samples:
        filename = args.samples_filename or f"{args.dataset_name}_samples.json"
        save_samples(requests, filename)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
SOURCESource: Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization, O'Reilly, Chapter 9 — LLM Optimization in Practice
